questions.question: At an events company, a clerk enters payments and a manager approves them, but the clerk can still edit a payment after approval. Which assessment should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: The duties are separated, since a manager approves every payment
options.B: The duties are combined, since the clerk can alter approved payments
options.C: The duties are combined, but logging the clerk's edits makes that acceptable
options.D: The duties are separated, since each person's account holds least privilege

questions.key_concept: Separation of duties holds only if no one person can complete the process alone, including by editing it after approval.
questions.pre_read: Count who can take a payment from entry to approval on their own.
questions.correct_explanation: Separation of duties works only if no one person can complete a sensitive process alone. Because the clerk can edit a payment after the manager approves it, the clerk alone still decides what is finally paid. Manager approval is the runner-up: it looks like a split, but an approval the clerk can change afterward checks nothing; edits after approval should need a fresh approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a manager does approve each payment. But the clerk can change the payment afterward, so the approval no longer controls what is paid.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs record each edit. But logging detects a change after it happens; it does not stop one person from deciding alone what is paid.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because each account is narrow. But least privilege limits what one account does; separation of duties makes sure no one person can finish the process alone.

tips: Eliminate: C accepts the combined duty because edits are logged, which detects but does not split, and D confuses least privilege with separation of duties.
Final two: B beats A because the clerk can still change a payment after approval; an approval one person can undo separates nothing.
Exam cue: test separation of duties by asking whether one person can still finish the task alone, including by changing it after the check.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)

questions.question: A cinema chain's admins check out passwords from a vault that logs each use, and a senior admin wants a permanent copy in a personal password manager. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Keep the password in the vault, checked out for every task
options.B: Allow the copy when multifactor authentication protects the password manager
options.C: Give admins one shared vault login for quicker check-out
options.D: Allow the copy, because senior admins are already trusted with it

questions.key_concept: Privileged credentials stay in the vault, where each check-out is logged and controlled; personal copies escape that control.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the vault records each time a password is used, and what a copy would record.
questions.correct_explanation: A vault controls privileged passwords by checking them out for a task, logging each use and often rotating them afterward. A permanent copy outside the vault escapes all of that: its use is never logged, and it lasts until someone notices. Allowing the copy behind multifactor authentication is the runner-up: it protects the copy from theft, but it still removes the logging and control the vault provides.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: multifactor authentication guards the copy. But the vault's logging and control of each use are lost, and the copy outlives any rotation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it speeds check-out. But a shared vault login cannot show which admin took which password.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the senior admin is trusted. But privileged controls guard against stolen accounts and mistakes, not just distrust; seniority changes nothing.

tips: Eliminate: D relaxes privileged controls because of seniority, and C shares one vault login so check-outs cannot be traced to a person.
Final two: A beats B because the vault logs and controls every use; a protected copy outside it is still unlogged and permanent.
Exam cue: privileged credentials stay in the vault: checked out for a task, logged and rotated, never kept as personal copies.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a vault checks admin credentials out, rotates them and logs each use' (notes 3.2.4 Privileged Access Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. questions.question: At an animation studio that uses discretionary access control, a designer opens a malicious attachment, and the malware reshares the designer's project files with an outside address. Which weakness does this MOST clearly show?

options.A: A central administrator set the files' labels too low
options.B: The designer's job role held more permissions than needed
options.C: Any program a user runs acts with the user's sharing rights
options.D: Owners often share files with more people than needed

questions.key_concept: Under discretionary access control, any program the owner runs, including malware, acts with the owner's rights to share and change files.
questions.pre_read: Trace each step from the attachment opening to the files being shared.
questions.correct_explanation: Under discretionary access control, the owner decides who may access their files, and any program the owner runs acts with those same rights. Malware launched by the designer could therefore reshare the files as if the designer had chosen to. Owner oversharing is the runner-up: it is a real weakness of the model, but here the designer made no sharing choice; the malware acted with their rights.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because labels control access in some models. But centrally set labels belong to mandatory access control, not to owner-decided sharing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because extra role rights cause harm. But job roles belong to role-based access control; here the file owner's own rights were used.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: oversharing is a classic weakness of this model. But the designer chose nothing here; the malware shared the files using the designer's rights.

tips: Eliminate: A describes labels from mandatory access control, and B describes job roles from role-based access control; neither fits owner-decided sharing.
Final two: C beats D because the designer shared nothing; malware ran with the owner's rights, which is the model's built-in weakness.
Exam cue: in discretionary access control, the owner's rights travel with whatever the owner runs, malware included.

questions.question: In a cruise line's role-based access control system, where role owners approve each role's rights, an access analyst finds 40 staff with permissions granted directly, outside any role. What should the analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep the grants; those 40 staff rely on them daily
options.B: Remove the 40 grants now; owners re-add those still needed
options.C: Have the role owners move needed grants into roles, remove others
options.D: Create a separate role for each of the 40 staff members

questions.key_concept: Role-based access control works when rights come through roles; the role owner decides whether a direct grant joins a role or goes.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can tell which of the direct grants are still needed.
questions.correct_explanation: Role-based access control works when rights come through roles; direct grants bypass the catalog and its reviews. The role owner decides whether each needed right belongs in a role, perhaps as a time-limited extra, or should go. Removing all 40 at once is the runner-up: it restores the model fast and lets owners re-add rights, but it acts before the owner decides and may cut access that live work still needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the access is in use. But use is not approval; direct grants escape role reviews and build privilege creep.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: direct grants should end, and owners can re-add rights. But removal comes before the owner's decision and may cut access live work needs; the owner decides first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it puts every right in a role. But one role per person is role explosion, which nobody can manage or review.

tips: Eliminate: A treats daily use as approval, and D creates one role per person, which is role explosion.
Final two: C beats B because the role owner decides which rights stay; removing all at once could cut access people need for live work.
Exam cue: in role-based access control, rights should flow through roles. Report direct grants to the role owner to fold in or remove.

questions.question: A mining company's rule blocks portal sign-ins from outside its two operating countries, and the rule's owner approved an exception for an engineer's trip to Chile. How should the access analyst BEST set it up?

options.A: Add Chile to the rule's allowed countries until the trip ends
options.B: Unblock each Chile sign-in when this engineer calls the help desk
options.C: Allow this engineer's sign-ins from Chile until the trip ends
options.D: Have this engineer use a consumer VPN app to appear in-country

questions.key_concept: An approved exception to an access rule is scoped to the need: only the person, place and period it covers, and then it expires.
questions.pre_read: For each option, note who could sign in, from where, and until when.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule-based access control applies one rule to everyone, so an exception should open only what the need requires. The owner approved one engineer's trip, so the analyst sets an exception for this engineer, from Chile, ending with the trip. Adding Chile to the rule until the trip ends is the runner-up: it is limited by place and time, but it changes the rule for every user, not just the engineer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it covers only Chile and ends with the trip. But editing the rule accepts sign-ins from Chile for every user; the owner approved an exception for one engineer.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a person checks each sign-in. But that is not the approved exception: each one waits on a call, and anyone posing as the engineer could get through.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it needs no rule change. But a consumer VPN disguises where the engineer really is, going around the owner's rule instead of using the exception the owner approved.

tips: Eliminate: D disguises the engineer's location with a consumer VPN to get around the rule, and B unblocks sign-ins for anyone who calls claiming to be the engineer.
Final two: C beats A because the owner approved an exception for one person; changing the rule itself opens Chile to every user.
Exam cue: scope an approved exception to the person, place and period the need covers, and let it expire on its own.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an approved exception covers only the person, place and period that need it, then expires' (notes 3.2.9 Rule-Based Access Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A city records office uses role-based access control for its applications, and staff now want to share low-sensitivity working folders with colleagues they choose. Which approach should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Discretionary control for the folders, role-based control for the apps
options.B: Role-based access control for both, adding a role for each sharing need
options.C: Attribute-based access control for both, replacing the existing roles
options.D: Discretionary access control for folders and apps, so owners grant both

questions.key_concept: Organizations mix access control models, using each where it fits the data and who should decide.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should decide access to the folders, and who should decide access to the applications.
questions.correct_explanation: Organizations mix models, choosing each where it fits. Low-sensitivity working folders suit discretionary access control, where the owner shares with chosen colleagues, while applications stay under role-based access control. Forcing everything into roles is the runner-up: it keeps one model, but a role for every sharing choice leads to role explosion, and nobody could manage or review the result.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: one model sounds tidy. But a role for every sharing choice causes role explosion; owner-decided sharing fits low-sensitivity folders better.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because attributes are flexible. But replacing a role model that works for the applications is a costly rebuild; only the folders need a different decider.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners know their data. But owner-decided access to business applications breaks the job-based control those systems need.

tips: Eliminate: C rebuilds both systems when only the folders need a change, and D lets folder owners decide application access too.
Final two: A beats B because mixing models is normal; forcing ad hoc sharing into roles creates role explosion.
Exam cue: choose the model per system, not per organization; keep what works and add another model only where the decider differs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'combine models where it helps; one model need not cover everything' (notes 3.2.10 Choosing an Access Control Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: A university's AI help desk agent only reads tickets and drafts replies, yet its account can also reset staff passwords. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep the right, since resets are logged in the help desk system
options.B: Remove the agent's right to reset any staff member's password
options.C: Alert the help desk whenever the agent resets a staff password
options.D: Scan each ticket for viruses before the agent reads it

questions.key_concept: AI agents get only the rights their task needs; removing an unneeded right beats detecting its misuse.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the agent's task needs with what its account can do.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent should hold only the rights its task needs. Reading tickets and drafting replies never requires resetting passwords, so removing that right means a hidden instruction in a crafted ticket, or a model error, cannot hand a staff account to someone else. Real-time alerts are the runner-up: they speed up detection, but a reset account may already be in use by then, and a right the task never needs should not exist.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a log leaves a trail. But it records a reset only after the account may be in someone else's hands; an unneeded right should be removed.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: alerts speed up detection. But a reset account may already be in use by then; a right the task never needs should simply be removed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tickets come from outside. But the risk here is excess rights that crafted text could trigger, which a virus scan does not address.

tips: Eliminate: D applies a malware scan to an excess-rights problem, and A keeps an unneeded right because its use is logged, which only records misuse afterwards.
Final two: B beats C because a right the agent lacks cannot be misused; an alert only reports a reset already made.
Exam cue: scope each bot or AI agent to its task. Removing unneeded rights prevents misuse; alerts only detect it.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'scope each bot or agent to the actions its task needs' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An ice arena evacuates after an ammonia alarm; ventilation needs admin rights, the system owner is unreachable, and the runbook lets the supervisor use break-glass access in emergencies. What should the supervisor do FIRST?

options.A: Keep calling the owner to approve the break-glass use
options.B: Start the ventilation with the on-call engineer's admin login
options.C: Ask the help desk to make the supervisor a permanent administrator
options.D: Use the break-glass account to switch on the ventilation

questions.key_concept: When lives are at risk and the runbook authorizes break-glass access, use it at once; alerting and review follow.
questions.pre_read: Note what the runbook allows, and whom it allows to act.
questions.correct_explanation: People's safety comes first, and the runbook already authorizes break-glass access for emergencies like this one, so the supervisor acts now. Every break-glass use raises an alert, is reviewed afterward, and the credential is changed. Calling the owner for approval is the runner-up: owner approval is normal for elevation, but the runbook has already granted it for this case, and each minute of delay lets the leak build while people are still near the building.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: elevation normally needs the owner's approval. But the runbook already authorizes the supervisor's break-glass use in emergencies, and each minute of waiting lets the ammonia build.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is quick. But a borrowed personal login cannot show who acted and bypasses the sealed, alerted emergency path.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would prevent future delays. But standing admin rights help attackers too, and a permanent grant needs the owner's approval, which cannot happen in time for this emergency.

tips: Eliminate: B borrows another person's login instead of the sealed emergency path, and C answers an emergency with permanent admin rights.
Final two: D beats A because lives are at risk and the runbook already authorizes break-glass use; the review comes after.
Exam cue: people's safety comes first. When a procedure already authorizes the emergency action, act on it, then record and review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(12) (Account Management | Account Monitoring for Atypical Usage)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'break-glass access is for when normal access fails, and every use is alerted and reviewed' (notes 3.2.12 Just-in-Time and Break-Glass Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A biotech company labels its clinical trial files Restricted, but each study leader may grant any colleague access to their own study's files at will. Which model should the access analyst MOST accurately record?

options.A: Role-based access control, since study leaders hold a defined job role
options.B: Mandatory access control, since the files carry Restricted labels
options.C: Discretionary access control, since study leaders choose who gets in
options.D: Attribute-based access control, as the Restricted label is an attribute

questions.key_concept: A label is not a model: access is mandatory only when the system enforces labels against clearances; owners granting access at will is discretionary.
questions.pre_read: Find who actually decides whether a colleague may open a study's file.
questions.correct_explanation: Read for the decider. Labels alone do not make a system mandatory: under mandatory access control, the system enforces labels against clearances and no owner can override them. Here each study leader grants access at will, so the owner decides, which is discretionary. Mandatory access control is the runner-up, because the Restricted label is the eye-catching clue, but nothing enforces it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because study leaders hold a job title. But nothing here grants access by job role; each study leader personally chooses who gets in.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: labels suggest mandatory control. But under that model the system enforces labels against clearances, and no study leader could grant access at will.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a label can be an attribute. But no policy checks it on each request; the study leader's choice alone decides.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses a job title with access granted by role, and D treats a label as a checked attribute when no policy evaluates it.
Final two: C beats B because the study leader decides access at will; a label nobody enforces does not make a model mandatory.
Exam cue: a label alone never makes access mandatory. Ask whether the system enforces it against the owner's wishes; if an owner can grant at will, the model is discretionary.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'check who decides; if the owner can grant access at will, it is discretionary, whatever the label' (notes 3.2.13 Access Model Scenarios: Worked Examples). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Identities and accounts
questions.question: A planetarium's access analyst finds an active account, 'show-tech2', with no owner recorded anywhere; procedure says only the system owner may disable, keep or remove an ownerless account. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the account, since no one can say who uses it
options.B: Disable the account now, then tell the system owner
options.C: Report the account to the system owner for a decision
options.D: Name the last person to sign in as its owner

questions.key_concept: Every account needs a named owner; an ownerless account goes to the system owner, who decides whether it stays.
questions.pre_read: Think about what you know, and do not know, about this account.
questions.correct_explanation: Every account needs a named owner who answers for it. Here the procedure reserves every decision on an ownerless account, disabling included, for the system owner, so the analyst reports this one and lets the owner decide. Disabling it first is the runner-up: it feels safe, but the procedure does not give the analyst that step, and nobody knows what the account runs, so cutting it off could break a live process.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an unknown account is a risk. But deletion is permanent, cuts the link between logs and the account, and the owner decides, not the analyst.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: disabling limits the risk quickly. But the procedure lets only the system owner disable an ownerless account, and nobody knows what this one runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because recent sign-ins hint at who uses it. But a user is not always accountable, and naming an owner keeps the account, which is the system owner's call.

tips: Eliminate: A deletes an account whose purpose is unknown, losing its history, and D makes the last person to sign in its owner, though they may not be accountable or even authorized.
Final two: C beats B because the procedure lets only the system owner disable, keep or remove an ownerless account; acting first oversteps it and could break a live process.
Exam cue: an account with no owner goes to whoever is accountable for the system. Find the decider in the stem before acting on an account yourself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an ownerless account goes to the system owner, who decides whether it stays' (notes 3.1.1 Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A car-sharing firm's access analyst drafts a 'fleet coordinator' role whose permissions include both issuing and approving customer refunds; the customer service director owns the role. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Raise the conflict with the director before anyone is assigned
options.B: Publish the role and have the director review refunds monthly
options.C: Split the refund rights into two roles and assign staff
options.D: Keep both rights, since coordinators are senior staff

questions.key_concept: Roles that mix conflicting duties are raised with the role owner before anyone is assigned them.
questions.pre_read: Look at what one person holding this role could do alone.
questions.correct_explanation: Issuing and approving refunds in one role lets one person pay out money with no check, a separation of duties conflict. The role owner approves what a role contains, so the analyst raises the conflict with the director before anyone gets the role. Splitting the role yourself is the runner-up: it is probably the right fix, but changing a role's contents is the owner's decision, not the analyst's.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the director, as owner, would see any misuse. But the conflict is live from day one, and a monthly review only finds refunds already paid.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: two roles is likely the right design. But the director owns the role's contents, so the split needs their approval before anyone is assigned.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because experienced staff seem low risk. But separation of duties is not about distrust; it protects the firm, and the staff, from fraud and error.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the conflict go live and checks only after refunds are paid, and D relies on seniority, which separation of duties never does.
Final two: A beats C because the director owns the role's contents; the analyst spots the conflict, but the owner approves how the role is fixed.
Exam cue: catch conflicting duties while a role is being designed, before anyone holds it, and take the fix to the role's owner.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'conflicting duties in a draft role go to the role owner before anyone is assigned' (notes 3.1.2 Defining Roles and Entitlements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A summer camp rehires a counselor whose disabled account still holds last year's group memberships, and the new start record lists this year's approved role. Which action is BEST for the help desk technician?

options.A: Re-enable it as it was, since last year's access was approved
options.B: Ask the counselor which of last year's groups they need
options.C: Re-enable the account with only this year's approved role
options.D: Re-enable the account now and trim its groups after a month

questions.key_concept: Returning staff are provisioned from the current start record and approved role, not by restoring old access.
questions.pre_read: Consider what may have changed since the counselor last worked at the camp.
questions.correct_explanation: Provisioning follows the current start record and its approved role, not what the person held before. Re-enabling the account with only this year's role clears memberships that may no longer fit. Restoring the account as it was is the runner-up: last year's access was approved, but for last year's job, and rights can change between seasons, so old memberships were never approved for this start.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the old access was once approved. But that approval covered last year's job; this year's record sets the role, and old memberships may no longer fit it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the counselor knows their own work. But people choosing their own access is not approval; the start record's approved role decides.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it gets the counselor working fast. But every extra group is live from day one, and trimming later often never happens.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the counselor choose their own access, which is not approval, and D grants first and trims later, leaving extra rights live.
Final two: C beats A because each start is provisioned from its own approved role; last year's approval does not carry over to this year's job.
Exam cue: for a rehire or returning worker, provision from the current record and role, never by restoring old access as it was.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.1 (Establish an Access Granting Process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'returning staff are provisioned from the current start record, not by restoring old access' (notes 3.1.3 Provisioning and Identity Proofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A racecourse's IT team is choosing between two fingerprint readers for staff tablets; one has a crossover error rate (CER) of 1%, the other 4%. Which conclusion is BEST supported?

options.A: The 4% reader is stricter, so it turns away more impostors
options.B: The 1% reader is the more accurate of the two overall
options.C: Tightening either reader's threshold will lower its CER
options.D: The 1% reader accepts fewer impostors at its factory setting

questions.key_concept: The crossover error rate compares biometric accuracy: lower is better, and moving the threshold trades errors without changing it.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the crossover error rate measures, and what it does not.
questions.correct_explanation: The crossover error rate is the point where false acceptances and false rejections are equal, so it compares readers' overall accuracy: lower is better. The 1% reader is the more accurate one. Claiming it accepts fewer impostors at its factory setting is the runner-up, but the CER says nothing about where the factory threshold sits; a loose setting could still let impostors in.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a higher number can look stricter. But a higher crossover error rate means more errors of both kinds where they meet; it is simply less accurate.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tightening cuts false acceptances. But it raises false rejections in step; the crossover point, and so the CER, stays where it is.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a more accurate reader usually helps. But false acceptances depend on the threshold chosen, and the CER does not show the factory setting.

tips: Eliminate: A reads a higher error rate as strictness, and C assumes moving the threshold changes the CER, which stays fixed for a reader.
Final two: B beats D because the CER compares overall accuracy; how many impostors get in depends on the threshold the team sets.
Exam cue: a lower crossover error rate means a more accurate biometric reader; the threshold then trades false acceptances against false rejections.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.3 (Use of Biometrics: false match and false non-match rates)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a lower crossover error rate means a more accurate biometric reader' (notes 3.1.4 Authentication Factors and MFA). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Attackers using stolen passwords keep flooding a ballet company's staff with push prompts, and look-alike login pages target the same staff. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Add number matching to every push approval staff receive
options.B: Replace push approvals with codes sent by text message
options.C: Remind staff in training to deny prompts they did not start
options.D: Replace push approvals with passkeys tied to the real site

questions.key_concept: Passkeys bind each sign-in to the real site, stopping both push floods and look-alike login pages.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against both attacks the staff face.
questions.correct_explanation: Passkeys are phishing-resistant: each sign-in is bound to the genuine site, and there is no prompt to approve, so neither the floods nor the fake pages work. Number matching is the runner-up: it stops blind approvals of a flood, but a look-alike page relaying the real sign-in as it happens can show the user the number to enter.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: number matching defeats blind approvals. But a look-alike page that relays the real sign-in can show the user the number, so phishing still works.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because codes end the prompt floods. But a fake login page can capture a texted code and relay it, and a SIM swap can move the number.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because aware staff deny more prompts. But tired people still slip, and training does nothing to stop the look-alike pages.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps prompts for codes a look-alike page can relay, and C relies on tired staff never slipping, which training cannot ensure.
Final two: D beats A because passkeys work only on the real site and need no approval; number matching still lets a relaying fake page through.
Exam cue: when the threat includes fake login pages, pick a site-bound method such as passkeys or FIDO2 keys, not a better prompt or code.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: phishing resistance); NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.5 (Phishing Resistance: manually entered codes can be relayed by an impostor verifier)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'passkeys stop both prompt floods and look-alike pages; number matching stops only blind approvals' (notes 3.1.5 Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A conference center's booking app, owned by its events director, now uses single sign-on (SSO) with MFA but still accepts users' old local passwords. What should the access analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the director to have the local logins switched off
options.B: Switch off the local logins in the app's settings directly
options.C: Ask the director to keep local logins as an SSO backup
options.D: Make the local passwords longer and expire them yearly

questions.key_concept: Local logins beside single sign-on bypass its MFA and central disabling, so they are raised with the system owner to close.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a user's local password lets them skip.
questions.correct_explanation: Local passwords beside single sign-on skip the MFA and central disabling the identity provider gives, so a leaver disabled centrally could still sign in. The events director owns the app, so the analyst raises the gap with the owner, who has the logins switched off through change control. Switching them off yourself is the runner-up: the right outcome, but it changes the owner's system without approval and could lock out anything still relying on them.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the local logins should go. But the app belongs to the events director, and an unplanned change could lock out anything still relying on them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because SSO outages happen and the director owns the app. But every local password skips MFA; emergencies need one sealed break-glass account, not a side door for all.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because stronger passwords sound safer. But the local logins would still skip MFA, and a leaver disabled at the identity provider could still use theirs.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps a login for everyone that skips MFA, when emergencies need one sealed account, and D strengthens passwords that still bypass the identity provider.
Final two: A beats B because the director owns the app; the analyst raises the bypass with the owner, who has it switched off through change control.
Exam cue: under single sign-on, any local login is a side door around MFA and central disabling. Take it to the system owner to close.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.7 (Centralize Access Control); NIST SP 800-63C-4 (Federation and Assertions)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'local logins beside SSO bypass its MFA and are reported to the system owner' (notes 3.1.7 Single Sign-On and Federation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Fix (4 Nov 2026, blind re-test): B says 'directly', not 'yourself', so no option stands out by person.

questions.question: A software vendor tells a science center that its AI sign-in scoring makes staff MFA unnecessary, since unusual sign-ins get flagged. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Drop MFA for everyone and let the AI flag unusual sign-ins
options.B: Use the scoring to add checks on top of MFA for everyone
options.C: Keep MFA for administrators and let the scoring cover other staff
options.D: Drop MFA once the model learns each person's habits

questions.key_concept: AI risk scoring adds checks on top of MFA; it decides when to ask for more proof and never replaces it.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a risk score can and cannot prove about the person signing in.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk scoring decides when to ask for more proof; it cannot replace the proof itself. A stolen password used at normal times would pass a score alone, so MFA stays for everyone and high scores trigger a stronger step. Keeping MFA only for administrators is the runner-up: admins matter most, but ordinary staff accounts are still a common way in, and scoring alone cannot verify who signs in.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the AI does catch many odd sign-ins. But an attacker with a stolen password who signs in at normal times looks ordinary and gets through.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: administrators need the strongest checks. But ordinary staff accounts are a common way in, and a score alone cannot prove who is signing in.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a trained model knows normal habits well. But attackers can mimic habits, and scoring decides when to ask for proof, not whether proof is needed.

tips: Eliminate: A treats flagging as proof of identity, and D lets a well-trained model stand in for a factor; scoring only judges risk.
Final two: B beats C because adaptive authentication adds checks on top of MFA; without MFA, an ordinary staff member's stolen password is enough to sign in.
Exam cue: adaptive or AI risk scoring decides when to ask for more proof. An option that drops MFA for anyone because of scoring is wrong.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-10 (Adaptive Authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI risk scoring adds to MFA and never replaces it' (notes 3.1.8 Adaptive Authentication and AI Behavior Analysis). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'with'; distractors reworded to drop 'since' and 'has'; same key and teaching point. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without a semicolon; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: At a tram operator, most staff who changed jobs this year still hold old-role rights; HR records each transfer, but nothing tells IT. Which fix should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Ask managers to email IT whenever someone joins their team
options.B: Have each HR transfer record open an access change request
options.C: Remove every old-role right found this year in one cleanup
options.D: Send HR's monthly transfer records to IT to process by hand

questions.key_concept: Each HR transfer should trigger an access change, so a mover's old rights are removed when the move happens.
questions.pre_read: Look for the step where information about each move is lost.
questions.correct_explanation: Privilege creep keeps coming back because the transfer event never reaches IT. Having each HR transfer record open an access change ticket makes every move trigger the removal of old rights when it happens. Sending a monthly list is the runner-up: it closes the information gap, but old rights stay live for up to a month and depend on someone working through the list by hand.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because managers know when people arrive. But it adds a manual step that relies on each manager remembering, when HR already records every transfer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it clears today's excess. But the cause remains, so creep returns with the next move, and the data owners never decided which rights could go.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a list does tell IT about moves. But old rights stay live for up to a month, and a manual list is easy to skip or misread.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a manual notice that depends on each manager remembering, and C cleans up once without fixing why moves are missed.
Final two: B beats D because a ticket per transfer removes old rights when the move happens; a monthly list leaves them live for weeks.
Exam cue: when the same access problem keeps repeating, fix the trigger: tie each HR joiner, mover or leaver event directly to an access change.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-5 (Personnel Transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(1) (Account Management | Automated System Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each HR transfer event triggers an access change, so movers lose old rights at the move' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A flight school's data owner for student records signed off the quarterly access review, marking 12 accounts for removal; two weeks later, the access analyst finds five still active. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: The review is complete, since the owner signed it off on time
options.B: The review stays open until every removal shows as done
options.C: The five users now decide whether they still need access
options.D: The sign-off was the weak step, as five removals are undone

questions.key_concept: An access review is complete only when every removal it decided shows as done in the system.
questions.pre_read: Separate the owner's decision from what has actually happened in the system.
questions.correct_explanation: An access review is a decision plus its follow-through. The owner's sign-off records the decision; the review is complete only when every removal shows as done in the system. Calling it complete on the sign-off date is the runner-up: the owner did their part on time, but five people the owner decided should lose access still have it, so the risk the review found is still open.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner certified on time. But signing records the decision only; while five removals are undone, those people keep access the owner said should go.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because users know their own work. But the owner already decided, and users judging their own access is a conflict of interest, not a review.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the five are still active. But the owner marked all 12 for removal; the gap is in carrying out the removals, not in the decision.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the decision to the users themselves, a conflict of interest, and D faults the sign-off, though the owner marked all 12 accounts correctly.
Final two: B beats A because a review closes when its removals are done and visible; a signature alone leaves five unwanted accounts live.
Exam cue: an access review is complete only when its decisions are carried out and shown in the system, not when the form is signed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(7) (Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an access review is complete only when its removals are done and visible' (notes 3.1.10 Access Reviews and Recertification). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A comedy club's departing marketing coordinator knew the password to the club's social media account, which four staff share. After disabling the coordinator's own account, what should the help desk technician do FIRST?

options.A: Nothing more: disabling their account ended their access
options.B: Watch the shared account's activity log for misuse each week
options.C: Ask the coordinator to promise in writing not to use it
options.D: Change the shared account's password and tell remaining users

questions.key_concept: Deprovisioning includes changing shared passwords a leaver knew; disabling their own account does not remove that access.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the coordinator still knows after their own account is disabled.
questions.correct_explanation: Disabling a leaver's own account does not touch secrets they still know. The shared password lets the coordinator sign in to the social media account from anywhere, so the technician changes it first and gives the new one only to remaining users. Watching the activity log is the runner-up: it might spot misuse, but only after a post or change is made in the club's name.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because their own account is now off. But a shared password is not tied to that account, so the coordinator can still sign in with it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the log could show misuse. But it only detects a post after the damage is public; changing the password prevents the sign-in.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a written promise feels like a control. But it cannot stop a sign-in, and the password would still work for anyone the coordinator told.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes disabling one account removes every secret the person knew, and C relies on a promise, which cannot block a sign-in.
Final two: D beats B because changing the password stops the coordinator signing in; watching the log only finds misuse after posts go out.
Exam cue: when someone leaves, list every secret they knew, such as shared passwords, codes and keys, and change each one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a leaver's known shared passwords are changed; disabling their own account is not enough' (notes 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: 'since' taken off option A; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A stationery maker's AI agent uses an access token that never expires, and the security manager wants to limit the damage if the token is stolen. Which change should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: A longer, harder-to-guess token with no expiry date
options.B: The token, moved into a vault and changed every 90 days
options.C: Tokens that expire quickly, which the agent renews automatically
options.D: One token shared by every agent the team runs, to cut secrets

questions.key_concept: Short-lived, automatically renewed tokens limit how long a stolen machine credential works; storing a permanent one better does not.
questions.pre_read: Think about what happens after an attacker copies the token.
questions.correct_explanation: Short-lived tokens limit how long any stolen copy works: the agent gets a fresh token as it needs one, and an old one soon expires, which limits the damage a theft can do. A vault with 90-day changes is the runner-up: it protects where the token is stored and caps its life, but a copy stolen from logs or memory could still work for up to three months.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because longer tokens are harder to guess. But a stolen token is copied, not guessed, and this one would still never expire.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a vault and regular changes both help. But a stolen copy still works until the next change, up to 90 days; a short-lived token soon expires.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fewer secrets seem easier to manage. But one theft would then expose every agent, and nobody could tell which agent made a call.

tips: Eliminate: A makes the token harder to guess, though stolen tokens are copied rather than guessed, and D shares one secret, so one theft exposes every agent.
Final two: C beats B because a short-lived token stops working soon after theft; a vault guards storage, and a 90-day change still leaves a stolen copy working for weeks.
Exam cue: match the control to the goal: vaults protect stored secrets, short lifetimes limit stolen ones, and separate identities contain one theft.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) NHI7 (Long-Lived Secrets); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'short-lived tokens limit how long a stolen AI agent credential works' (notes 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'short'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: At a printing company, administrators sign in to servers with the backup service account's password, since it skips MFA. Which change should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Add MFA to the service account, requiring a code for each backup
options.B: Change the service account's password and give it to the admins
options.C: Give admins named logins, then block people from the service account
options.D: Log each interactive sign-in by the service account and review them weekly

questions.key_concept: People should never sign in with a service account; block interactive sign-in and use named, MFA-protected admin accounts.
questions.pre_read: Think about who a service account is meant for.
questions.correct_explanation: A service account is for software, not people. When administrators sign in with it, their actions cannot be traced to a person and they dodge the MFA their own accounts require. Giving admins named logins of their own, then blocking people from the service account, fixes both. Logging and a weekly review is the runner-up: it would show the misuse, but the shared, MFA-free sign-ins keep happening.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because MFA is the missing control. But the backup software signs in unattended and cannot answer an MFA prompt, so the backups would fail.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a new password limits who knows it. But admins would still share one MFA-free login, and actions would still not trace to a person.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: logs would show the misuse. But detection does not stop it; admins would keep sharing an MFA-free login that hides who acted.

tips: Eliminate: A puts an MFA prompt on unattended software, which would break the backups, and B keeps people sharing the same MFA-free login.
Final two: C beats D because blocking human sign-in stops the shared, MFA-free use; a weekly log review only reports it afterward.
Exam cue: service accounts are for software only. When people use one, stop the human sign-in and give them named accounts of their own.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) NHI10 (Human Use of NHI); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'people must not sign in with service accounts' (notes 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and' or 'with'; 'so' taken off option A; same key and teaching point. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without a semicolon, as an ordered 'before' step; same key and teaching point. Word-tell sweep polish, 18 Nov 2026: key now names the service account it blocks, and D names it too so the key is not the longest option; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A watchmaker's HR system sends starts and exits to its cloud directory through a connector, which failed unnoticed for ten days. Which risk should the access analyst check FIRST?

options.A: Leavers from those ten days may still have working accounts
options.B: Starters from those ten days may still have no accounts
options.C: Sign-ins during those ten days may have skipped MFA
options.D: HR may have lost its start and exit records for those days

questions.key_concept: When the HR-to-directory feed fails, exits stop reaching accounts, so leavers keeping access is the first risk to check.
questions.pre_read: Trace what the connector carries from HR to the directory.
questions.correct_explanation: When the HR feed stops, exits never reach the directory, so people who left keep working accounts: a live security gap nobody sees. That is the risk to check first. Missing accounts for starters is the runner-up: it is real, but it fails safe, since a new hire with no account cannot get in and will soon report it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: starters may be missing accounts. But that fails safe and gets noticed fast; leavers keeping access is silent and can be misused.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a failure sounds like weaker sign-in. But the connector carries HR changes; MFA is enforced at sign-in and does not depend on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data seems at risk. But the connector failed, not the HR system; its records remain, waiting to be sent.

tips: Eliminate: C ties MFA to the HR feed, which does not enforce sign-in, and D assumes HR lost data, when only the connector failed.
Final two: A beats B because leavers keeping access is a silent security gap; starters without accounts fail safe and soon report it.
Exam cue: when an identity feed or process breaks, check the leaver side first: missed removals stay hidden, while missed grants get reported.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(1) (Account Management | Automated System Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a failed HR-to-directory feed leaves leavers with working accounts first' (notes 3.1.13 IAM Frameworks and Tools). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A seafood wholesaler's data owner for supplier contracts is on leave, and procedure lets a named delegate approve requests; the delegate approved a buyer's ticket. What should the help desk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Hold the delegate's approval until the owner returns
options.B: Ask the security team to record a second approval
options.C: Grant the access on the delegate's recorded approval
options.D: Grant wider access so the buyer needs no further tickets

questions.key_concept: A named delegate's recorded approval, where the procedure allows it, carries the owner's authority; the help desk then fulfills it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the procedure says about approvals while the owner is away.
questions.correct_explanation: Resource owners approve access, and a procedure can name a delegate to approve while the owner is away. The delegate's approval is recorded on the ticket, so the analyst fulfills it as the procedure assigns. Holding it for the owner is the runner-up: it looks cautious, but it sets aside the delegation the procedure created and leaves the buyer waiting for no gain in control.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: waiting for the owner feels safest. But the procedure names a delegate for exactly this, and their recorded approval carries the owner's authority.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because two approvals sound stronger. But the security team does not own the contracts, and the procedure already names who approves while the owner is away.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it saves future tickets. But the delegate approved one specific request; extra access goes beyond what anyone approved.

tips: Eliminate: B adds an approver who does not own the contracts, and D grants more than the approved request, which nobody authorized.
Final two: C beats A because the procedure lets the named delegate approve while the owner is away; the analyst then fulfills the recorded approval.
Exam cue: escalation is not a free win. When the procedure gives approval to a named delegate, their recorded approval is enough to fulfill.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.1 (Establish an Access Granting Process); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a named delegate's recorded approval carries the owner's authority' (notes 3.1.14 Access Requests and Approvals). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A wildlife sanctuary's procedure has the access analyst disable guest accounts whose sponsor leaves until the data owner names a new sponsor; the sponsor for eight researchers just left. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the eight guest accounts now that their sponsor has gone
options.B: Disable the eight accounts until the owner has named a sponsor
options.C: Ask the data owner whether the eight accounts should be disabled
options.D: Ask the partner which of its researchers still need access

questions.key_concept: Guest accounts need a current sponsor; when the procedure assigns it, the analyst disables unsponsored accounts until the owner names one.
questions.pre_read: Think about who each option leaves deciding the accounts' future.
questions.correct_explanation: Every outside account needs an internal sponsor who confirms it is still needed. Here the procedure gives the analyst a clear task: disable unsponsored guest accounts until the data owner names a new sponsor, and the owner's part is only that naming. Asking the owner whether to disable is the runner-up: involving the owner sounds careful, but the procedure already decided, and the accounts stay open while the analyst waits.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the accounts lost their sponsor. But deleting is permanent and loses their history; the procedure disables them until a new sponsor is named.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the data owner does decide on sponsors. But the procedure already assigns disabling to the analyst, and asking first leaves eight unsponsored accounts open.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the partner knows its staff. But the partner does not decide access to the sanctuary's data; the sanctuary's owner and sponsor do.

tips: Eliminate: A deletes accounts the procedure only disables, losing their history, and D lets the partner decide access to data the sanctuary owns.
Final two: B beats C because the procedure assigns disabling to the analyst; the owner's part is naming a new sponsor, not approving the disable.
Exam cue: when a procedure gives you the task, do it, even if an owner is named. Escalate only what the procedure leaves to someone else.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'unsponsored guest accounts are disabled when the procedure assigns it' (notes 3.1.15 Third-Party, Guest and Federated Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; 'since' taken off option A; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A mountain rescue base's console locks after five idle minutes under the security manager's standard; unlocking it delayed help to an injured climber, and every second counts. What should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Exempt the console from locking but keep it in a locked room
options.B: Keep the idle lock and train rescuers to unlock it faster
options.C: Give rescuers one shared password to unlock the console fast
options.D: Remove the idle lock from every console across the organization

questions.key_concept: When a session control endangers people, a narrow, approved exception with a compensating control keeps both safety and protection.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what the idle lock protects against what its delay put at risk.
questions.correct_explanation: People's safety comes first, and every second of an unlock delays help to an injured climber. The fix is a narrow exception for this console, for the security manager who owns the standard to approve, with the lock's risk handled another way: a locked room only rescue staff enter. Keeping the lock and training faster unlocking is the runner-up: it respects the standard, but even a fast unlock still costs seconds.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: keeping the standard's lock is usually right. But every second counts, so even a fast unlock delays help; standards allow approved exceptions when a control endangers people.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems faster. But a shared password still has to be typed during a callout, and it hides who acted on the console.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes the delay. But only this console has the safety need; dropping idle locks everywhere leaves every other unattended screen open.

tips: Eliminate: C still needs typing during a callout and cannot show who acted, and D removes idle locks everywhere for one console's need.
Final two: A beats B because people's safety comes first; a faster unlock still costs seconds, while a narrow exception with room controls keeps dispatch fast and the console protected.
Exam cue: when a control endangers people, keep the protection but change its form through an approved exception for that case, never a blanket removal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-11 (Device Lock); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'when a session lock endangers people, use a narrow approved exception with a compensating control' (notes 3.1.16 Sessions, Timeouts and Reauthentication). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A climbing gym's AI scheduling agent, set up by the front-desk manager, asks the booking system to read the instructors' calendar. In this access decision, which is MOST accurately the subject?

options.A: The AI agent that asks to read the calendar
options.B: The instructors' calendar the agent wants to read
options.C: The front-desk manager who set up the agent
options.D: The access rule that decides whether reading is allowed

questions.key_concept: In an access decision, the subject is the party asking for access, such as a user, process or AI agent; the object is the resource.
questions.pre_read: Picture who or what is making the request at the moment it is checked.
questions.correct_explanation: In an access decision, the subject is the active party making the request, and the object is the resource it wants. Here the AI agent asks to read, so it is the subject; the calendar is the object. The manager who set it up is the runner-up: they answer for the agent, but the agent itself makes the request and is checked against its own rights.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the calendar is central to the request. But it is the resource being reached, which makes it the object, not the subject.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the manager answers for the agent. But the request comes from the agent, so the access check runs against the agent's own identity and rights.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the rule makes the decision. But a rule is the policy being applied, not a party asking for access.

tips: Eliminate: B is the resource being reached, the object, and D is the policy that decides, not a party asking for access.
Final two: A beats C because the agent itself makes the request; its owner is accountable but is not the party being checked.
Exam cue: the subject asks, the object is reached, and the policy decides. Software, including an AI agent, can be a subject.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the subject is the party asking for access, which can be an AI agent' (notes 3.2.1 Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: 'last month' taken off option C; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A model railway museum hires a contractor to rewrite only its events page over the next two weeks. Which access should the access analyst set up as BEST?

options.A: Edit rights to the events page under a shared staff login
options.B: View access, with staff pasting in the contractor's new text
options.C: Site-wide edit rights set to expire when the two weeks end
options.D: Edit rights to the events page that expire after two weeks

questions.key_concept: Least privilege limits scope and time: only the access a task needs, ending automatically when the task should be done.
questions.pre_read: Check each option for how much it grants, and for how long.
questions.correct_explanation: Least privilege limits how far access reaches as well as how long it lasts: the contractor needs edit rights to one page, for two weeks. Page-only rights that end automatically fit both limits. Site-wide rights with the same end date are the runner-up: the timing is right, but the task touches one page, so edit rights to every other page go beyond what the work needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the scope is exactly right. But a shared staff login hides who made each edit, and the rights outlive the contractor's job.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it grants the least access possible. But least privilege means what the task needs, and the contractor cannot do the work without edit rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the end date is right. But the task is one page, so rights to the whole site go beyond what the work needs.

tips: Eliminate: A puts the contractor on a shared staff login, so no edit traces to them, and B grants less than the work needs; least privilege is what the task needs, no more, no less.
Final two: D beats C because least privilege limits how far rights reach as well as how long they last; the job is one page.
Exam cue: size temporary access on both axes: only what the task touches, and only for as long as it runs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(2) (Account Management | Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'least privilege limits both scope and duration' (notes 3.2.2 Least Privilege and Need to Know). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Fix (4 Nov 2026, blind re-test): distractor A changed to a shared staff login so the key no longer combines A's scope with C's timing. Options C and D reworded so the key shares no phrase with both other options.

questions.question: At a tool hire firm, one clerk both records cash takings and reconciles them; the duty moves to a different clerk each month, which the manager calls separation of duties. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Separation is in place, as no clerk keeps the role for long
options.B: Separation is missing, but a till camera covers the gap
options.C: Separation would exist if the duty rotated weekly instead
options.D: Separation is missing, as one clerk still does the whole task

questions.key_concept: Job rotation surfaces problems after the fact; it does not separate duties when one person still completes the whole task.
questions.pre_read: For any single month, ask what one clerk can do alone.
questions.correct_explanation: Separation of duties means no one person can complete a sensitive task alone. Each month one clerk both records the takings and reconciles them, so they could hide their own error or theft. Rotation is the runner-up because it helps: the next clerk may spot old problems, but only after the fact. It is a detective backstop, not a split of duties.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: rotation is a real control. But for a whole month one clerk still records and checks the same cash, and rotation finds problems only afterward.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because cameras deter theft at the till. But a camera records the cash, not the reconciliation, so one person can still hide a gap on paper.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because shorter periods reduce exposure. But each week one clerk would still record and check the same cash; only a second person splits the duty.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on a camera that cannot see a falsified reconciliation, and C shortens the rotation, which still leaves one clerk doing both duties.
Final two: D beats A because one clerk still completes the whole task each month; rotation only surfaces problems after they happen.
Exam cue: separation of duties asks whether one person can finish a sensitive task alone. Rotation and monitoring help find problems but do not split the task.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'job rotation detects problems later; it does not separate duties' (notes 3.2.3 Separation of Duties and Two-Person Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A canal boat hire firm's new storage server has a built-in 'admin' account with a published default password, and named admin accounts are already set up. Which step should the system administrator take as BEST?

options.A: Rename the 'admin' account to hide it from attackers
options.B: Keep the default password as a backup for when named accounts fail
options.C: Share the 'admin' password with the team for quick emergency fixes
options.D: Replace the default password and lock the new one in the vault

questions.key_concept: Built-in admin accounts with default passwords are changed and vaulted at once; renaming them hides nothing an attacker needs.
questions.pre_read: Think about who else knows the default password.
questions.correct_explanation: A built-in administrator account with a published default password is an open door: anyone can look the password up. Replacing it and locking the new one in the vault closes that door and keeps the account under the same check-out controls as other privileged credentials. Renaming the account is the runner-up: it hides the name, but the published password still works for anyone who finds the account.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a renamed account is harder to target. But the published default password still works, and account names are easy to discover.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a fallback sounds useful. But a published password is a backup for attackers too; emergency access belongs in a sealed, vaulted account.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because emergencies need speed. But a shared admin password cannot show who acted, and it spreads the most powerful credential across the team.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps a published password live as a fallback, and C shares an admin password, so nobody can tell who used it.
Final two: D beats A because replacing the default password stops anyone using the published one; renaming only hides the account's name.
Exam cue: default credentials are public knowledge. Change them before use, and control built-in admin accounts like any other privileged account.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'default admin passwords are replaced and vaulted, not hidden' (notes 3.2.4 Privileged Access Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: 'so' taken off option A; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A student union's treasurer shares a budget file under discretionary access control and wants only the committee to open it. Which sharing setting BEST fits?

options.A: Share with named committee members who sign in to open it
options.B: Share by a link anyone can open until the committee meets
options.C: Share by a long, random link sent to the committee by email
options.D: Share publicly, but leave the file out of search results

questions.key_concept: Under discretionary access control, sharing with named, signed-in people keeps the owner's decision; links let in whoever holds them.
questions.pre_read: Think about what happens if the message carrying the file is forwarded.
questions.correct_explanation: Under discretionary access control the owner decides who gets in, and sharing with named people keeps that decision real: each person must sign in, and a forwarded message lets nobody else open the file. An expiring link is the runner-up: it limits how long the risk lasts, but until then anyone holding the link, including someone it was forwarded to, can open the file.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an end date limits exposure. But until the meeting anyone with the link can open the file, including people it was forwarded to.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a long random link is hard to guess. But links are forwarded, not guessed, and anyone holding this one can open the file.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because hidden files seem private. But public sharing lets anyone who finds the address open it; leaving it out of search only hides it.

tips: Eliminate: C protects against guessing when links leak by forwarding, and D makes the file public and only keeps it out of search, so anyone with the address gets in.
Final two: A beats B because only the named members can sign in and open it; an expiring link lets anyone holding it in until it ends.
Exam cue: under discretionary control the owner's sharing choice is the control. Named people who must sign in beat any link anyone can use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'under discretionary access control, sharing with named people keeps the owner's control; links do not' (notes 3.2.5 Discretionary Access Control (DAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At a government agency using mandatory access control, the security manager lowers an engineer's clearance from Secret to Confidential after a vetting review. Which statement about the Secret files the engineer wrote is MOST accurate?

options.A: The engineer keeps access, since they created and own the files
options.B: The engineer keeps access until a line manager confirms the new clearance
options.C: Access ends once the help desk edits each file's permissions
options.D: Access ends, as the new clearance is below each file's label

questions.key_concept: Under mandatory access control, the system compares clearance with each label, so a lowered clearance ends access to higher-labeled files, whoever owns them.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the system compares each time someone opens a file under this model.
questions.correct_explanation: Under mandatory access control, the system compares a person's clearance with each file's label whenever access is requested. Once the security manager lowers the engineer's clearance to Confidential, the Secret files are refused from then on, and nobody has to edit them. Keeping access as the files' creator is the runner-up: under discretionary control, ownership decides access, but under mandatory control it gives no say over labels or clearances.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: creators control their files under discretionary control. But under mandatory control, ownership gives no rights; the clearance is now below the files' Secret label.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because line managers often approve access changes. But under mandatory control they neither grant nor remove access; the system applies the security manager's new clearance on every request.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because removing access often means editing permissions. But mandatory control needs no change to each file; the system compares clearance with label on every request.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for a line manager to confirm the new clearance, though line managers have no say under mandatory control, and C waits for edits to each file, though the system checks labels itself.
Final two: D beats A because under mandatory control the label outranks ownership; with a Confidential clearance, the engineer is refused the Secret files, whoever wrote them.
Exam cue: under mandatory access control, access follows clearance against label. Change either one and access changes with it, whoever owns the file.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-3 (Personnel Screening)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'under mandatory access control a lowered clearance ends access to higher-labeled files, whoever owns them' (notes 3.2.6 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026; re-angled in fix-up round 1 so it no longer repeats cc_d3_016 or the notes worked example.
