questions.question: An ice rink's booking system uses role-based access control, and the owner wants the Rink Staff role usable only during opening hours. Which change should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Add an opening-hours rule to the Rink Staff role's access
options.B: Remove staff from the role each night and re-add them each morning
options.C: Create a second Rink Staff role reserved for daytime use
options.D: Ask rink staff to sign out when opening hours end

questions.key_concept: Plain role-based access control checks only role membership; limits on time or place need an added rule or attributes.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a role-based check actually looks at.
questions.correct_explanation: Plain role-based access control checks only whether someone holds a role; it has no sense of time. Adding a time rule to the Rink Staff role enforces opening hours automatically, every day. Removing and re-adding staff daily is the runner-up: it would limit access, but it relies on someone making changes twice a day, and one missed evening leaves the role live all night.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: membership changes would limit access. But they depend on someone acting twice daily, and one missed change leaves the role live overnight.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because roles organize access. But a daytime role still checks only membership, not the clock, so it works at midnight too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because signing out ends sessions. But staff could sign back in after hours; nothing in the system would stop them.

tips: Eliminate: C adds a role, but roles check membership, not the time, and D relies on staff behavior the system does not enforce.
Final two: A beats B because a time rule enforces hours automatically every day; daily manual membership changes fail the first time someone forgets.
Exam cue: role-based control answers 'which job?' Conditions such as time or location need a rule or attribute added on top.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'plain role-based access control does not check time; add a rule' (notes 3.2.7 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A fashion retailer's attribute-based policy opens payroll reports to anyone whose profile job title is Manager, and staff can edit their own job title. Which weakness should the access analyst rate MOST serious?

options.A: The policy checks too few attributes to be fine-grained enough
options.B: The policy also needs a separate role for each job title
options.C: Any employee can grant themselves this access at will
options.D: The title can go stale when managers step down

questions.key_concept: Attribute-based access control is only as trustworthy as its attributes, so they must come from sources users cannot edit.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can change each value the policy relies on.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute-based access control trusts its attributes, so they must come from an authoritative source users cannot change. Because staff can edit their own job title, anyone can make themselves a Manager and open payroll reports at will. Staleness is the runner-up: it is a real attribute risk, but it happens by accident and slowly, while self-editing is an open, deliberate way in.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more attributes can sharpen a policy. But adding attributes does not help if users can set them; trust in the source is the problem.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because roles are familiar. But attribute-based control needs no role per case; one policy covers them, provided its attributes are trustworthy.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: stale attributes are a real risk. But they cause accidental, gradual errors; a title staff can edit gives anyone payroll access today.

tips: Eliminate: A adds attributes without fixing who can set them, and B treats attribute-based control as needing roles, which it does not.
Final two: C beats D because a self-editable attribute lets anyone grant themselves access now; staleness causes slower, accidental errors.
Exam cue: attribute-based decisions are only as good as their attributes. Check that each one comes from a source the user cannot change.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-162 Section 3.2.3.1 (Confidence in Access Control Decisions: accurate and timely attributes from authoritative sources); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(13) (Access Enforcement | Attribute-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'attribute-based access control attributes must come from sources users cannot edit' (notes 3.2.8 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A network technician reviews a cable car operator's remote-access gateway: it allows sign-ins from three listed office addresses, and its last rule blocks everything else. Which principle does that last rule MOST directly apply?

options.A: Default deny, refusing whatever no earlier rule allows
options.B: Least privilege, giving each user the minimum rights their job needs
options.C: Role-based control, letting each rule grant access by job role
options.D: Discretionary control, letting each owner choose who signs in

questions.key_concept: A final deny-all rule applies default deny: anything not explicitly allowed by an earlier rule is refused.
questions.pre_read: Think about what happens to a sign-in from a fourth address.
questions.correct_explanation: Default deny means anything not explicitly allowed is refused. The gateway's final block-everything rule does exactly that: only the three listed addresses get through, and every other sign-in attempt meets the last rule. Least privilege is the runner-up: it is a related idea, but it limits each user's rights to their job, while this rule refuses every source not already allowed.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: least privilege is a close cousin. But it sizes each user's rights to their job; this rule refuses every source address not explicitly allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 'rule-based' and 'role-based' sound alike. But this rule treats every sign-in the same way, whatever the person's job role.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because someone set the rule. But an administrator's rule applied to everyone is non-discretionary; no owner chooses case by case.

tips: Eliminate: C mixes up rule-based and role-based control, and D calls an administrator's rule for everyone discretionary, though no owner decides case by case.
Final two: A beats B because the last rule refuses anything not explicitly allowed, which is default deny; least privilege sizes each user's rights.
Exam cue: a final block-everything rule puts default deny into practice: anything not explicitly allowed is refused.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(5) (Boundary Protection | Deny by Default — Allow by Exception)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a final deny-all rule applies default deny' (notes 3.2.9 Rule-Based Access Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A national archive labels each diplomatic cable by classification, and policy says no holder may pass one to anyone uncleared, even by mistake. Which model should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Discretionary access control, with each holder deciding who may see a cable
options.B: Role-based access control, with roles granted by each archivist's job
options.C: Rule-based access control, with one rule blocking shares outside the archive
options.D: Mandatory access control, with the system enforcing each cable's level

questions.key_concept: Mandatory access control fits labeled, classified data where the system, not users, must enforce who sees each item.
questions.pre_read: Find the condition that users' own choices must never be able to break.
questions.correct_explanation: Mandatory access control fits when data carries classification labels and policy must hold whatever users intend: the system compares each person's clearance with each cable's label, and no holder can override it, so even an accidental share fails. Role-based control is the runner-up: it suits most business systems, but it grants by job, not by label against clearance, so it cannot enforce each cable's classification.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because holders know the cables. But under discretionary control a holder can pass a cable to anyone, by choice or by mistake, which the policy forbids.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: roles fit most business systems. But they grant by job, not by each cable's label against a person's clearance, so classification is not enforced.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one rule binds every holder. But it still lets a holder pass a cable to an uncleared colleague inside the archive; only comparing label with clearance stops that.

tips: Eliminate: A lets holders share at will, which the policy forbids, and C blocks only sharing outside the archive, so an uncleared colleague inside could still see a cable.
Final two: D beats B because the system checks clearance against each label and nobody can override it; roles grant by job, not classification.
Exam cue: labels plus a rule that users must not be able to share, even by mistake, point to mandatory access control. Otherwise, roles usually fit.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'mandatory access control fits labeled data that users must not be able to share' (notes 3.2.10 Choosing an Access Control Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: A language-learning app company plans to have a second copy of its AI coding agent approve each change the agent writes before it merges. Which assessment should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: It is independent, as no change merges without a second check
options.B: It is independent once both copies log every change they make
options.C: It is not needed, as the agent already tests its own changes
options.D: It is not independent, as both copies share the same flaws

questions.key_concept: Separation of duties needs an independent approver; a copy of the same AI agent shares its flaws and inputs, so it is not one.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the approver could fail in a different way from the writer.
questions.correct_explanation: Separation of duties works only when the approver is independent of whoever made the change. A second copy of the same agent runs the same model on the same inputs, so a flaw or injected instruction that fooled one copy will likely fool the other. Calling it independent because every change gets a second check is the runner-up: the check exists, but it repeats the same judgment, so a person should approve instead.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a second check sounds like separation of duties. But both copies share the same model and inputs, so they tend to make the same mistake and approve it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because logs support oversight. But logging records what happened; it does not make one copy's approval independent of the other.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing catches many errors. But a writer checking its own work is exactly what separation of duties forbids, for agents as for people.

tips: Eliminate: B treats logging as if it made the approval independent, and C lets the agent check its own work, which separation of duties forbids.
Final two: D beats A because the second copy shares the first's flaws and inputs; a check that repeats the same judgment is not independent.
Exam cue: separation of duties needs an approver who can fail differently. A copy of the same AI agent is not a second person.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a copy of the same AI agent is not an independent approver' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: Before go-live, an orchard cooperative's AI purchasing agent must stop for staff approval before paying any supplier. Which check should the security analyst run as BEST evidence the control works?

options.A: Read the agent's design document showing the approval step
options.B: Get the vendor's signed statement that its tests passed
options.C: Send test payments, some meant to trick it, and see it pause
options.D: Confirm the agent's payment logs are kept for a whole year

questions.key_concept: The best evidence an AI agent's approval step works is testing it live, including inputs crafted to make it skip the step.
questions.pre_read: Separate evidence that a step was planned from evidence that it happens.
questions.correct_explanation: The best evidence that a control works is watching it work under realistic pressure. Sending test payment requests, including ones meant to talk the agent past the step, shows whether it really stops for approval every time. The design document is the runner-up: it shows the step was intended, but a document cannot show the live agent obeys it, especially when inputs try to trick it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the design shows the intended step. But intent is not operation; only testing the live agent shows it really stops, even when inputs try to trick it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor tested its product. But the vendor's claim about its own tests is not evidence that this setup stops as intended.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs support later checks. But keeping logs shows nothing about whether the agent waits for approval before paying.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a vendor's claim in place of evidence, and D checks log retention, which says nothing about whether the agent waits.
Final two: C beats A because testing the live agent, including with inputs meant to trick it, shows the step works; a design document only shows it was planned.
Exam cue: to show a control works, test it in operation, including attempts to get around it. Designs and promises show intent only.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'test that an AI agent really stops at its approval step' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor A no longer names the vendor; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: During an outage, a harbor pilot service's on-call engineer used the sealed break-glass account as the runbook allows, and the incident is recorded. What is the system administrator's BEST next step?

options.A: Keep the same password, since this use was approved and recorded
options.B: Reseal it with a new password, since the old one is exposed
options.C: Give the engineer the account for future outages
options.D: Disable the account, since normal sign-in is working again

questions.key_concept: After a break-glass account is used, its password is changed and resealed so it stays ready but unexposed.
questions.pre_read: Think about who now knows the account's password.
questions.correct_explanation: After a break-glass account is used, its password is no longer sealed: the engineer has seen it. Sealing away a new password restores the account to a ready, unused emergency state. Disabling it is the runner-up: it removes the exposed access, but it also removes the emergency path, so the next outage would find no working way in.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the use was proper. But approval does not reseal the password; the engineer now knows it and could use it again without any emergency.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the engineer handled the outage well. But a permanent admin login is standing privilege, the opposite of a sealed emergency account.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: disabling stops misuse of the exposed password. But it also leaves no emergency path for the next outage, which is the account's whole purpose.

tips: Eliminate: A treats approval as resealing, though the engineer now knows the password, and C turns an emergency account into standing privilege.
Final two: B beats D because a new sealed password keeps the account ready and unexposed; disabling it leaves no way in during the next outage.
Exam cue: after any break-glass use, reset it: new secret, sealed again, still ready. Emergency access should stay available but unexposed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'after break-glass use, change and reseal the password' (notes 3.2.12 Just-in-Time and Break-Glass Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and', now giving its reason; same key and teaching point. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded per blind-test flag (the old wording read backwards); same key and teaching point.

questions.question: At a defense supplier, engineers share their notes with anyone they choose, while design files open only to staff whose clearance matches each file's label. Which description should the access analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Mandatory for the notes and for the design files alike
options.B: Discretionary for the notes and mandatory for the design files
options.C: Role-based for the notes and mandatory for the design files
options.D: Discretionary for the notes and rule-based for the design files

questions.key_concept: One site can run several models; name each system's model by who decides there, not by how sensitive the site's work is.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decides access for the notes, and who decides for the design files.
questions.correct_explanation: Name each model by who decides. Engineers choosing who sees their notes is discretionary: the owner decides. Design files that open only when clearance matches the label, whatever anyone wants, are mandatory: the system decides. Mandatory for both is the runner-up, because classified work suggests it everywhere, but the notes are shared at each engineer's own choice, so that part is discretionary.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: classified work points to mandatory control. But engineers share their notes with anyone they choose, so the owner decides there; that part is discretionary.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because engineers share a job. But nothing grants the notes by role; each engineer chooses who sees their own notes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a fixed check applies to everyone. But it compares clearance with each file's label, which is mandatory control, not a general rule such as an hours limit.

tips: Eliminate: C grants by job when each engineer chooses, and D calls a clearance-against-label check rule-based, though matching labels to clearances is mandatory control.
Final two: B beats A because the notes are shared at each owner's choice; classified work elsewhere does not make every system mandatory.
Exam cue: sensitive work at a site does not make every system there mandatory. Judge each system on its own: does an owner or the system decide?
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'classified work at a site does not make every system there mandatory' (notes 3.2.13 Access Model Scenarios: Worked Examples). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Identities and accounts
questions.question: A chocolate factory's warehouse scanner signs in daily with an account whose recorded owner, a supervisor, left in June, and nobody has taken it over. Which term BEST describes this account?

options.A: Orphaned: still active, but with no accountable owner
options.B: Dormant: left unused past the set inactivity period
options.C: Shared: used by several people under one login
options.D: Privileged: lets its owner change system settings

questions.key_concept: An orphaned account is active with no accountable owner; a dormant account is one left unused for a set period.
questions.pre_read: Separate two facts about any account: who answers for it, and whether it is still being used.
questions.correct_explanation: An orphaned account is still active but has no accountable owner, here because the supervisor left and nobody took it over. Orphaned accounts are risky because nobody notices misuse or decides whether they are still needed. Dormant is the runner-up, since old accounts are often unused, but this one signs in every day, so it is not dormant; its problem is the missing owner.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: old accounts are often unused. But the scanner signs in daily, so the account is active; what it lacks is an owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because warehouse staff all handle the scanner. But one device signs in with the account; no group of people shares the login.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because an unexplained account feels powerful. But nothing in the stem gives it admin rights; the defining fact is the owner who left.

tips: Eliminate: C needs several people signing in to one login, and D needs admin rights; the stem shows neither.
Final two: A beats B because the account signs in daily, so it is not dormant; it is orphaned because its owner left and nobody replaced them.
Exam cue: orphaned is about the owner; dormant is about use. Read which fact the stem gives before naming the account.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an orphaned account is active with no accountable owner' (notes 3.1.1 Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A glassworks' system administrator is explaining the access control list (ACL) on the design team's shared folder to a new technician. Which description of it is MOST accurate?

options.A: Firewall rules that filter traffic to the folder by address
options.B: A list of the access roles each employee holds across systems
options.C: A log on the folder recording who accessed it, how and when
options.D: A list on the folder naming who holds which permissions

questions.key_concept: An access control list on an object names who may access it and with which rights; logging each access is accounting.
questions.pre_read: Picture where an ACL is kept and what happens when someone tries to open the folder.
questions.correct_explanation: An access control list sits on the object, here the folder, and names which users or groups may access it and with what rights, such as read or edit. It is an authorization tool. The log is the runner-up because it also sits on the folder, but recording who opened it is accounting: it traces actions afterward and grants or blocks nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because firewalls also use access lists. But those filter network traffic by address; a folder's ACL names which people may use the folder.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because roles do grant access. But a list of each employee's roles is kept with the people, not on the folder, and is not an ACL.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it sits on the folder too. But recording who opened it is accounting, which traces actions; an ACL decides who may open it.

tips: Eliminate: A describes network access lists that filter traffic, and B describes role assignments kept with the people; neither is a list on the folder.
Final two: D beats C because an ACL grants or refuses access before it happens; a log only records it afterward.
Exam cue: ask whether the thing described decides access or records it. Deciding is authorization, such as an ACL; recording is accounting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an access control list on an object names who may access it and how' (notes 3.2.1 Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and' or 'how'; option C reworded; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A toy maker's role owner must approve the new 'warehouse picker' role, but its entitlements are listed only as group codes such as GRP_INV_RW_07. What should the access analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Refer the role to IT to approve, since IT understands the codes
options.B: Send the owner the technical permission export to sign
options.C: Copy a similar warehouse role that was already approved
options.D: Rewrite each entitlement in plain terms the owner can judge

questions.key_concept: Role owners approve entitlements described in business terms, so the approval reflects a real decision.
questions.pre_read: Consider who approves the role and what they must be able to read to do it.
questions.correct_explanation: An owner can only approve what they understand. Rewriting each code as the task it allows, such as updating stock counts, lets the role owner judge whether a picker needs it. Sending the technical export is the runner-up: it is complete, but an owner who cannot read GRP_INV_RW_07 will guess or rubber-stamp, so the approval means little.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because IT builds the groups. But building a role is not owning it; the role owner knows the work and must approve its contents.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the export is complete. But codes the owner cannot read lead to guessing or rubber-stamping; the owner needs each entitlement in plain terms.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it saves time. But a copied role can carry rights the picker job never needed, and the owner still cannot judge it.

tips: Eliminate: A hands the owner's approval to IT, which builds roles but does not own them, and C copies another role, which can carry rights this job never needed.
Final two: D beats B because an approval counts only when the owner understands what they approve; complete but unreadable codes invite rubber-stamping.
Exam cue: make entitlements readable to the business owner before any role approval or review; an owner who cannot read the list cannot really decide.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'role owners approve entitlements they can understand' (notes 3.1.2 Defining Roles and Entitlements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At a map publisher, the help desk role can reset passwords and also add anyone to the domain administrators group, which technicians never need to do. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Delete the admin-group right from the help desk role
options.B: Log every admin-group change made through the help desk role
options.C: Keep both rights, since technicians are trusted staff
options.D: Give each technician a second, standard account for email

questions.key_concept: Least privilege removes rights a role's tasks never use; logging those rights does not shrink the risk.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the help desk does every day with everything its role can do.
questions.correct_explanation: Least privilege gives a role only what its tasks need. Resetting passwords is help desk work; adding people to the domain administrators group is not, and a stolen technician account could use it to take over the domain. Logging every change is the runner-up: it shows misuse afterward, but the excess right stays, and least privilege removes it rather than watching it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: logs help trace misuse. But they record a domain takeover after it happens; removing the right the role never uses prevents it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because technicians are trusted. But least privilege is about the role, not trust; a phished technician account would hand that right to an attacker.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because separate admin accounts are good practice. But the excess right sits in the help desk role itself, so a second account leaves it in place.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps an unneeded right out of trust, though least privilege sizes rights to the task, and D adds a second account while the excess right stays in the role.
Final two: A beats B because removing the unneeded right prevents misuse; logging only reveals it after the domain is taken.
Exam cue: when a role holds a right its tasks never use, remove it. Monitoring backs up rights that must stay; it is no substitute for removal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.2 (Privileged access rights)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'least privilege removes rights a role's tasks never use' (notes 3.2.2 Least Privilege and Need to Know). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A whale-watching firm's start records give 30 seasonal guides the approved Guide role, but the operations manager messages the help desk to add Bookings Admin for all. Which action is BEST for the technician?

options.A: Set up one shared Guide login for the 30 seasonal guides
options.B: Give each guide both roles, with Bookings Admin ending in a week
options.C: Hold the start records until the security manager approves the change
options.D: Give each guide the Guide role that their start record lists

questions.key_concept: Provision exactly the approved role on the start record; extra access asked for in a message needs its own approved request.
questions.pre_read: Look at what each start record already says about the guides' access.
questions.correct_explanation: Provisioning follows the trusted record: each start record already carries the approved Guide role, so the technician grants exactly that. A message is not an approved request; if guides need booking rights, the manager can raise a request for the bookings owner to approve. Holding the records for the security manager is the runner-up, but nothing about the Guide role needs deciding, and the security manager does not own booking access.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one login is quick to set up for seasonal staff. But a shared login hides which guide acted and cannot be removed for one person.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the extra role expires. But for a week, 30 newcomers hold admin rights that nobody approved, granted on a message.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: checking first sounds careful. But the start records already approve the Guide role, and bookings access is the bookings owner's call, not the security manager's.

tips: Eliminate: A gives 30 guides one shared login, so no action traces to a person, and B grants an admin role on a message that no approved request backs.
Final two: D beats C because the approved role is already on each start record, so provisioning it is the technician's job; holding the records only delays the guides.
Exam cue: provision exactly what the trusted record approves. Extra access asked for in a message needs its own approved request first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.1 (Establish an Access Granting Process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'provision exactly the approved role from the trusted record; extra access needs its own approved request' (notes 3.1.3 Provisioning and Identity Proofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Re-angled in fix-up round 2: the shortcut is an extra role asked for by message, not copied access, which cc_d3_128 teaches.

questions.question: A national mint's security manager is listing the mint's controls. Which arrangement is MOST clearly two-person control rather than separation of duties?

options.A: One officer orders die steel, and another receives the deliveries
options.B: Two trained officers take turns on die vault duty each month
options.C: One officer opens the vault with a badge and a PIN
options.D: Two officers enter separate codes together to open the die vault

questions.key_concept: Two-person control needs two people for the same action; separation of duties gives different steps of a process to different people.
questions.pre_read: Recall how two-person control and separation of duties each stop one person acting alone.
questions.correct_explanation: Two-person control needs two people for the same action, so neither can complete it alone; the officers' separate codes, entered together, open the vault. Ordering steel and receiving it is the runner-up: it is separation of duties, splitting a process into different functions done by different people. Both stop one person acting alone, but only the vault codes need two people for one action.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it also stops one person acting alone. But ordering and receiving are different steps of a process, each done by one person; that is separation of duties.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because two officers take part. But job rotation moves a duty between people over time; at any moment one person still acts alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a badge plus a PIN is multifactor. But it is one person proving identity strongly; no second person takes part.

tips: Eliminate: B rotates one duty between people over time, and C is one person with two factors; neither needs a second person for the same action.
Final two: D beats A because both officers must act on the same action to open the vault; ordering and receiving are different steps, which is separation of duties.

Exam cue: two people acting together on one action, such as two codes entered at once, is two-person control. Different people doing different steps, such as entering and approving, is separation of duties.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(2) (Access Enforcement | Dual Authorization); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'two-person control needs two people acting together' (notes 3.2.3 Separation of Duties and Two-Person Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A county courthouse clerk reports losing the smart card they unlock with a PIN to sign in. Which action is BEST for the help desk technician?

options.A: Revoke the card's certificate and issue the clerk a new card
options.B: Leave the card active, because nobody can use it without the PIN
options.C: Reset the clerk's PIN and leave the lost card active
options.D: Disable the clerk's whole account until the card is found

questions.key_concept: A lost authenticator is revoked and replaced at once; a PIN slows a finder but does not make the card safe to leave active.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a finder could still do with a card that stays valid.
questions.correct_explanation: A lost authenticator is treated as compromised, so the technician revokes the card's certificate, which makes the card useless to anyone who finds it, and issues a new card so the clerk can keep working. Leaving the card active because it needs a PIN is the runner-up: the PIN does slow a finder, but PINs are short and can be guessed or watched being typed, and only revoking the card removes the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the PIN does protect the card. But a PIN can be guessed or seen, so a lost card left valid is still a way in.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a new PIN blocks anyone who saw the old one. But the lost card itself stays valid, and the clerk still has no card to sign in with.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shuts out any finder. But it also locks the clerk out of their work; revoking only the card stops a finder and keeps the clerk's account.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the PIN but leaves the lost card valid, and D locks the clerk out of all work when only the card needs to stop working.
Final two: A beats B because only revoking the card makes a found card useless; a PIN slows a finder but can be guessed or seen.
Exam cue: a lost or stolen authenticator is revoked and replaced at once. Its second factor slows a finder, but never makes it safe to leave active.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 4.3 (Loss, Theft, Damage, and Compromise: a lost authenticator is assumed compromised and is promptly suspended, invalidated or destroyed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'authenticators have a life cycle: revoke a lost one and enroll a replacement' (notes 3.1.4 Authentication Factors and MFA). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Re-angled in fix-up round 2 from factor counting, which cc_d1_114 teaches, to the authenticator life cycle. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: 'since' taken off option B; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A new system administrator at a marionette workshop is told to use the team's shared 'itadmin' login for convenience until a named admin account is set up next week. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Use the shared login until the named account is set up
options.B: Ask to have the named account set up before any admin work
options.C: Use the shared login and record each change in a ticket
options.D: Ask for admin rights on their everyday account instead

questions.key_concept: Each administrator uses a named admin account; a shared admin login hides who acted, however convenient it is.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the logs could show after a change made under the shared login.
questions.correct_explanation: Admin actions must trace to one person, so admin work waits for the named admin account, and the administrator asks to have it set up before making any changes. Using the shared login and recording each change in a ticket is the runner-up: it adds a paper trail, but the system still logs only 'itadmin', and anyone else using the login could make changes no ticket explains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is only for a week. But every change that week is logged as 'itadmin', so nobody can show which person made it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: tickets add a record. But the system still logs every change as 'itadmin', and others using the login leave no ticket; only a named account proves who acted.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids the shared login. But admin rights on an everyday account expose them to email and web threats; admin work needs a separate named admin account.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts a week of changes nobody can trace to a person, and D puts admin rights on an everyday account used for email and browsing.
Final two: B beats C because only a named admin account ties each change to one person in the system's own logs; a ticket is a note beside an untraceable login.
Exam cue: convenience never justifies a shared admin login. Each administrator gets a named admin account, kept separate from their everyday one.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 5.4 (Restrict Administrator Privileges to Dedicated Administrator Accounts); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each administrator needs a named admin account, never a shared one' (notes 3.2.4 Privileged Access Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A law firm's partner asks whether a look-alike login page could capture the PIN that unlocks their new passkey and reuse it. Which reply should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: Yes, a fake page catches the PIN sent at each sign-in
options.B: Yes, if the fake page copies the real site closely enough
options.C: No, the PIN stays on the device, where it unlocks the passkey
options.D: No, the browser encrypts the PIN before it goes to the site

questions.key_concept: A passkey's PIN or biometric unlocks the key on the user's own device and is never sent to any website.
questions.pre_read: Picture where the PIN is checked when the partner signs in with a passkey.
questions.correct_explanation: A passkey's PIN is an activation secret: it unlocks the private key on the partner's own device and is never sent to any website, so a real sign-in gives a look-alike page nothing to capture. Even a PIN typed into a fake form is useless without that device. The browser-encryption reply is the runner-up: it also says no, but it wrongly implies the PIN travels.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because passwords are sent at sign-in. But a passkey PIN only unlocks the key on the device; no site, real or fake, receives it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because phishing relies on convincing copies. But passkeys work only on the real site's address, and the PIN is never sent to any site, so looks do not matter.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it also says no. But the PIN is never sent to any site; if it were, a fake page would receive it readable, like any site.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the PIN as a password sent to the site, and B thinks a close copy can fool a passkey, which works only on the real site.
Final two: C beats D because the PIN is checked locally and never sent to any website; encryption in transit would not help, since a fake page receives whatever is sent to it.
Exam cue: a passkey's PIN or fingerprint unlocks a key on the device. Nothing a fake site could capture and reuse is ever sent.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.1.1 (Passwords: activation secrets such as an unlock PIN are not sent to the verifier); NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.5.2 (Verifier Name Binding)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a passkey's unlock PIN never leaves the device' (notes 3.1.5 Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An architecture firm uses discretionary access control for its cloud documents, and staff keep sharing client drawings with personal email addresses. Which control should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Switch every document to mandatory access control with labels
options.B: Remind staff to check that each recipient is approved before sharing
options.C: Block sharing outside the firm unless an exception is approved
options.D: Let the firm's IT team approve every share instead of owners

questions.key_concept: Discretionary access control is limited with organization-wide sharing restrictions, such as blocking outside recipients, not by abandoning the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what lets staff send drawings to personal addresses, and which control limits that.
questions.correct_explanation: Discretionary access control lets owners share freely, so the fix is an organization-wide limit that keeps owner sharing inside the firm: block outside recipients, with approved exceptions for genuine client needs. Reminders are the runner-up; awareness helps, but staff already share out of habit or convenience, and a technical limit stops the personal-address shares that reminders only discourage.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because mandatory control is strict. But labels and clearances are rigid and costly for an architecture firm; a sharing limit fixes this one leak.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: awareness helps. But staff already share by habit, and a reminder only discourages it; a block on outside sharing stops it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because central approval stops mistakes. But it ends owner sharing and floods IT with requests; a limit on outside recipients keeps owner choice inside the firm.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps in mandatory control, too rigid for a design firm's documents, and D takes every share away from owners; both give up owner sharing to fix one leak.
Final two: C beats B because a block on outside recipients stops the leak; a reminder only discourages it.
Exam cue: oversharing is discretionary control's weak spot. Keep owner sharing, but add organization-wide limits, such as blocking outside recipients.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'organizations limit discretionary sharing with restrictions rather than abandoning it' (notes 3.2.5 Discretionary Access Control (DAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An observatory's security manager is writing the password rule for an internal wiki where staff sign in with a password alone. Which rule BEST follows NIST SP 800-63B-4?

options.A: At least 8 characters, mixing capitals, digits and symbols
options.B: At least 12 characters, with a password change every 90 days
options.C: At least 8 characters, checked against a list of breached passwords
options.D: At least 15 characters, checked against a breached-password list

questions.key_concept: NIST SP 800-63B-4 sets a 15-character minimum for passwords used alone, with blocklist screening and no composition or expiry rules.
questions.pre_read: Recall what current NIST guidance says about password length, character mixes and scheduled changes.
questions.correct_explanation: For a password used alone, NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires at least 15 characters and screening against blocklisted values, such as breached passwords, with no composition rules or scheduled changes. Eight characters with screening is the runner-up: the same guidance allows an 8-character minimum only when the password is part of multifactor sign-in, and this wiki uses the password alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because character mixes look strong. But the guidance forbids composition rules, which push people toward predictable patterns; length and screening matter more.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because regular changes feel safe. But the guidance drops scheduled changes, and 12 characters is short for a password used alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: screening is right. But an 8-character minimum applies only when the password is one factor of MFA; used alone, it needs at least 15.

tips: Eliminate: A demands character mixes and B forces scheduled changes; current NIST guidance drops both.
Final two: D beats C because a password used alone needs at least 15 characters; the 8-character minimum is only for passwords paired with another factor.
Exam cue: for NIST password rules, think length and breach screening, no character mixes and no calendar changes: 15 alone, 8 with MFA.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: password requirements); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5(1) (Authenticator Management | Password-based Authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'passwords used alone need at least 15 characters and blocklist screening' (notes 3.1.6 Passwords and Modern Password Standards). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A defense contractor is moving a project's files from discretionary to mandatory access control. Which change should the access analyst warn the project's staff about as MOST noticeable?

options.A: Each file's access will follow its owner's job role
options.B: Staff will choose a clearance level for each colleague
options.C: Staff can no longer decide who opens files they create
options.D: Staff can share files, but only with colleagues they name

questions.key_concept: Under mandatory access control, file creators cannot grant access or change labels; the system enforces central labels and clearances.
questions.pre_read: Think about who decides access under each model, before and after the move.
questions.correct_explanation: Under mandatory access control the system decides, comparing each person's clearance with each file's label under central policy; creators cannot share or relabel, even their own files. That loss of owner choice is what staff will notice most. Sharing only with named colleagues is the runner-up, as it sounds stricter, but it is still discretionary: the owner still decides.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because job roles also centralize access. But that describes role-based control; mandatory control compares clearances with labels.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because clearances are central to mandatory control. But a central security authority sets clearances after vetting; staff never set them for colleagues.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it narrows sharing. But owners still choose who gets in, which is discretionary; under mandatory control, owners cannot grant access at all.

tips: Eliminate: A describes role-based control, and B gives staff the security authority's job of setting clearances.
Final two: C beats D because mandatory control takes the decision away from file owners; sharing with named people is still the owner deciding.
Exam cue: in mandatory access control, owners lose discretion. Labels and clearances, set centrally, decide every access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'under mandatory access control, owners cannot decide who opens their files' (notes 3.2.6 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An adaptive sign-in vendor offers to sharpen a public library's AI risk scoring by feeding it staff's full web browsing histories. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Accept the feed, since the model needs more data to be accurate
options.B: Accept the feed once staff are told what it collects
options.C: Turn off adaptive sign-in so no staff data is collected
options.D: Limit the feed to the sign-in signals scoring needs

questions.key_concept: AI behavior scoring should collect only the signals sign-in needs; telling staff is required but does not justify over-collection.
questions.pre_read: Consider what data a sign-in risk score actually uses to do its job.
questions.correct_explanation: Behavior data is personal data, so adaptive sign-in should collect only the signals its purpose needs, such as device, location and time. Full browsing histories go far beyond judging a sign-in. Telling staff is the runner-up: notice is required, but telling people about over-collection does not make it necessary; the first question is whether the data is needed at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models often improve with data. But sign-in scoring needs signals about the sign-in, not everything staff browse; extra data adds privacy risk, not accuracy.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: staff should be told what is collected. But notice does not justify gathering browsing histories that sign-in scoring never needs; minimization limits what is collected.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it collects nothing. But it drops a useful layer against stolen passwords; collecting only the sign-in signals keeps both protection and privacy.

tips: Eliminate: A collects everything on the belief that more data means better scores, and C drops adaptive sign-in entirely when a narrower feed would do.
Final two: D beats B because the first privacy question is whether the data is needed; telling staff about browsing-history collection still collects far more than sign-in needs.
Exam cue: for AI that watches behavior, collect only what the purpose needs. Notice and protection are still required, but neither justifies collecting extra data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-10 (Adaptive Authentication); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-8(33) (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles | Minimization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'behavior data is personal data: collect only what is needed and tell users' (notes 3.1.8 Adaptive Authentication and AI Behavior Analysis). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: In a brewery's role-based access control system, policy forbids anyone holding both the Supplier Setup and Payment Release roles. Which control should the access analyst propose to enforce this BEST?

options.A: A monthly report listing anyone who holds both roles
options.B: One combined role holding both sets of rights for small teams
options.C: Let each role's members approve who else joins the role
options.D: Mark the roles mutually exclusive, so no account gets both

questions.key_concept: Mutually exclusive roles let a role-based system refuse conflicting role pairs, enforcing separation of duties at assignment.
questions.pre_read: Think about how role-based systems can carry separation of duties rules.
questions.correct_explanation: Role-based systems can mark roles as mutually exclusive, so the system refuses to give one account both. That enforces the separation of duties policy at the moment of assignment. A monthly report of people holding both is the runner-up: it finds conflicts, but only after someone already holds both roles and could set up a fake supplier and pay it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it does find conflicts. But it finds them after assignment, leaving a window to set up and pay a fake supplier; exclusive roles prevent the pairing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because small teams find combined roles convenient. But it builds the forbidden conflict into a role; one holder could create and pay a fake supplier.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because members know their team. But role membership is set through the organization's approved process; letting members add others makes it discretionary.

tips: Eliminate: B builds the forbidden pairing into one role, and C lets members hand out roles, which breaks role-based control's central assignment.
Final two: D beats A because the system refuses the conflicting pair before anyone holds it; a report only finds it afterward.
Exam cue: when policy forbids two roles together, enforce it at assignment with mutually exclusive roles; reports and reviews are the backstop.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'mutually exclusive roles stop one person holding conflicting roles' (notes 3.2.7 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: During a wildfire, AI sign-in scoring blocks crew leaders' genuine evacuation-app sign-ins from shelters; the runbook lets the security analyst add emergency exceptions, though the security manager sets thresholds. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add a temporary exception for the named crew leaders' sign-ins
options.B: Report the blocked sign-ins to the security manager to retune
options.C: Reset the crew leaders' passwords and have them sign in again
options.D: Add an AI scoring exception for every user until it is over

questions.key_concept: When AI scoring blocks genuine users in an emergency, use the narrow exception the runbook allows; thresholds stay with their owner.
questions.pre_read: Think about how adaptive sign-in rules are adjusted during an emergency.
questions.correct_explanation: People's safety comes first, and the runbook gives the analyst authority to add emergency exceptions, so a temporary exception for the named crew leaders restores the evacuation app while scoring still protects everyone else; the exception is recorded and reported. Reporting to the security manager is the runner-up: retuning thresholds is the manager's call and worth raising, but crews leading an evacuation cannot wait for it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the security manager owns the thresholds. But the runbook already lets the analyst add emergency exceptions, and an evacuation cannot wait for a retune.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a reset is the usual fix for sign-in trouble. But the block comes from the risk score on location and device; a reset changes nothing the score sees.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one exception clears every block. But it strips AI protection from all users during a crisis attackers exploit; an exception for the named crew leaders frees them alone.

tips: Eliminate: C resets passwords, but the block comes from the risk score, not the password, and D exempts every user from AI scoring when only the crews are blocked.

Final two: A beats B because the runbook gives the analyst the exception power, while retuning belongs to the security manager; the crews need the evacuation app now, and the retune request can follow.
Exam cue: sort the powers a procedure gives you from those it keeps with an owner. Use yours, kept narrow, and send the rest to the owner with the evidence.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-10 (Adaptive Authentication); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a narrow emergency exception, allowed by the runbook, protects people when AI scoring blocks genuine users' (notes 3.1.8 Adaptive Authentication and AI Behavior Analysis). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A canal boat tour company's new attribute-based policy should open passenger lists only to crew rostered on that sailing. Which test is BEST for the access analyst to run before go-live?

options.A: Ask the policy owner to read the policy and sign it off
options.B: Check each crew member's roster attribute against the rota
options.C: Run requests meant to pass, then ones meant to be refused
options.D: Have every rostered crew member confirm the list opens for them

questions.key_concept: Test an attribute-based policy with requests that should be allowed and requests that should be denied before go-live.
questions.pre_read: List the ways an attribute-based policy could give the wrong answer.
questions.correct_explanation: An attribute-based policy can fail two ways: blocking people who should get in, or letting in people who should not. Running requests that should pass and others that should be refused, such as a crew member not rostered on that sailing, shows both. Having rostered crew confirm the list opens is the runner-up: it shows the right people get in, but a policy open to every crew member would pass it too.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because owners approve policies. But reading the rule is not testing it; only real requests show how the policy engine treats each attribute.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because attributes must match their source. But correct inputs do not prove the policy's logic; only test requests show how it decides on them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it does test the policy. But it only checks who gets in; a policy that opened the lists to every crew member would pass it too.

tips: Eliminate: A signs off the policy text without testing it, and B checks the attribute inputs, not the decisions the policy makes from them.
Final two: C beats D because a test of allowed requests alone would also pass a policy open to everyone; only requests that should be refused prove the limit works.
Exam cue: test access controls both ways, with a case that should pass and a case that should be refused.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-162 (Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) Definition and Considerations); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3(2) (Configuration Change Control | Testing, Validation, and Documentation of Changes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'test an attribute-based policy with allowed and denied cases' (notes 3.2.8 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; same key and teaching point. Final cross-domain gate, 19 Nov 2026: key C reworded without 'plus'.

questions.question: A perfume maker moves its AI agent from summarizing human resources case notes to drafting marketing copy, but the agent keeps its case-note access. Which action should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep the access in case HR needs the agent again
options.B: Add marketing access now; remove case notes at month end
options.C: End the case-note access; grant only the rights marketing needs
options.D: Add a marketing account, keeping the old one as a spare

questions.key_concept: An AI agent moved to a new task is a mover: remove its old access and grant only what the new task needs.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the agent's new task uses with what it can still reach.
questions.correct_explanation: A repurposed agent is a mover: its new task gets new access, and the old access goes at the move. Leaving human resources case notes readable by a marketing agent exposes sensitive data to a tool that no longer uses it. Removing case-note access at month end is the runner-up: the old access does go, but until then the case notes stay readable, and the risk of a manipulated agent reading them remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the agent might move back. But access follows the current task; if HR needs it again, that is a new, approved request.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the case-note access does go in the end. But until month end a marketing agent can still read HR case notes; old access goes at the move.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a fresh account seems clean. But the old one keeps case-note access as a spare; unused identities with rights are what attackers look for.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps old access in case of a move back, and D leaves the old account active as a spare; both keep rights the new task does not use.
Final two: C beats B because a mover's old access is removed at the move; waiting for month end leaves HR case notes open to a marketing agent.
Exam cue: treat an AI agent given a new job like a human mover. Remove the old access, then add only what the new task needs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) NHI5 (Overprivileged NHI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an AI agent given a new task is a mover whose old access is removed' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and' or 'what'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A new access analyst at a translation agency keeps mixing up rule-based and role-based access control. Which description of rule-based access control is MOST accurate?

options.A: Owners write rules deciding who may open their own files
options.B: Administrator rules apply the same way to every user
options.C: Permissions attach to job roles that people are assigned
options.D: A policy engine weighs several attributes on each request

questions.key_concept: Rule-based access control applies administrator-set rules the same way to every subject, unlike role-based access by job.
questions.pre_read: Recall who writes the rules in rule-based control, and whom they apply to.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules, written by an administrator, to every subject alike, such as a firewall rule or a ban on sign-ins after hours. Who you are or what job you do does not change the rule. A policy weighing several attributes is the runner-up, because it also sounds rule-driven, but that is attribute-based control, which decides each request on many characteristics.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because owners can set conditions. But owners choosing who opens their files is discretionary control, not administrator rules for all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the names sound alike. But permissions tied to job roles describe role-based access control, the model this one is confused with.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it also follows a written policy. But weighing many attributes of each request is attribute-based control; rule-based applies one fixed rule to all.

tips: Eliminate: A describes owners deciding, which is discretionary, and C describes job roles, which is role-based; neither is one rule for all.
Final two: B beats D because rule-based control applies the same fixed rule to everyone; weighing several attributes per request is attribute-based control.
Exam cue: the same rule for everyone, such as hours or addresses, is rule-based. Access by job is role-based. Many conditions together is attribute-based.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'rule-based access control applies administrator rules to every subject alike' (notes 3.2.9 Rule-Based Access Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A satellite operator's managers barely finish one yearly review of every account, including the ground-station administrator accounts. Which change to the review schedule should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Review privileged and sensitive access more often than the rest
options.B: Review every account monthly, whatever access it holds
options.C: Review only the accounts that usage reports show as unused
options.D: Keep yearly reviews and require MFA on the administrator accounts

questions.key_concept: Access reviews run more often for privileged and sensitive access than for routine access, matching effort to risk.
questions.pre_read: Think about which accounts would do the most harm if a wrong right went unnoticed.
questions.correct_explanation: Review effort should follow risk: privileged and sensitive access, such as the ground-station administrator accounts, is reviewed more often, while everyday access stays on a longer cycle. Monthly reviews of every account are the runner-up; they reach the administrators sooner too, but managers who barely finish one review a year would face twelve, and rushed reviewers rubber-stamp.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it reviews administrators more often too. But managers who barely finish one yearly review would rubber-stamp twelve; frequency should follow the risk of each access.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because unused access is a clue. But use is not need; rarely used rights can be needed, and daily-used rights can be wrong.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because MFA protects admin accounts. But it strengthens sign-in, not the yearly check of whether each admin right is still needed.

tips: Eliminate: C reviews only what usage reports flag, though use is not need, and D adds MFA, which protects sign-in but does not check whether rights are still needed.
Final two: A beats B because review frequency should follow risk; monthly reviews of everything would swamp managers who barely finish one, inviting rubber-stamping.
Exam cue: more risk, more often. Schedule reviews of privileged and sensitive access more frequently than routine access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(7) (Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'privileged and sensitive access is reviewed more often' (notes 3.1.10 Access Reviews and Recertification). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A table tennis association is buying a system for its players' ranking records, and the vendor asks which access control model to configure. What should the access analyst establish FIRST?

options.A: Which model would protect the records most strictly
options.B: Which model the vendor's product supports most easily
options.C: Who should decide access to the records, and on which basis
options.D: How many staff will need access when the system launches

questions.key_concept: Choosing an access control model starts with who should decide access and on what basis, not with the strictest or easiest option.
questions.pre_read: Recall what separates the access control models from one another.
questions.correct_explanation: Choosing a model starts with who or what should decide access, and on what: the record owner, central labels, job roles, attributes or fixed rules. That answer, matched to the risk, points to the model. What the vendor's product supports most easily is the runner-up, a real constraint later, but letting the tool choose puts technology before the access decision it must carry out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because strict sounds safe. But the strictest model, mandatory control, is rigid and costly; the model should fit who decides and the risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: product support matters. But it comes after deciding how access should work; picking what is easiest to configure lets the tool set the rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because size affects effort. But account numbers do not say who should decide access; small and large systems can use any model.

tips: Eliminate: A picks the strictest model by default, though mandatory control is rigid and costly, and D counts accounts, which says nothing about who should decide.
Final two: C beats B because the access decision comes before the tool; what a product configures easily is checked afterward.
Exam cue: to choose an access control model, first ask who should decide and on what basis, then match the model to that and to the risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'choosing a model starts with who decides and on what basis' (notes 3.2.10 Choosing an Access Control Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'what'; option A reworded without 'is' or 'so'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A herbarium's quarterly access review lists its backup service account and its AI cataloging agent's identity, each with a named owner. Who should MOST appropriately confirm their access?

options.A: The administrators named in each account's setup record
options.B: The named owner of each account, for each right it holds
options.C: Nobody, since neither account signs in like a person
options.D: The AI agent's vendor, as the owner of the agent's model

questions.key_concept: Service accounts and AI agent identities are reviewed like staff accounts, with each one's named owner confirming its access.
questions.pre_read: Recall how access reviews treat accounts that no person signs in with.
questions.correct_explanation: Non-human identities go through the same reviews as people, and their named owners, who answer for what each one does, confirm whether its access is still needed. The administrators who created the accounts are the runner-up: they know how the accounts were set up, but building access is not owning it, and the creators would be confirming their own work.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the setup record names who built each account. But building is not owning; the named owner answers for its purpose and confirms its access.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because nobody signs in with them interactively. But service accounts and agents often hold broad, long-lived access that attackers target.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the agent's model. But the vendor does not own the herbarium's data or decide what its agent may reach.

tips: Eliminate: C skips non-human accounts, which often hold broad standing access, and D hands the decision to a vendor that does not own the herbarium's data.
Final two: B beats A because the named owner answers for each account's purpose; the administrators who built them would be checking their own work.
Exam cue: service accounts and AI agents are reviewed like people, and their named owner confirms each right.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(7) (Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'non-human identities are reviewed by their named owners like staff accounts' (notes 3.1.10 Access Reviews and Recertification). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: An AI scheduling agent's vendor asks a community choir for administrator rights over its whole email system, citing strong security certifications; the agent only books rooms. Which response should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Grant the calendar rights that room booking needs
options.B: Grant the administrator rights the vendor says it needs
options.C: Grant the administrator rights for a 30-day trial only
options.D: Refuse the agent and keep booking rooms by hand

questions.key_concept: AI agents get only the access their task needs, whatever the vendor's reputation; limiting how long excess access lasts does not limit what it reaches.
questions.pre_read: Compare what booking rooms requires with what the vendor is asking for.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI agent gets only the access its task needs, whoever made it. Room booking needs calendar rights, not administrator power over every mailbox; a manipulated or faulty agent with broad rights could read or send any email. A 30-day trial with administrator rights is the runner-up: it limits how long the excess lasts, but for that month the agent can still reach every mailbox.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certifications show a careful vendor. But a reputable agent can still be manipulated or faulty; access is sized to the task, not the vendor.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a trial limits how long. But for 30 days the agent holds power over every mailbox; access is sized to the task, not just the time.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no access means no risk. But it drops a useful tool when scoped calendar rights would let it book rooms safely.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the vendor's certifications instead of sizing access to the task, and D refuses a tool that scoped rights would make safe.
Final two: A beats C because scoping to calendar rights removes the excess power; a trial only shortens how long the agent holds it.
Exam cue: for AI agents, size access to the task, not to the vendor's reputation or a trial period: the least access that does the job.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an AI agent gets only the access its task needs, whatever the vendor's reputation' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A kite maker's designer leaves on good terms; procedure disables leavers on their last day, but the manager wants the account kept a month for its cloud files. Which action is BEST for the technician?

options.A: Move the files to the manager, then disable it on schedule
options.B: Keep it active a month, giving the manager a new password
options.C: Delete the account on the last day so nothing is left behind
options.D: Disable it now, days before the designer's last day

questions.key_concept: Disable a friendly leaver's account on the last day, and meet ongoing needs such as file access without keeping the account live.
questions.pre_read: Separate the account's timing from the manager's need for the designer's files.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure sets the timing, and for a friendly exit that is the last day: the account is disabled then, and the manager's real need, the design files, is met by moving them to the manager. Keeping the account live with a new password is the runner-up, since it meets the need too, but it leaves a leaver's account usable, with its actions untraceable to one person.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it gives the manager the files. But a live leaver account used by someone else hides who acts and stays open to misuse; move the files instead.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deletion feels thorough. But deleting can lose data and breaks the link between logs and the person; disable first, delete later under retention rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because early removal feels safe. But this is a friendly exit, and the procedure sets the last day; cutting access early only stops the designer finishing work.
