tips: Eliminate: C deletes the account, which loses data and breaks log links, and D cuts access early, though a friendly exit follows the last-day rule.
Final two: A beats B because moving the files meets the manager's need without leaving a leaver's account live under someone else's use.
Exam cue: for a leaver, disable on schedule and meet business needs another way, such as moving files to a new owner; never keep the account alive for them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.2 (Establish an Access Revoking Process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'disable a leaver on schedule and meet ongoing needs without keeping the account live' (notes 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded as 'X before Y' without a comma clause; distractor B given one; same key and teaching point. Word-tell sweep polish, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded to say the files are moved, matching the explanation and tips; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A hydroelectric dam operator's break-glass account, held by the system owner, has not been tested in two years; the runbook has the system administrator test it each quarter. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Report the missed tests to the system owner and wait for direction
options.B: Run the test the runbook sets, then reseal the credentials
options.C: Delete the account, since two years unused shows it is not needed
options.D: Share its credentials with every administrator named in the runbook

questions.key_concept: Break-glass accounts are tested on schedule so they work in an emergency; the person the runbook assigns runs the test.
questions.pre_read: Recall why emergency accounts are tested even though they are rarely used.
questions.correct_explanation: The runbook assigns the quarterly test to the system administrator, so the administrator runs it: an untested break-glass account may fail in the very emergency it exists for. Afterward the credentials are changed and resealed, since the test opened them. Reporting the missed tests to the system owner is the runner-up; the owner should hear of the gap, but the procedure already gives the administrator the task.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner should learn of the gap. But the runbook already makes the test the administrator's task; waiting leaves an untested emergency account.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it has sat unused. But a break-glass account is rarely used by design; it exists for when normal access fails.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it makes the account easy to reach. But break-glass credentials are held by few people and sealed, so every use is deliberate and alerted.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes an account meant to sit unused until an emergency, and D spreads credentials that should stay sealed and held by few.
Final two: B beats A because the runbook gives the administrator the test; the owner can be told, but the procedure already assigns the task.
Exam cue: when the procedure assigns a task to you, do it, even if an owner is named; escalate only what is outside your authority.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'break-glass accounts are tested regularly so they work when needed' (notes 3.2.12 Just-in-Time and Break-Glass Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An esports team's three AI agents, including one that answers public fan messages, share one service account for scheduling, video editing and replies. Which risk should the access analyst rate as MOST serious?

options.A: The shared account may hit the platform's rate limits sooner
options.B: The account's secret may expire for all three agents at once
options.C: A tricked fan-reply agent could use every agent's rights
options.D: Activity logs may not show which of the three agents acted

questions.key_concept: Each AI agent needs its own scoped identity; a shared account lets one tricked agent use every agent's rights.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a shared non-human account lets each agent reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Each agent should have its own identity scoped to its task. Here the fan-reply agent reads public messages, which can carry hidden instructions, and through the shared account a tricked agent could edit videos or change schedules too. Unclear logs are the runner-up: losing track of which agent acted is a real weakness, but the bigger harm is one exposed agent carrying every agent's rights.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because shared accounts do pool usage. But rate limits are an availability nuisance, not a route for an attacker to gain wider rights.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a shared secret is a single point of failure. But an expiry is fixed by renewing it; it hands nobody more access.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: shared accounts do blur who acted. But that hampers tracing after the harm; the greater risk is one tricked agent carrying every agent's rights.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are operational nuisances, rate limits and a shared expiry, that give nobody wider access.
Final two: C beats D because the public-facing agent is the likeliest to be tricked, and the shared account hands it every agent's rights; muddy logs matter, but after the harm.
Exam cue: give each workload or agent its own identity. A shared non-human account lets one compromise reach everything it can.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) NHI9 (NHI Reuse); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-4 (Identifier Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each workload or AI agent needs its own identity, never a shared one' (notes 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At a lifeboat charity, the IT team puts each new volunteer into a group matching their job, and volunteers cannot share files beyond those groups. Which model should the access analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Discretionary access control, because access is granted to groups
options.B: Role-based access control, because job decides group membership
options.C: Mandatory access control, because volunteers cannot share files
options.D: Rule-based access control, because one rule applies to every group

questions.key_concept: Job-based groups set centrally are role-based access control; being unable to share shows a non-discretionary model, not necessarily a mandatory one.
questions.pre_read: Find who places volunteers in groups, and on what basis.
questions.correct_explanation: Read for the decider: the IT team assigns each volunteer to a group by job, so the job decides access, which is role-based access control, and volunteers cannot hand out rights. Mandatory control is the runner-up, because volunteers cannot share files, but mandatory control decides by labels and clearances, and nothing here is labeled; being unable to share only shows the model is non-discretionary.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because groups also appear in owner sharing. But here the IT team, not a file owner, picks each group, and it picks by job.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: volunteers cannot pass on access. But mandatory control compares clearances with labels, and none appear; role-based control also stops users sharing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because group setup follows a standard process. But rule-based control applies one condition, such as hours, to everyone; here access differs by job.

tips: Eliminate: A treats groups as owner sharing, though the IT team picks them, and D needs one rule for everyone, while access here differs by job.
Final two: B beats C because job-based groups set by the organization are role-based; mandatory control needs labels and clearances, which the stem never mentions.
Exam cue: users who cannot share point to a non-discretionary model, not automatically mandatory. Look for labels and clearances before choosing mandatory control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'users who cannot share does not by itself mean mandatory access control' (notes 3.2.13 Access Model Scenarios: Worked Examples). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A rowing club is connecting an identity governance platform to create, change and remove staff accounts. Which source is BEST for the access analyst to set as authoritative for who works there?

options.A: The cloud directory, since it already holds every staff account
options.B: The human resources system, since it tracks every employee
options.C: Managers' emails telling IT who has joined or left their teams
options.D: The door badge system, since staff badge in each day

questions.key_concept: The human resources system is the trusted source that drives joiner, mover and leaver changes through IAM tools.
questions.pre_read: Recall how IAM tools connect, from the first record of a hire to the accounts.
questions.correct_explanation: Identity governance needs one trusted record of who works there, and that is the human resources system, where hires, moves and exits are formally recorded; it then drives account changes in the directory. The cloud directory is the runner-up because it holds every account, but it sits downstream: it shows accounts that exist, including ones that should not, not who is actually employed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it holds every staff account. But it is what the platform updates; using it as the source would treat leftover accounts as current staff.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because managers know their teams. But emails are informal, easy to fake and often forgotten; a formal record should trigger each change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because badges show who comes in. But badge records miss remote staff and track entry, not employment; they are another system to update.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on informal emails, which are no formal record, and D tracks building entry, not employment.
Final two: B beats A because the directory sits downstream of the employment record; it shows accounts that exist, not who still works there.
Exam cue: identity life cycle changes start from a trusted record, usually human resources, which then drives the directory and applications.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(1) (Account Management | Automated System Account Management); NIST SP 800-162 Section 3.2.3.1 (Confidence in Access Control Decisions: accurate and timely attributes from authoritative sources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'human resources is the trusted source that drives IAM tools' (notes 3.1.13 IAM Frameworks and Tools). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key now gives its reason with 'since', parallel to options A and D; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A bonsai nursery's bookings data owner approves a ticket giving a new booking clerk 'the same access as Jo', a clerk there for eight years. What should the help desk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Copy Jo's access to the clerk, as the owner has approved it
options.B: Ask the owner to approve the specific access the clerk needs
options.C: Grant Jo's access, then remove whatever the clerk does not use
options.D: Grant only the booking screens the analyst thinks the clerk needs

questions.key_concept: Access requests name the specific access a task needs; a 'same as a coworker' approval hides what is being granted.
questions.pre_read: Think about what an access request should state before anyone fulfills it.
questions.correct_explanation: A request names the exact access, the reason and how long. 'The same as Jo' approves an unknown bundle, which may include rights Jo gathered over eight years, so the analyst asks the owner to approve the specific access the clerk's work needs. Copying Jo's access on the approval is the runner-up: the owner did sign, but nobody can tell what they actually approved.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner did approve. But 'the same as Jo' hides what is granted, possibly rights Jo gathered over eight years; approval must name specific access.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because unused rights would be trimmed. But the extra access is live from day one, and trimming later rarely happens.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids copying. But the help desk fulfills approved access; deciding what the clerk needs is the owner's call.

tips: Eliminate: C grants everything and trims later, leaving extra access live, and D has the help desk decide access, which is the owner's call.
Final two: B beats A because an approval must name the specific access; 'the same as Jo' approves whatever Jo has collected, which nobody has checked.
Exam cue: 'same as a coworker' is not a specific request. Get the exact access approved by the owner before fulfilling.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.1 (Establish an Access Granting Process); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an access request names the specific access, not 'the same as a coworker'' (notes 3.1.14 Access Requests and Approvals). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Re-set in fix-up round 2 (setting was shared with cc_d1_114); cc_d3_105 now teaches trusted request sources, so this item alone keeps the copied-access lesson.

questions.question: A stamp museum's help desk technician is creating a guest account for a visiting consultant's three-month cataloging project. Who should MOST appropriately be the account's sponsor?

options.A: The consultant's own firm, which employs and vouches for them
options.B: The help desk technician who creates the guest account
options.C: The museum's collections manager who hired the consultant
options.D: The museum's security manager, who oversees all outside access

questions.key_concept: Each guest or contractor account needs an internal sponsor who requests the access, answers for it and confirms when it ends.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a sponsor does for an outside user's account.
questions.correct_explanation: A sponsor is an internal person who requests an outsider's access and answers for it, confirming it is still needed and ending it when the work ends. The collections manager who hired the consultant knows the project and its dates. The consultant's firm is the runner-up, because it vouches for its own staff, but it sits outside the museum and cannot answer for access to the museum's systems.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the firm vouches for who the consultant is. But a sponsor must be inside the museum, answering for the access and its end date.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because they set up the account. But creating an account is fulfillment; the sponsor must know the project and why the access exists.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because security oversees outside access. But the security manager does not know this project's needs or dates; the person who hired the consultant does.

tips: Eliminate: B only fulfills the request, and D oversees security without knowing this project; neither can say whether the consultant still needs access.
Final two: C beats A because a sponsor must be inside the museum to answer for the access; the consultant's firm can vouch for identity, not for the museum's access.
Exam cue: every outside account needs an internal sponsor, the person who brought the outsider in, requests their access and answers for its end.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-7 (External Personnel Security); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'every outside user has an internal sponsor who answers for their access' (notes 3.1.15 Third-Party, Guest and Federated Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A permit office's staff sometimes keep portal sessions open for 20 hours; the security manager wants each one ended 12 hours after sign-in, however active. Which setting should the system administrator apply as BEST?

options.A: A 12-hour overall timeout, counted from each sign-in
options.B: An inactivity timeout of 12 hours with no user activity
options.C: A screen lock after 15 idle minutes on each computer
options.D: Multifactor sign-in required at the start of every session

questions.key_concept: An overall session timeout ends a session a set time after sign-in, however active; an inactivity timeout needs idle time.
questions.pre_read: Recall the two kinds of session timeout and what triggers each.
questions.correct_explanation: An overall timeout ends a session a set time after sign-in, however active the user is, which is exactly the 12-hour cap the manager wants; NIST describes it beside the inactivity timeout. An inactivity timeout of 12 hours is the runner-up, but it ends only sessions left idle for 12 hours, so busy staff working for 20 hours would never be signed out.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it is a session timeout too. But it fires only after 12 idle hours; an active user's session would still run for 20 hours.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because idle locks protect unattended screens. But a 15-minute lock leaves the session itself running; staff unlock it and carry on for 20 hours.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because strong sign-in protects the start. But MFA does not limit how long the session lasts after that sign-in.

tips: Eliminate: C locks idle screens without ending the session, and D strengthens the sign-in but sets no limit on what follows it.
Final two: A beats B because only an overall timeout ends a busy session; an inactivity timeout waits for idleness that never comes.
Exam cue: an overall timeout is a fixed limit from sign-in, however active the user. An inactivity timeout ends a session after a period with no activity.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 5.2 (Reauthentication: an overall timeout limits session length after authentication and an inactivity timeout ends a session without activity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-12 (Session Termination)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an overall timeout ends a session a set time after sign-in, however active' (notes 3.1.16 Sessions, Timeouts and Reauthentication). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Identities and accounts
questions.question: A seed bank's IT team wants each new AI agent's account created only from a trusted record, as staff accounts come from human resources (HR) start records. Which trigger BEST fits?

options.A: A service desk ticket the agent's builder opens and approves
options.B: The vendor's email confirming the license is paid and active
options.C: Its first sign-in, which creates the account automatically
options.D: An approved inventory entry naming the agent's owner and purpose

questions.key_concept: Every identity, AI agents included, starts its life cycle from a trusted, approved record that names who answers for it.
questions.pre_read: Recall what starts each stage of the identity life cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: Each life cycle stage starts from a trusted record: an HR start record for staff and, for an AI agent, an approved inventory entry naming its human owner and purpose. That gives the account an accountable owner from day one. The builder's ticket is the runner-up, since tickets are the usual request path, but a builder who approves their own request gives no independent approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: tickets are the normal request path. But the builder both asks and approves, so nobody independent has agreed the agent should exist.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it comes from the supplier. But a license email proves a purchase, not that anyone inside approved the agent or owns it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it saves setup work. But an account created on first sign-in exists before any approval, owner or inventory record.

tips: Eliminate: B is an outside license notice, and C creates the account before anyone approves it; neither is a trusted internal record.
Final two: D beats A because the inventory entry is approved and names an owner; a ticket the builder approves for themselves has no independent check.
Exam cue: for any identity, human or AI, find the trusted record that starts its life cycle and names who answers for it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-4 (Identifier Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a trusted record triggers each stage of the life cycle, AI agents included' (notes 3.1.1 Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: option B reworded; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A hat maker's new access analyst reads that the 'order clerk' role bundles nine entitlements. Which item is MOST accurately one of those entitlements?

options.A: Permission to issue credit notes in the order system
options.B: The order clerk job title held in the human resources record
options.C: The clerk's password and authenticator app enrollment
options.D: The manager's approval recorded for the clerk's access

questions.key_concept: An entitlement is one specific permission in a system; a role bundles the entitlements a job needs.
questions.pre_read: Recall how roles and entitlements relate.
questions.correct_explanation: An entitlement is a specific permission in a system, such as issuing credit notes, and a role bundles the entitlements a job needs. The job title in the human resources record is the runner-up, because it decides which role a person receives, but it describes the person; it is not a permission the role grants.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the job title links a person to the role. But it describes the person; entitlements are the permissions the role grants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because credentials come with access. But they prove who is signing in; they grant no permission in the order system.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because approval is part of granting access. But an approval is a decision about access, not a permission itself.

tips: Eliminate: C is how the clerk proves who they are, and D is the decision to grant access; neither is a permission the role holds.
Final two: A beats B because an entitlement is a permission in a system; the job title only decides who receives the role.
Exam cue: roles are bundles; entitlements are the individual permissions inside them, each a specific action in a specific system.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a role groups the entitlements a job needs' (notes 3.1.2 Defining Roles and Entitlements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A cinema's new policy has every box-office clerk issue refunds from next month; the box-office manager owns the clerk role and approves its changes. What should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Have the role owner approve refund rights for each clerk separately
options.B: Add refunds to the clerk role once the role owner approves
options.C: Add refunds to the clerk role now, as the policy requires it
options.D: Let clerks use the supervisor's login for refunds at the desk

questions.key_concept: When a job changes for everyone who holds it, change the role through its owner, not with one-off grants.
questions.pre_read: Recall when a role itself should change.
questions.correct_explanation: When a job changes for everyone who holds it, the role changes, so access stays standard and reviewable; one-off grants are for one person's temporary need. The role owner approves the change and checks it for conflicts. Separate grants for each clerk are the runner-up, since the owner still approves them, but they scatter one-off rights that reviews must track person by person.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner does approve each grant. But the whole job changed, so separate grants scatter access that the role itself should carry.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the policy requires refunds. But a policy sets the duty; the role owner still approves the role's rights and checks for conflicts.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it needs no setup. But a shared login hides which clerk issued each refund.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the role without its owner's approval, and D shares a login so refunds cannot be traced.
Final two: B beats A because the job changed for every clerk; the role should carry the new right, not a pile of one-off grants.
Exam cue: when a job changes for everyone, change the role through its owner; one-off grants are for one person's temporary need.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'when the job changes for everyone, change the role through its owner' (notes 3.1.2 Defining Roles and Entitlements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): re-angled from one clerk's temporary need (the notes 3.1.2 example, cc_d3_034, cc_d3_088) to a role change for every holder; key letter unchanged.

questions.question: A credit bureau is hiring a mailroom assistant who gets no system access and a database administrator who will reach every consumer file. Which identity proofing plan should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: The same quick check of an emailed ID scan for both hires
options.B: The administrator's level of checks, applied to the assistant too
options.C: A criminal background check for the administrator, not identity checks
options.D: Stricter identity checks for the administrator than for the assistant

questions.key_concept: Identity proofing confirms a person is who they claim, and its strength should match the access at stake.
questions.pre_read: Recall what identity proofing proves and how its strength is chosen.
questions.correct_explanation: Identity proofing confirms a person is who they claim, and its strength should match the access at stake; NIST ties stronger evidence to higher assurance, so the administrator who can reach every consumer file gets stricter checks than an assistant with no system access. Giving both hires the administrator's checks is the runner-up, as it feels safest, but it spends effort where no access is at stake without making the risky hire any safer.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the administrator does need those checks. But the assistant gets no system access, so those checks add cost and delay without lowering risk; proofing strength follows access.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one process is simple. But an emailed scan is weak evidence, and the administrator's access needs stronger proof.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because powerful roles deserve screening. But a background check reviews the claimed person's history; it does not prove the applicant is that person, so it cannot replace identity proofing.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts weak emailed evidence for the administrator, and C swaps identity proofing for a background check, which screens a history without proving who the applicant is.
Final two: D beats B because proofing strength follows the access at stake; the assistant gets no system access, so the administrator's checks would add cost without cutting risk.
Exam cue: proofing asks whether this is really them, screening asks whether to trust them; set proofing strength by the access each person will get.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-12 (Identity Proofing); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-3 (Personnel Screening)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'proofing checks evidence more strictly for riskier access' (notes 3.1.3 Provisioning and Identity Proofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): option C names the administrator so the stem's high-risk hire is not on the key alone. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): option B is now an over-control distractor (the same in-person checks for both), not a second negation. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): stem states the assistant's lack of system access; B is now the over-control runner-up (it names the assistant too, so that stem word is not on the key alone), and the tips name it.

questions.question: A kayak maker's help desk technician says a stolen fingerprint template does more lasting harm than a stolen password. Which reply from the access analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree, as a finger cannot be replaced if its template leaks
options.B: Disagree, as a template is just numbers, not an image
options.C: Disagree, as a fingerprint, unlike a password, stays secret if leaked
options.D: Agree, as a fingerprint is something you have, like a smart card

questions.key_concept: A copied body trait cannot be changed like a password, so biometric data needs strong protection and pairing with another factor.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes each authentication factor category different after theft.
questions.correct_explanation: A fingerprint is something you are, and unlike a password it cannot simply be changed once copied, so stolen biometric data can stay useful to an attacker; NIST notes revoking biometrics is possible only with schemes of limited availability. That a template is only numbers is the runner-up, because it is not a picture, but it is still unique to the person and still matches them.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: templates are not images. But they are still unique to the person, can still be matched, and cannot be changed like a password.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because biometrics feel private. But fingerprints are not secrets; people leave them on everything they touch, so a leaked template adds to what an attacker can already gather.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the conclusion is right. But a fingerprint is something you are; a smart card is something you have.

tips: Eliminate: C treats fingerprints as secrets, though people leave them everywhere, and D puts fingerprints in the wrong factor category.
Final two: A beats B because a template, numbers or not, still matches the person and cannot be reissued; that is what makes the theft lasting.
Exam cue: passwords and cards can be replaced after theft; body traits cannot, so protect biometric data and pair it with another factor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.3 (Use of Biometrics: biometric characteristics are not secrets, and schemes to revoke them have limited availability); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a copied trait cannot be changed' (notes 3.1.4 Authentication Factors and MFA). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): stem no longer states the reason the key gives. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): option A uses 'as' like the other options. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): option C now argues against the technician's point (a leak exposes no secret) and names a password too, so that stem word is not on the key alone, the misconception SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.3 refutes. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded with 'if' (shared with option C); same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A bowling alley chain's system administrator added number matching to staff push approvals and now calls sign-in phishing-resistant. Which assessment should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: Not phishing-resistant, as a fake page can show the real number
options.B: Phishing-resistant, as tired staff can no longer approve blindly
options.C: Not phishing-resistant, as push approvals are not true MFA
options.D: Phishing-resistant, as the number ties each sign-in to the real site

questions.key_concept: Number matching stops blind approvals, but only methods bound to the real site, such as passkeys, are phishing-resistant.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes a sign-in method phishing-resistant.
questions.correct_explanation: Number matching stops staff approving prompts they did not start, but a fake login page can relay the password, receive the number from the real site and show it, so the user approves the attacker. NIST counts out-of-band methods as not phishing-resistant. Ending blind approvals is the runner-up: a real gain against prompt flooding, but it still relies on the user spotting the fake page.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it does stop blind approvals of prompt floods. But a fake page can show the real number, so the user approves the attacker.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because push feels weaker than other methods. But a password plus approval on an enrolled phone is still two factors.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the number links screen and phone. But only site-bound methods such as passkeys check the site's address.

tips: Eliminate: C wrongly says push is not MFA, and D gives number matching the site binding that only passkeys and security keys have.
Final two: A beats B because ending blind approvals is not phishing resistance; a relaying fake page can pass the real number to the user.
Exam cue: phishing-resistant means the method itself checks the real site; anything a person reads, types or approves can be relayed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.5 (Phishing Resistance: manually entered codes can be relayed by an impostor verifier); NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.1.3 (Out-of-Band Devices: out-of-band authentication is not phishing-resistant)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'number matching stops blind approvals but is not phishing-resistant' (notes 3.1.5 Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): option D carries 'number' too, so the word is not on the key alone. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): the claim is now made by the system administrator, not the IT manager, so the speaker's role does not predict the key.

questions.question: A tea importer's security manager owns a password standard that has the help desk force resets on proof of compromise. Three staff passwords leak in a breach; what should the help desk do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the security manager to approve resets for the three staff
options.B: Force resets of the three passwords, then tell the staff why
options.C: Leave the passwords, as current guidance bans forced changes
options.D: Force every employee to reset their password this week

questions.key_concept: No scheduled password changes, but a forced change whenever there is evidence a password is compromised.
questions.pre_read: Recall when current guidance requires a password change.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST advises against scheduled password changes but requires a change when there is evidence of compromise, and this standard gives that task to the help desk. Forcing resets of the three leaked passwords closes the exposure. Asking the security manager is the runner-up: the manager owns the standard, but it already authorizes these resets, so waiting only leaves leaked passwords working.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the manager owns the standard. But the standard already gives compromise resets to the help desk, so asking first only delays them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because NIST discourages routine changes. But it still requires a change when a password is known to be compromised.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems thorough. But only three passwords leaked; resetting everyone disrupts staff without removing more risk.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses scheduled changes with a change after compromise, and D resets everyone when only three passwords leaked.
Final two: B beats A because the owner's standard already assigns compromise resets to the help desk; no fresh approval is needed.
Exam cue: no scheduled password changes, but always a change on evidence of compromise; when the procedure gives you the task, do it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.1.1.2 (Password Verifiers: no periodic changes, but a forced change on evidence of compromise); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5(1) (Authenticator Management | Password-based Authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'force a change on evidence of compromise, never on a schedule' (notes 3.1.6 Passwords and Modern Password Standards). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; same key and teaching point. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded as 'X, then Y' without an -ing clause; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: An access analyst is explaining a vineyard's single sign-on (SSO), which uses Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML), to a new technician. What does the ordering app MOST accurately receive at sign-in?

options.A: The staff member's password, passed on by the identity provider
options.B: A signed note from the identity provider naming who signed in
options.C: An OAuth 2.0 access token that proves who the user is
options.D: A one-time code that the staff member also types into the app

questions.key_concept: In SAML single sign-on, the identity provider sends the app a signed assertion of who signed in; the app never sees the password.
questions.pre_read: Recall what an identity provider sends an application in single sign-on.
questions.correct_explanation: With SAML, the identity provider checks the user and sends the app a signed assertion saying who signed in, often with a few attributes; the app trusts the signature and never sees the password. An OAuth 2.0 access token is the runner-up, since tokens also travel in sign-in flows, but OAuth grants limited access to data and does not itself prove who the user is.

wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: tokens appear in many sign-in flows. But an OAuth 2.0 access token grants limited access, proves no identity, and SAML sends an assertion.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the app must trust the sign-in somehow. But in SSO only the identity provider checks the password; apps never receive it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because codes add a factor. But any second factor is checked once at the identity provider, not typed again into each app.

tips: Eliminate: A would hand every app the password SSO keeps at the identity provider, and D moves the factor check away from the identity provider.
Final two: B beats C because SAML sends a signed assertion of identity; an OAuth 2.0 access token grants access but proves nobody's identity.
Exam cue: in SSO and federation, the identity provider vouches with a signed message; the app trusts the signature, never a password.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63C-4 (Federation and Assertions)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the identity provider vouches to the app, which never sees the password' (notes 3.1.7 Single Sign-On and Federation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): notes 3.1.7 how_it_works now teaches the signed SAML assertion and that an OAuth 2.0 access token does not prove identity.

questions.question: A science museum guide moves to the gift shop, whose manager approved the new access. Whom should the access analyst MOST appropriately ask to confirm which tour-booking rights served only the old job?

options.A: The guide's former manager, who ran the guide's old team
options.B: The gift shop manager, who approved the guide's new access
options.C: The guide, who knows best which rights they still need
options.D: The help desk, which can see which rights the guide used

questions.key_concept: In a move, the new manager approves new access and the former manager confirms which old rights can go.
questions.pre_read: Recall who decides what a mover keeps and what they lose.
questions.correct_explanation: In a move, the new manager approves what the new job needs, and the former manager confirms which old-job rights can now go, since they know what the tour role required. The gift shop manager is the runner-up, being accountable for the guide now, but they judge the shop job's needs, not which tour-booking rights served only the old job.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: they are now accountable for the guide. But they approve what the shop job needs; which tour-booking rights only the old job used is the former manager's call.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the guide knows their own work. But nobody confirms their own access; that is a conflict of interest.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because usage reports seem objective. But usage shows what was used, not what is needed, and the help desk owns no access decision.

tips: Eliminate: C has the guide vouch for their own access, and D treats usage as need and gives the decision to the help desk.
Final two: A beats B because the former manager knows what the tour role required; the new manager can judge only the new job.
Exam cue: in a move, the new manager approves what comes; the former manager confirms what goes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-5 (Personnel Transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the new manager approves new access; the old manager confirms what can go' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): stem asks which rights served only the old job; option A shortened. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): option A no longer echoes the stem's tour-booking rights.

questions.question: In a seaplane charter's quarterly access review, the booking system's data owner finds their own administrator account among the lines they must confirm. What is the access analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Let the owner confirm it, as they own the booking system
options.B: Route that line to the owner's own manager, who confirms it
options.C: Skip the line, as owners' accounts sit outside the review
options.D: Confirm the line themselves, since the analyst runs the review

questions.key_concept: Nobody confirms their own access in a review; that line goes to someone accountable for the person, such as their manager.
questions.pre_read: Recall who may confirm a line in an access review.
questions.correct_explanation: Nobody confirms their own access, so the line for the owner's administrator account goes to someone accountable for the owner, usually their own manager. Confirming it themselves is the runner-up, because the analyst is independent of the account, but running a review is not being accountable for the access; the analyst gathers decisions rather than making them.

wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the analyst is independent of the account. But running the review does not make them accountable for whether the owner needs admin rights.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner decides access to the system. But confirming one's own account is a conflict of interest.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owners are senior and trusted. But privileged accounts are exactly the lines a review must cover.

tips: Eliminate: A lets the owner confirm their own access, and C exempts an administrator account from the review.
Final two: B beats D because confirmation needs someone accountable for the owner's access; the analyst runs the process but decides nothing.
Exam cue: in any access review, find the line where reviewer and reviewed are the same person and send it one level up.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(7) (Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the reviewer is never the person whose access is reviewed' (notes 3.1.10 Access Reviews and Recertification). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A glider club's leaver procedure has the help desk technician delete accounts 60 days after disabling them. A departed coach's account, its files already moved, reaches day 60 today; what is the technician's BEST action?

options.A: Delete the account and note the deletion on the ticket
options.B: Keep it disabled for good, in case logs or audits need it
options.C: Ask the security manager to approve deleting the account
options.D: Re-enable it briefly and check that nothing is left behind

questions.key_concept: When the leaver procedure assigns a disabled account's deletion and sets its date, the technician deletes it on that date without seeking fresh approval.
questions.pre_read: Recall the order of disabling and deleting a leaver's account.
questions.correct_explanation: Disable first and delete later is the leaver rule: the account was disabled at exit, its files have moved, and the procedure sets day 60 for deletion and gives that step to the technician, so the technician deletes it and records it. Asking the security manager is the runner-up, as deletion feels final, but the procedure already authorizes it, and holding the account only keeps another dormant identity around.

wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: deletion cannot be undone. But the procedure already authorizes deletion on day 60, so a fresh approval only delays it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deletion feels risky for investigations. But the 60 days were the safety period for tracing logs; after that, a dormant identity could be re-enabled and misused.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it double-checks the files. But re-enabling a leaver's account reopens access, and the files were already moved.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps a dormant account forever, and D reopens a leaver's access to check files already moved.
Final two: A beats C because the procedure sets day 60 for deletion and assigns it to the technician; asking again adds delay, not control.
Exam cue: when the procedure names the step, the person and the date, carry it out and record it; that is where 'disable now, delete later' ends.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'disable first and delete later under the retention policy' (notes 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): option A no longer echoes the stem's procedure and day 90. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): explanation of B now agrees with notes 3.1.11 on why accounts are disabled before deletion. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): day 60 instead of 90 and a key_concept on carrying out an assigned, dated step, so the item no longer retells cc_d3_054; explanation of B no longer overstates a disabled account's risk. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: options B and D reworded ('or' added to B; D given the key's two-step form); same key and teaching point.

questions.question: An e-bike maker's developer pushed the AI translation service's application programming interface (API) key to a public repository, then deleted the commit within an hour. Which assessment should the access analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: The leak is closed, since the commit no longer shows the key
options.B: The key works for anyone who copied it until it is revoked
options.C: The risk is low, as the key was public under an hour
options.D: The key is safe once the repository's history is rewritten too

questions.key_concept: Deleting a leaked secret does not revoke it; it stays usable until its owner revokes and replaces it.
questions.pre_read: Recall what ends the risk from a leaked secret.
questions.correct_explanation: Deleting a secret from code or chat does not revoke it: automated scanners can copy keys from public repositories within minutes, and a copied key keeps working until its owner revokes and replaces it. Rewriting the repository's history is the runner-up, since it removes every trace there, but copies already taken still work; only rotation ends them.

wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: rewriting history removes the key from the repository. But copies taken before that still work until the key is revoked and replaced.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the key is no longer visible. But any copy already taken still works; hiding the commit does not revoke it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the window was short. But automated scanners can harvest public keys within minutes, so an hour is plenty.

tips: Eliminate: A treats hiding the commit as revoking the key, and C assumes an hour is too short for anyone to copy it.
Final two: B beats D because copies taken before the cleanup still work; only revoking and replacing the key ends them.
Exam cue: a leaked secret stays dangerous until it is rotated; deleting the post or file only hides it.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) NHI2 (Secret Leakage); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'deleting a leaked secret from chat or code does not revoke it' (notes 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A pottery manufacturer's access analyst wants a recognized, free guide for deciding how strong proofing and sign-in must be for each of its online services. Which source BEST fits?

options.A: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, the incident response recommendations
options.B: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, with its identification and authentication controls
options.C: NIST SP 800-63-4, the Digital Identity Guidelines
options.D: FIRST CVSS v4.0, the vulnerability scoring standard

questions.key_concept: NIST SP 800-63-4 is the identity framework that sets assurance levels for proofing, authentication and federation, chosen for each service by risk.
questions.pre_read: Recall which published frameworks guide identity and access practice.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-63-4, the Digital Identity Guidelines, is built for this decision: organizations choose an assurance level for proofing, authentication and federation for each service, based on risk, and each level carries its own requirements. NIST SP 800-53 is the runner-up, since its identification and authentication controls require users to sign in, but it lists controls to apply rather than sizing how strong proofing and sign-in must be.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: its identification and authentication controls do require sign-in. But it is a control catalog; the assurance levels that size proofing and sign-in come from SP 800-63-4.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because incidents often involve stolen accounts. But SP 800-61 guides incident response, not how strong proofing or sign-in must be.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it rates how serious things are. But CVSS scores software vulnerabilities; it says nothing about checking users.

tips: Eliminate: A guides incident response and D scores vulnerabilities; neither sets how strongly to prove or check identity.
Final two: C beats B because SP 800-63-4 sets assurance levels for proofing and sign-in; SP 800-53 lists controls without sizing their strength.
Exam cue: for how strongly to prove identity or authenticate, think NIST SP 800-63-4 and its assurance levels; for which controls to have, think SP 800-53.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63-4 Section 1.2 (How to Use This Suite of SPs: organizations select an assurance level for identity proofing, authentication and federation for each service based on risk); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'frameworks set out good practice, such as the NIST identity guidelines' (notes 3.1.13 IAM Frameworks and Tools). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ticket asks for 'access to the finance share' for a new accountant, naming no folders, rights or end date. Procedure requires all three before routing; what should the help desk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Return it so the requester can add the missing details
options.B: Send it to the finance data owner to decide what to grant
options.C: Grant read access to the whole share as a safe default
options.D: Grant full rights now and trim them once the work is clearer

questions.key_concept: A valid access request names the exact access, the reason and how long it is needed before anyone approves it.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a complete access request contains.
questions.correct_explanation: A request must name the exact access, the reason and how long it is needed, and this procedure will not route one without its folders, rights and end date. Returning it gets a specific request the owner can approve. Sending it straight to the finance data owner is the runner-up, since the owner approves finance access, but the procedure routes only complete requests, and the requester is the one who knows what the job needs.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the owner does approve finance access. But this procedure routes only complete requests, and the requester, who knows the job, names the folders, rights and end date.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because read access seems harmless. But a whole share may hold data the accountant has no need to see.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids delay. But broad access is live from day one, and trimming later rarely happens.

tips: Eliminate: C grants a whole share by default, and D grants everything now and trims later.
Final two: A beats B because the procedure routes only complete requests; the requester fills in the folders, rights and end date before the owner approves.
Exam cue: a valid access request names what, why and for how long; fix the request before anyone approves or grants it.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.1 (Establish an Access Granting Process); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the requester names the exact access, the reason and how long it is needed' (notes 3.1.14 Access Requests and Approvals). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): option A no longer echoes 'all three' and is no longer the shortest. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): key rests on the procedure's routing rule, not on owners being unable to approve an unspecified request (consistent with cc_d3_128).

questions.question: A marine survey firm's quarterly access review covers 300 staff accounts, and its security manager proposes leaving out 40 contractor guest accounts, all with contract end dates. What should the access analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Have sponsors review the guest accounts yearly, as end dates exist
options.B: Leave them out, as the contractors' firms manage their staff
options.C: Ask each contractor to confirm they still need the account
options.D: Include the guest accounts, with sponsors confirming each one

questions.key_concept: Guest and contractor accounts are reviewed like staff accounts, confirmed by their internal sponsors; end dates are only a backstop.
questions.pre_read: Recall how outside users' accounts are kept in check.
questions.correct_explanation: Guest and contractor accounts sit on the firm's own systems, so they belong in every access review, confirmed by the internal sponsor who answers for them. End dates help, but people finish early or change roles. Reviewing them yearly is the runner-up, because end dates already cap exposure, but a contractor who leaves mid-contract would keep access for months.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: sponsors are right and end dates cap exposure. But contractors leave before them, and a yearly check leaves that access open for months.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the firms employ the contractors. But the access is to this firm's systems, so its own sponsors must answer for it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because contractors know their own work. But nobody confirms their own access; the sponsor decides.

tips: Eliminate: B hands the decision to outside firms, and C has each contractor vouch for their own access.
Final two: D beats A because people leave before contracts end; quarterly sponsor checks catch that, while a yearly check leaves access open for months.
Exam cue: outside users are reviewed like staff, by their internal sponsor; an end date is a backstop, not a review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-7 (External Personnel Security); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'guest access is time-limited and included in access reviews' (notes 3.1.15 Third-Party, Guest and Federated Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): runner-up A also names sponsors, so the choice turns on review frequency. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): the proposal now comes from the security manager, not the IT manager, so the speaker's role does not predict the key.

questions.question: An auction house's AI filing agent, with read and write permissions on a cloud storage bucket, saves edits but is refused when deleting old drafts. Which explanation from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: Write permission includes deleting, so the system is at fault
options.B: The agent's sign-in had lapsed before it tried the delete
options.C: Accounting refused it, as the audit log records every action
options.D: Delete is a separate permission the agent was never given

questions.key_concept: Permissions are granted action by action: a person or AI agent holding read and write can still be refused a delete it was never given.
questions.pre_read: Recall how a system decides whether a subject may perform an action.
questions.correct_explanation: Logical access controls decide each action separately: cloud storage buckets, like Windows file permissions, grant delete as its own permission, and anything not explicitly allowed is refused. The agent holds read and write only, so its delete request fails. Write including delete is the runner-up, since some systems, such as Linux folders, do work that way, but cloud storage buckets do not, so the system worked as set.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: on some systems, such as Linux folders, write does allow deleting. But cloud storage buckets grant delete as its own permission, so the system worked as set.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a lapsed sign-in does cause refusals. But the agent is still saving edits, so it is signed in; the refusal is about what it may do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the refusal shows up in the log. But accounting only records each decision; the permissions, through authorization, allow or refuse the action.

tips: Eliminate: B blames sign-in, though the agent is still saving edits, and C gives the audit log a blocking role; accounting records decisions but makes none.
Final two: D beats A because cloud storage buckets grant delete on its own; read and write do not include it, so the system worked as set.
Exam cue: when a subject can do some actions but is refused another, check whether that exact action was granted; one right does not imply the next.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'anything not explicitly allowed is refused' (notes 3.2.1 Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): explanations no longer state that write and delete are separate in every system (on POSIX systems, folder write permission allows deletion). Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): arguable owner-only option C replaced with the accounting-blocks-actions misconception; A is now the runner-up. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): stem names the system (a cloud storage bucket) and that the agent still saves edits, so the case against A is no longer circular; B is now the lapsed-sign-in misconception instead of an absolute; key_concept and Exam cue no longer copy cc_d3_060.

questions.question: A dog show organizer's booking website runs its web server under a full administrator account, though the server only serves pages and writes one log folder. Which change should the system administrator make as BEST?

options.A: Add multifactor sign-in to the admin account the server uses
options.B: Run it under a dedicated account limited to the server's tasks
options.C: Run it under a named administrator's personal account
options.D: Run it under a standard user account with no admin rights

questions.key_concept: Least privilege applies to processes as well as people: each runs with only the rights its task needs.
questions.pre_read: Recall how least privilege applies to software services.
questions.correct_explanation: Least privilege applies to processes as well as people: the web server only serves pages and writes one log folder, so a dedicated account limited to those tasks means a software flaw gives an attacker little. A standard user account is the runner-up, as dropping admin rights is a real gain, but an ordinary user can still reach far more than the server needs, such as shared folders.

wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: removing admin rights does shrink the damage. But a standard user can still reach shared files and settings the server never uses; least privilege fits the task.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because MFA protects accounts. But services do not sign in interactively, and MFA would not shrink the rights an attacker inherits.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it makes the account traceable. But it gives the service a person's rights and ties it to a human login.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens sign-in without cutting rights, and C runs a service on a person's admin account.
Final two: B beats D because non-admin is not the same as least privilege; the server needs to serve pages and write one log folder, and a standard user can reach far more.
Exam cue: for any process, ask what the least is that it can run with; 'not admin' is a start, not the answer.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'start with no access and add only what the task requires' (notes 3.2.2 Least Privilege and Need to Know). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): option B shortened to remove a length cue. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): runner-up D is now a process-specific need (the server writes files), not monitoring, which cc_d3_104 and cc_d3_068 already teach; option A reworded so A and D no longer share an opener. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): runner-up D is now 'a standard user account' (non-admin is not least privilege), not an option the stem refutes, so the item no longer retells cc_d3_012 and cc_d3_021. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'those'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A newspaper's printing plant needs two operators to approve any press configuration change. The press's system owner asks whether its emergency stop should need two operators too; what should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Require two operators for the stop, as for config changes
options.B: Require a supervisor's approval before any stop takes effect
options.C: Let any single operator stop the press with no second approval
options.D: Keep two operators for the stop, both posted beside the press

questions.key_concept: Two-person control suits deliberate high-impact changes; actions that protect people, such as an emergency stop, must work for one person at once.
questions.pre_read: Recall where two-person control fits and where people's safety comes first.
questions.correct_explanation: Two-person control suits deliberate, high-impact changes, but an emergency stop exists to protect people in seconds, so any single operator must be able to use it without waiting for anyone. Keeping two operators posted beside the press is the runner-up, as it keeps the control and puts both close, but in an emergency the second person may be busy, hurt or away.

wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it keeps both operators close by. But a second person may be away or hurt in an emergency, and any delay can cost lives.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because consistent rules seem safer. But dual control is for deliberate changes; a safety stop must work in seconds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because supervisors oversee the press. But waiting for approval delays the stop while people are in danger.

tips: Eliminate: A applies the change rule to an emergency, and B makes the stop wait for a supervisor; both delay a safety action.
Final two: C beats D because people's safety cannot depend on a second person being free; keep dual control for changes and leave the stop to anyone.
Exam cue: human safety comes first; controls that add a second person belong on deliberate changes, never on the action that protects lives.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(2) (Access Enforcement | Dual Authorization); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 2.4 (Comparing OT and IT System Security: human safety is paramount, followed by protection of the process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'two-person control requires two people to act together on a sensitive task' (notes 3.2.3 Separation of Duties and Two-Person Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sailcloth mill's scan finds nine local administrator accounts on servers missing from the vault's inventory, and procedure has the system administrator bring such accounts under the vault. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Remove all nine, as the vaulted named accounts suffice
options.B: Leave them off the inventory, as built-in accounts are exempt
options.C: Disable all nine at once until their owners come forward
options.D: Add the nine accounts to the inventory, then vault their passwords

questions.key_concept: Privileged access management starts with an inventory of every privileged account, built-in ones included, each with an owner.
questions.pre_read: Recall the first step in managing privileged accounts.
questions.correct_explanation: Privileged access management starts with an inventory: every privileged account, built-in ones included, gets an owner, and its password goes into the vault, where it is rotated and each use is logged. The procedure gives this to the administrator, and the inventory entry names each account's owner. Disabling all nine is the runner-up, as it cuts exposure fast, but unknown accounts may run services, and nothing shows misuse.

wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: disabling cuts exposure quickly. But unknown accounts may run services, and the procedure says to bring them under the vault, not switch them off blind.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because named admin accounts exist. But removing unknown accounts unchecked can break services that depend on them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because built-in accounts come with the server. But they hold full rights, so they are among the first a vault must cover.

tips: Eliminate: A removes accounts nobody has checked, and B exempts built-in accounts that hold full rights.
Final two: D beats C because the procedure is to bring the accounts under the vault; disabling blind may break services and still leaves them unowned.
Exam cue: you cannot protect privileged accounts you have not listed; inventory and owner first, then the vault.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'inventory every privileged account, including built-in, service and cloud console accounts' (notes 3.2.4 Privileged Access Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and' or 'owner'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: At a puppet theater using discretionary access control, the coordinator who created the volunteers folder has left, and requests to join it go unanswered. What should the help desk technician do FIRST?

options.A: Take ownership and approve the requests themselves
options.B: Open the folder to all staff so volunteer work can carry on
options.C: Ask the coordinator's manager to name a new folder owner
options.D: Move the folder under mandatory access control labels

questions.key_concept: Under discretionary access control the owner decides who gets in; when the owner leaves, an accountable person must name a new owner.
questions.pre_read: Recall who decides access under discretionary access control.
questions.correct_explanation: Under discretionary access control the owner decides who gets in, so an owner who has left leaves nobody entitled to decide. The coordinator's manager, accountable for that work, should name a new owner. Taking ownership is the runner-up, because the help desk can do it technically, but then the help desk would be deciding access to data it does not own.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the help desk can technically take ownership. But it would then decide who sees the volunteers' data, which is the business's call.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it unblocks the work. But opening volunteers' personal data to everyone is oversharing, the main weakness of DAC.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes owner choice. But changing the model for one folder is a large change that leaves the real gap, a missing owner.

tips: Eliminate: B overshares the folder to everyone, and D swaps the whole access model to fix one missing owner.
Final two: C beats A because someone accountable for the work must hold the owner role; a help desk that takes it ends up deciding access it does not own.
Exam cue: in DAC, the owner decides; when the owner is gone, get a new owner named rather than deciding yourself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the owner sets permissions on their own files' (notes 3.2.5 Discretionary Access Control (DAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At a space agency test center using mandatory access control, where the security manager sets labels, a Secret-cleared analyst finds Secret test data in a report labeled Confidential. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Relabel the report Secret, as the analyst holds Secret clearance
options.B: Remove the report to keep lower-cleared staff from seeing it
options.C: Leave the label as it is and alert the security manager
options.D: Copy the data to a new Secret file, telling the security manager

questions.key_concept: Under mandatory access control, users never change labels, even on their own files; they report errors to the authority that sets them.
questions.pre_read: Recall who may change labels under mandatory access control.
questions.correct_explanation: Under mandatory access control the system trusts each object's label, so a Secret report labeled Confidential is open to anyone cleared to Confidential. Users cannot change labels, even when cleared higher; the security manager, who sets them, must correct it. Relabeling it is the runner-up, because the analyst knows the right level, but MAC keeps labels in central hands.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the analyst knows the correct level. But under MAC only the central authority changes labels, whatever a user's clearance.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it closes the exposure. But it destroys a classified record and its evidence, and records are not the analyst's to remove.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it informs the security manager. But copying spreads the data, and the original stays open to Confidential-cleared staff meanwhile.

tips: Eliminate: B removes a classified record the analyst does not control, and D spreads the data while the mislabeled original stays open.
Final two: C beats A because MAC lets only the central authority change labels; a user relabeling, even correctly, breaks that control.
Exam cue: in MAC, users never change labels or clearances; report errors to the authority that sets them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-16 (Security and Privacy Attributes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'users cannot change labels, even on their own files' (notes 3.2.6 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: 'so' taken off option B; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: In a weather service's role-based access control system, team leads add anyone to their team's role unapproved, and one added a friend from payroll. Which change should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Let staff choose their own roles, approved by any team lead
options.B: Remove the friend and remind leads to add just their own staff
options.C: Replace the roles with each file owner's own sharing choices
options.D: Route each role assignment through the role owner's approval

questions.key_concept: Role-based access control is non-discretionary: the organization assigns roles through an approved process, not at a lead's choice.
questions.pre_read: Recall who decides role membership in role-based access control.
questions.correct_explanation: Role-based access control is non-discretionary: the organization decides role membership through an approved process, usually the role owner's approval, so a lead cannot add whoever they like. Removing the friend and reminding leads is the runner-up, since it fixes this case, but leads could still add anyone tomorrow; the assignment step itself needs the control.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it removes the friend's access now. But leads could still add anyone tomorrow, so the gap in the assignment process stays open.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because staff know their work. But choosing your own role defeats role-based control, and any lead's approval is not the role owner's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owners know their data. But owner sharing is discretionary control, the looser model this problem already resembles.

tips: Eliminate: A lets staff pick their own roles, and C swaps roles for owner sharing; both make access more discretionary.
Final two: D beats B because the flaw is the unapproved assignment step; removing one friend leaves every lead free to do it again.
Exam cue: in role-based control the organization assigns roles through an approved process; nobody adds people to roles at will.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the organization sets role membership through an approved process' (notes 3.2.7 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A historic house trust's attribute-based policy opens loan records only to Collections staff, for Active records, during opening hours. Which condition should the access analyst document as MOST accurately an environment attribute?

options.A: The staff member's department being Collections
options.B: The loan record's status being Active
options.C: The request arriving during opening hours
options.D: The action requested being to open a record

questions.key_concept: Attribute-based access control weighs subject, object, action and environment attributes; environment attributes describe the moment, such as time.
questions.pre_read: Recall the kinds of attributes an attribute-based policy checks.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute-based access control checks attributes of the subject, the object, the action and the environment. Environment attributes describe conditions of the request itself, such as time or location, independent of who asks and what they ask for, so opening hours is the environment attribute. The record's Active status is the runner-up, because it also changes over time, but it describes the object.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: status changes over time too. But it describes the record being requested, which makes it an object attribute.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is checked on every request. But department describes the person asking, a subject attribute.
