wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the policy names the action. But opening a record is the action itself, a separate attribute type.

tips: Eliminate: A describes the person asking and D the action asked for; neither describes the conditions of the moment.
Final two: C beats B because environment attributes describe the moment of the request; the record's status describes the record.
Exam cue: subject is who asks, object is what is asked for, action is what they want to do, environment is when, where or how.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-162 Section 1.4 (Notes on Terminology: environment conditions, such as time and location, are independent of subject and object); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(13) (Access Enforcement | Attribute-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'environment attributes describe the moment, such as time or device health' (notes 3.2.8 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A change record approved by the finance director, who owns the after-hours ledger rule, has the access analyst remove its year-end evening exception when close ends. Close ended yesterday; what should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the finance director to approve removing the exception
options.B: Delete the evening exception so the after-hours block applies again
options.C: Keep the exception in case finance needs to work late again
options.D: Switch off the whole after-hours rule, since year-end close is over

questions.key_concept: A rule's exception covers only the people and period that need it, then ends as its approval set out.
questions.pre_read: Recall how exceptions to an access rule should end.
questions.correct_explanation: Exceptions to a rule cover only the people and period that need them, then end. The change record, approved by the rule's owner, already tells the analyst to remove this one when close ends, so deleting it restores the block. Asking the finance director is the runner-up, since they own the rule, but they approved the removal in advance; asking again keeps evening access open longer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the director owns the rule. But the approved change record already sets the removal, so asking again only keeps evening access open longer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because late work may recur. But an exception left in place becomes a standing gap; a new need gets a new approval.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the exception and rule seem linked. But the block itself stays; only the time-limited exception ends.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps a time-limited exception open-ended, and D removes the whole rule instead of the exception.
Final two: B beats A because the owner already approved the removal in the change record; the step is the analyst's to carry out.
Exam cue: an approved exception has an end; when the record assigns its removal to you, remove it on time.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an exception the rule's owner approves covers only the person, place and period that need it, then expires' (notes 3.2.9 Rule-Based Access Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. questions.question: A food rescue charity has three stable job types and no system holding volunteers' other details, and a vendor proposes attribute-based access control on 40 attributes. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Attribute-based access control, as more attributes give finer control
options.B: Role-based access control, with one role for each kind of task
options.C: Mandatory access control, as donor data is highly sensitive
options.D: Discretionary access control, letting each record's creator share it

questions.key_concept: Attribute-based control needs accurate attribute sources; with a few stable jobs and no such source, role-based control fits better.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each access control model fits best.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute-based control is only as good as its attributes, and nothing here would supply or maintain 40 of them, while three stable job types map neatly to three roles that are simple to build, review and explain. Attribute-based control is the runner-up, as it gives finer control, but its decisions would rest on attributes no system keeps.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: ABAC does give fine-grained control. But with no system keeping volunteers' details, 40 attributes would go stale, and three stable jobs do not need them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because donor data is sensitive. But MAC is rigid and costly; sensitive business data is normally protected with roles and least privilege.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because creators know the records. But donor data belongs to the charity, and owner sharing invites oversharing.

tips: Eliminate: C brings classified-style labels to business data, and D lets whoever creates a record share it.
Final two: B beats A because three stable jobs map neatly to roles, and ABAC's 40 attributes would have no source to keep them accurate.
Exam cue: before choosing attribute-based control, ask where each attribute comes from and who keeps it accurate; with few stable jobs, roles fit.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); NIST SP 800-162 Section 3.2.3.1 (Confidence in Access Control Decisions: accurate and timely attributes from authoritative sources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'attribute-based control needs maintained attribute sources; with few stable jobs, roles fit' (notes 3.2.10 Choosing an Access Control Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): deciding fact is now the missing attribute source, so the item no longer retells cc_d3_036; key letter unchanged. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): stem no longer signals that the vendor's proposal is wrong ('yet' removed). Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): option B no longer echoes the stem's 'job types' and is no longer the lone shortest option.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: A florist's invoice-entry AI agent can also edit suppliers' bank details, and the vendor says the agent's instructions forbid it. Which assessment should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: Safe, as the agent's instructions were tested thoroughly
options.B: Safe enough, once invoices are screened for hidden instructions
options.C: Unsafe, as instructions guide the agent but enforce nothing
options.D: Unsafe, as AI agents should be limited to read access

questions.key_concept: An AI agent's instructions are not access control; only the permissions on its account reliably limit what it can do.
questions.pre_read: Recall what actually limits the actions an AI agent can take.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent's instructions shape its behavior but enforce nothing: hidden text in an invoice, or a model error, can lead it to ignore them, while its account's permissions still allow the edit. Only removing the bank-details right stops that. Screening invoices is the runner-up and worth adding, but filters miss new tricks, and the right would remain.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: screening does catch some hidden instructions. But filters miss new tricks, and the agent would still hold a right its task never needs.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors test their products. But testing cannot foresee every crafted input; the permission, not the instruction, decides what the agent can do.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because agents need tight limits. But this agent must write invoice entries; least privilege removes unneeded rights, not every write right.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts vendor testing to cover every input, and D strips the write rights the agent's task needs.
Final two: C beats B because only permissions are enforced; screening helps, but a missed trick would still find the bank-details right in place.
Exam cue: when a vendor says an AI agent won't do something, check whether its account can; only the permissions are enforced.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.4 (Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations: attackers plant instructions in resources the model reads)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an AI agent's instructions are not access control; limit it with its account's permissions' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): re-angled from removing an unneeded agent right (cc_d3_068, cc_d5_045) to instructions versus enforced permissions; setting moved off 'garden center'; key letter unchanged. Shares the 'instructions are not a control' point with cc_d5_045 (fixing a test finding, 5.5); this item instead tests judging a vendor's claim against the agent's actual permissions. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): exam cue now targets judging a vendor's claim against the agent's permissions. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor A no longer names the vendor; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A cheese maker's just-in-time admin tool lets an administrator request database rights for a task and then approve that same request. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Require a different person to approve every elevation
options.B: Keep self-approval, as every elevated session is logged
options.C: Give administrators standing rights with no approval step
options.D: Allow self-approval for requests lasting under one hour

questions.key_concept: Just-in-time access limits standing rights only when someone other than the requester approves each elevation.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes a just-in-time elevation a real control.
questions.correct_explanation: Just-in-time access limits standing rights only if someone other than the requester agrees to each elevation; self-approval turns the request into a formality. A second approver keeps separation of duties inside the tool. Keeping self-approval because sessions are logged is the runner-up, since logs show what happened, but they detect misuse afterwards rather than preventing an unjustified elevation.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: session logs do show what was done. But they detect misuse after it happens; nobody independent checks the elevation was justified.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes delay. But standing admin rights are what just-in-time access exists to avoid; attackers use them too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because short grants limit exposure. But even a one-hour elevation goes unchecked when the requester approves it, and an hour is enough to do harm.

tips: Eliminate: C returns to standing admin rights, and D still lets administrators approve their own short elevations.
Final two: A beats B because an independent approver prevents unjustified elevation; logs only reveal it afterwards.
Exam cue: an approval step is real only when the approver is not the requester, in tools as well as on paper.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an administrator requests elevation for a named task, and an approver agrees' (notes 3.2.12 Just-in-Time and Break-Glass Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): option D is now a stronger distractor (self-approval for short requests) and option A no longer the longest.

questions.question: A seismology institute's datasets open only to requesters whose employment type is Staff and whose office region matches each dataset's region tag. Which model should the access analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Mandatory access control, as each dataset carries a region tag
options.B: Role-based access control, with Staff as the job role
options.C: Attribute-based access control, as the policy compares several facts
options.D: Discretionary access control, as the owners tag their own datasets

questions.key_concept: A tag is not always a classification label; matching user and data attributes under a policy is attribute-based access control.
questions.pre_read: Recall how to name an access control model from who or what decides.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute-based access control decides each request by comparing attributes of the user, such as employment type and office region, with attributes of the resource, such as its region tag. Mandatory access control is the runner-up, because the datasets carry tags, but MAC compares a subject's clearance, and any compartments it is granted, with a label set by a central authority; here no clearance is involved, only ordinary user facts matched by a policy.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the datasets carry tags, and MAC labels can include compartments. But MAC checks a centrally granted clearance against each label; employment type and office region are ordinary attributes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Staff sounds like a role. But employment type is one attribute among several the policy compares, not a job role holding permissions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because someone set each tag. But nothing lets an owner choose who gets in; the policy decides for everyone.

tips: Eliminate: B treats one attribute as a job role, and D invents an owner's choice the scenario does not describe.
Final two: C beats A because the policy matches ordinary user facts, employment type and office region, to a data tag; MAC checks a clearance, plus any compartments, against a label.
Exam cue: a tag is not always a classification label; if access rests on a clearance granted centrally, it is MAC, and if it rests on everyday user and data facts, it is ABAC.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(13) (Access Enforcement | Attribute-based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'find the decider: an owner, a central label, a job role, attributes or one rule for all' (notes 3.2.13 Access Model Scenarios: Worked Examples). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 1 (5 Nov 2026): option C no longer echoes the stem's 'matches'. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): option C uses an 'as' reason clause like the other options. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): explanations allow for MAC compartments (cc_d3_042, notes 3.2.13) and rest the case on the absence of any clearance. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and' or 'data'; option B reworded without 'is'; same key and teaching point.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Identities and accounts
questions.question: Three night-shift bakers at a commercial bakery need identical access to its ordering tablet, and their supervisor asks for one shared 'nightshift' login. Which setup should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: One shared login, with each user named in a written shift log
options.B: Separate named accounts for each person, all holding the same role
options.C: One shared login whose password changes at the end of each week
options.D: Their supervisor's own account, signed in on the tablet nightly

questions.key_concept: Each person gets their own account, even when several need the same access, so every action traces to one person.
questions.pre_read: Recall the account types in the identity life cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: Separate named accounts for each baker, all holding the same role, give identical access while the system records which person placed each order, and one leaver can lose access without disturbing the others. A shared login with a written shift log is the runner-up, because it tries to keep a record, but a hand-written log is easily skipped or wrong, and the system itself still sees one identity.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the shift log tries to record who used the login. But the system still sees one identity, and a hand-written log is easily skipped or wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because changing the password feels like control. But the three bakers still share it, so nobody can tell who placed an order.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the supervisor is accountable. But the bakers would act under someone else's identity, and every order would look like the supervisor's.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the shared password but leaves one identity for three people, and D has the bakers act under the supervisor's identity.
Final two: B beats A because named accounts let the system itself record who acted; a paper log beside a shared login depends on people remembering.
Exam cue: the same access does not mean the same account; give each person their own login and put the shared access in a role.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a shared team login hides who acted; give each person an account holding the same role' (notes 3.1.1 Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ski school's access analyst drafts new roles by grouping the rights current instructors already hold, and the head instructor owns the roles. What should the analyst do FIRST, before the roles go live?

options.A: Let the head instructor publish the roles exactly as drafted
options.B: Have the head instructor confirm which rights each role should hold
options.C: Add every right instructors hold, so nobody loses access
options.D: Have each instructor confirm the rights they use in their role

questions.key_concept: Roles built from today's access copy its leftovers, so the role owner confirms each right before anyone is assigned.
questions.pre_read: Recall who decides what a role should contain.
questions.correct_explanation: Roles drafted from today's access copy whatever rights people have collected over time, including leftovers from old jobs. The head instructor, who owns the roles, must confirm which rights each role should hold before anyone is assigned. Having each instructor confirm their own rights is the runner-up, because they know the work, but people rarely give up access they have, and confirming your own access is a conflict of interest.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner signs off. But publishing the draft unchanged approves every leftover right copied from today's access.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids complaints. But merging everyone's rights gives each instructor the access of all, the opposite of least privilege.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: instructors know their daily work. But people rarely give up access they hold, and confirming your own access is a conflict of interest.

tips: Eliminate: A publishes leftover rights copied from today's access, and C merges every instructor's rights into one oversized role.
Final two: B beats D because the role owner judges what the job needs; instructors confirming their own rights tend to keep what they have.
Exam cue: roles mined from current access inherit its creep; have the role owner confirm each right before anyone is assigned.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'roles drafted from current access inherit leftover rights, so the role owner confirms each one' (notes 3.1.2 Defining Roles and Entitlements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A fintech startup ships remote hires a laptop, with a card in the box giving a password to change at first sign-in. Which change should the help desk technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Release the password after a live check of the hire's ID
options.B: Mail the password card separately, a day later, to the same address
options.C: Print a longer, random password on the card instead
options.D: Give the password to the hire when they phone the help desk

questions.key_concept: A working credential goes to a person only after their identity has been checked.
questions.pre_read: Recall how identity proofing fits into onboarding.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever opens the box gets the password, and the first-sign-in change then lets them lock the real hire out. A credential should reach a person only after their identity is checked, so the password is released once a live check shows the person holding the laptop matches the hire's ID. Mailing the card separately is the runner-up, because two parcels are harder to intercept, but whoever receives both still signs in unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: separate parcels make interception harder. But nobody checks who receives them, so anyone at that address, or a thief holding both, still signs in.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because longer passwords resist guessing. But the problem is who receives the password, not how strong it is.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the help desk speaks to the person first. But a caller who simply asks proves nothing; whoever opened the box can make the call.

tips: Eliminate: C strengthens a password still handed to whoever opens the box, and D gives it to any caller who asks.
Final two: A beats B because only A confirms the person receiving the password is the new hire; separate parcels still go unchecked.
Exam cue: prove who someone is before giving them a working credential; delivery tricks do not replace identity proofing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-12 (Identity Proofing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'identity proofing comes before credentials are issued' (notes 3.1.3 Provisioning and Identity Proofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A land registry's staff sign in with a smart card and its PIN, and a technician calls this single-factor because a PIN is a short password. Which reply from the access analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree, as a PIN and a password are both something you know
options.B: Disagree, as a PIN is something you are, tied to the user
options.C: Agree, as the card merely holds the PIN the reader then checks
options.D: Disagree, as the card adds something you have to the PIN

questions.key_concept: A smart card unlocked by a PIN combines something you have with something you know, so it is multifactor.
questions.pre_read: Recall the three authentication factor categories and how to count them.
questions.correct_explanation: The PIN is something you know, but it only unlocks the smart card, which holds a key the person must physically possess: something you have. Two different categories make this multifactor authentication. Agreeing because a PIN is like a password is the runner-up: that part is true, but it overlooks the card, which an attacker who learns the PIN still needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a PIN is indeed something you know. But the sign-in also needs the card, a second category, so it is not single-factor.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a PIN is personal. But it is memorized, so it is something you know, not something you are.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the card is used with the PIN. But the card holds its own secret key, so possessing it is a separate factor.

tips: Eliminate: B puts a memorized PIN in the wrong category, and C treats the card as a mere PIN holder rather than something you have.
Final two: D beats A because the PIN alone is something you know, but the card adds a second, different category.
Exam cue: count categories, not steps; a card or key you hold plus a PIN or fingerprint to unlock it is multifactor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.1.7 (Multi-Factor Cryptographic Authentication: the authenticator is something you have, activated by something you know or something you are); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'MFA combines different categories: a smart card is something you have, its PIN something you know' (notes 3.1.4 Authentication Factors and MFA). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ceramics studio's booking-system vendor wants staff able to paste passwords from a password manager, but the IT manager wants pasting blocked. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree with the IT manager, as pasting exposes passwords to other apps
options.B: Agree with the vendor, as pasting makes long, unique passwords easy
options.C: Agree with the IT manager, as blocking paste stops automated guessing
options.D: Agree with the vendor, as pasted passwords skip length rules

questions.key_concept: Current guidance supports password managers and pasting, because they make long, unique passwords practical.
questions.pre_read: Recall what current NIST guidance says about password managers.
questions.correct_explanation: Current NIST guidance says sign-in pages must allow password managers and should allow pasting, because managers make long, unique passwords practical; blocking paste pushes people back to short, memorable ones. The clipboard worry is the runner-up: it is a real but small risk, outweighed by the weak and reused passwords that blocking paste encourages.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: other apps can sometimes read the clipboard. But that risk is small next to the weak, reused passwords people choose when they must type them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because blocking seems to slow bots. But automated guessing is stopped by rate limiting, not by blocking paste in a sign-in field.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it backs the vendor. But a pasted password must meet the same rules as a typed one; the verifier still checks it.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on paste blocking to stop guessing, which is rate limiting's job, and D wrongly lets pasted passwords skip the rules.
Final two: B beats A because NIST favors password managers; the small clipboard risk is outweighed by the weak passwords that blocking encourages.
Exam cue: modern password guidance favors long, unique passwords and the tools that make them easy; rules that fight password managers backfire.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.1.1.2 (Password Verifiers: verifiers allow password managers and autofill, and should permit pasting passwords); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5(1) (Authenticator Management | Password-based Authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'NIST favors long passwords and password managers over rules that make long passwords harder' (notes 3.1.6 Passwords and Modern Password Standards). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At an engineering college, staff signing in through single sign-on (SSO) keep approving an AI note-taking app's request to read their whole mailbox and files. Which control should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Have the security team approve apps before they reach staff mailboxes
options.B: Train staff to read each app's access request before approving it
options.C: Require multifactor authentication each time the AI app is opened
options.D: Block single sign-on for all outside apps the college uses

questions.key_concept: In an organization, the organization, not each user, decides which apps may receive broad access to its data.
questions.pre_read: Recall how single sign-on lets outside apps reach staff data.
questions.correct_explanation: During each SSO sign-in, one staff member's click on the app's request lets an outside app reach their data, so one careless approval can expose a whole mailbox. In an organization, the organization should decide which apps may receive broad access, so the security team reviews such requests and staff approve only low-risk ones. Training is the runner-up: it helps, but staff are already clicking Accept, and awareness alone leaves the decision with whoever clicks.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: informed staff decline more requests. But staff are already approving these, and training alone leaves each decision with whoever clicks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because MFA protects sign-in. But it proves who opened the app; it does not limit what the app may read once approved.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shuts the door completely. But it breaks approved apps and pushes staff to separate passwords, losing central control.

tips: Eliminate: C strengthens sign-in but not what the app may read, and D drops single sign-on for all outside apps, losing central control.
Final two: A beats B because the organization, not each user, should decide which apps get broad access; training leaves the click with the user.
Exam cue: when users can hand data to outside apps, move the decision on broad access to the organization and leave users the low-risk cases.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'single sign-on concentrates trust, so the organization controls what apps can reach through it' (notes 3.1.7 Single Sign-On and Federation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A coworking firm's AI monitoring marks a session jumping to a new country and device; the playbook says the security analyst handles such alerts directly. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the flagged session to the incident response lead
options.B: Lower the model's sensitivity to stop ending travelers' sessions
options.C: End the flagged session, which forces the user to sign in again
options.D: Require a new password at the user's next sign-in

questions.key_concept: When monitoring flags a likely stolen session, ending it and requiring a fresh sign-in stops the thief but not the real user.
questions.pre_read: Recall what session monitoring looks for.
questions.correct_explanation: A session that suddenly moves to another country and device suggests a stolen session token. Since the playbook has the analyst handle such alerts directly, the analyst ends the session and requires a fresh sign-in, which the real user can pass and a token thief cannot. Reporting to the incident response lead is the runner-up, because escalation is often right, but here it leaves the suspect session running when the task is already the analyst's.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: escalation is often right. But the playbook has the analyst handle these alerts, and passing it on leaves the suspect session open meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because AI alerts can be false alarms. But a mid-session jump in country and device is a classic sign of a stolen session.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a new password fixes a stolen one. But the attacker holds a live session, which a change at the next sign-in does not end.

tips: Eliminate: B tunes the model down instead of acting on a classic stolen-session sign, and D waits for a later sign-in while the live session continues.
Final two: C beats A because the playbook gives the analyst this step; escalating first leaves the suspect session running.
Exam cue: when a procedure assigns the response to you, act within it; escalate when the action is outside your authority.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 5.3 (Session Monitoring: when potential fraud is detected during a session, reauthenticate, terminate the session or notify support personnel); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(12) (Account Management | Account Monitoring for Atypical Usage)
