Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; 'so' taken off option B; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A hotel group's access report shows staff who have changed jobs most often hold the most rights, though each now does one job. Which term should the access analyst use as MOST precise?

options.A: Privilege escalation
options.B: Orphaned accounts
options.C: Dormant accounts
options.D: Privilege creep

questions.key_concept: Rights that pile up through approved job changes are privilege creep; escalation means gaining rights that were never granted.
questions.pre_read: Recall how privilege creep differs from privilege escalation.
questions.correct_explanation: Privilege creep is the slow build-up of rights as people move between jobs and keep access their old jobs needed. Every right here was granted properly and never taken away. Privilege escalation is the runner-up, because these staff do hold more than they need, but escalation means gaining rights that were never granted, usually through a flaw or misconfiguration.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: these staff hold more than their jobs need. But each right was granted at some point; escalation means seizing rights that were never granted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because orphaned accounts are a common finding. But these accounts belong to current staff with known owners.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because old rights sound unused. But dormant describes accounts left unused for a set period, and these staff use their accounts in their current jobs.

tips: Eliminate: B describes accounts with no accountable owner, and C describes unused accounts, but these staff are active.
Final two: D beats A because these rights were granted properly and never removed; escalation means gaining rights nobody granted.
Exam cue: rights that pile up through approved job changes are privilege creep; rights gained beyond what was granted are privilege escalation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-5 (Personnel Transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(7) (Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'privilege creep builds when moves add access without removing the old' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: In a quarterly review, a broadcaster's music-archive data owner confirms a sound engineer keeps delete rights, noting the engineer runs the archive's clean-ups. Which action is BEST for the access analyst running the review?

options.A: Remove the delete rights, citing the risk of archive deletions
options.B: Ask the sound engineer to confirm and record they still use them
options.C: Accept the owner's confirmation, logging the reason they gave
options.D: Ask the security manager to check the owner's decision first

questions.key_concept: In an access review the accountable owner decides whether each right is still needed, and the reviewer records the decision.
questions.pre_read: Recall the roles of the owner and the person running an access review.
questions.correct_explanation: In an access review the data owner, who knows the work, decides whether each right is still needed; the analyst running it records that decision. Here the owner gives a clear business reason, so the analyst accepts it and records the reason. Removing the rights is the runner-up, because delete rights carry real risk, but the owner has weighed that against the work, and overruling their business judgment is outside the reviewer's role.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: delete rights do carry risk. But the owner has judged that the work needs them, and the analyst running the review records that decision rather than overruling it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the engineer knows their own work. But self-confirmation is a conflict of interest; the accountable owner confirms access.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a second check feels safer. But the data owner is the accountable approver; the security manager does not re-decide routine business needs.

tips: Eliminate: B has the engineer confirm their own access, and D sends a routine owner decision to someone who is not accountable for the data.
Final two: C beats A because the owner weighs a right's risk against the work; the analyst records the decision and its reason rather than overruling it.
Exam cue: in an access review, the owner decides and the person running it records; send a decision back only when the evidence contradicts it, such as a leaver kept on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6(7) (Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'in a review, the accountable owner confirms each right and the person running it records the decision' (notes 3.1.10 Access Reviews and Recertification). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and' or 'record'; same key and teaching point. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor A reworded with a comma clause like the key's; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A university's leaver checklist has the help desk technician revoke leavers' personal access keys; a departed data scientist's key for an AI platform owned by research computing still works. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Ask research computing, as platform owner, to decide on the key
options.B: Revoke the key after the scientist's projects are handed over
options.C: Disable the leaver's directory account and let that end the key
options.D: Revoke the key and note it on the leaver's offboarding ticket

questions.key_concept: A leaver's keys keep working until revoked, and a checklist that assigns the revocation lets the practitioner act.
questions.pre_read: Recall which credentials can outlive a leaver's main account.
questions.correct_explanation: The leaver checklist assigns revoking personal access keys to the technician, and a key keeps working after its creator leaves until someone revokes it. Revoking it and noting it on the offboarding ticket completes the step. Asking research computing is the runner-up, because they own the platform, but the procedure already gives this task to the technician, and waiting leaves a departed person's working key in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: research computing owns the platform. But the checklist already assigns revoking leavers' keys to the technician, and waiting leaves a working key in place.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because handover feels considerate. But a personal key belongs to the leaver, and projects should run under their own accounts, not a departed person's key.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the directory account is the main identity. But keys issued on another platform often keep working after the account is disabled.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps a departed person's key working for handover, and C assumes disabling the directory account also ends keys issued elsewhere.
Final two: D beats A because the checklist assigns this revocation to the technician; owning the platform does not make research computing the one to act.
Exam cue: a named owner does not always mean escalate; if the procedure assigns the step to you, do it and record it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.2 (Establish an Access Revoking Process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'disabling the main account does not end every credential; revoke keys and tokens too' (notes 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Human resources (HR) tells a bottling plant's help desk technician that a just-dismissed supervisor threatened to come back for coworkers; the leaver checklist covers the badge and all accounts. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Revoke the supervisor's network accounts and alert the IT manager
options.B: Collect the supervisor's badge, laptop and phone at the exit
options.C: Disable the supervisor's building badge and alert site security
options.D: Reset the door codes and passwords the supervisor knew

questions.key_concept: When a leaver may harm people, cutting physical access and involving security comes before protecting data.
questions.pre_read: Recall what deprovisioning a leaver covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Deprovisioning a leaver removes every identity they hold, and the checklist lists the building badge beside the accounts. The threat against coworkers decides the order: a working badge would let the supervisor back into the plant, so disabling it and alerting site security protects staff at once. Revoking network accounts is the runner-up, since it is on the same checklist and protects data, but it does nothing to stop the supervisor walking back in.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the accounts must go and the IT manager should know. But data can wait minutes; a working badge lets someone who threatened coworkers back inside.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the badge must come back. But confronting a person who has just made threats risks staff safety; disabling the badge remotely does not.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because known codes must change. But resetting them takes time while the badge still opens the doors, the immediate risk to people.

tips: Eliminate: B has staff confront someone who just made threats, and D changes codes while the supervisor's badge still opens the doors.
Final two: C beats A because people's safety comes first; the badge is the access that could put coworkers at risk.
Exam cue: when a leaver threatens people, cut physical access and involve security first; protect people before data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'deprovisioning covers badges and devices too, and people's safety comes first' (notes 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A record label's eight apps each keep their own user list, so staff juggle eight passwords and each leaver needs eight removals. Which tool type should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Password manager for staff, holding the eight app passwords
options.B: Central directory service that every app checks at staff sign-in
options.C: Privileged access vault for administrator passwords
options.D: Log management system that gathers each app's sign-in records

questions.key_concept: A directory service gives each person one identity that apps check, so access can be removed everywhere at once.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a directory service does in identity and access management.
questions.correct_explanation: A central directory gives each person one identity that every app checks at sign-in, often through single sign-on, so staff need one password and disabling one account ends access everywhere. A password manager is the runner-up: it eases the juggling, but the eight separate accounts remain, and each leaver still needs eight removals, any of which can be missed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a password manager eases juggling eight passwords. But the eight separate accounts remain, so each leaver still needs eight removals that can be missed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vaults guard passwords. But a privileged access vault protects administrator accounts, not everyday staff identities across apps.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs show who signed in. But they record activity after the fact; they do not give staff one identity to disable.

tips: Eliminate: C guards administrator accounts only, and D records sign-ins rather than giving staff one identity.
Final two: B beats A because one directory identity can be disabled once for every app; a password manager still leaves eight accounts to remove.
Exam cue: scattered user lists call for a central directory; one identity, checked everywhere, can be disabled everywhere at once.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.7 (Centralize Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each IAM tool does one job: a directory stores identities, governance runs requests and reviews, PAM guards admins' (notes 3.1.13 IAM Frameworks and Tools). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sculpture park's coordinator asks the help desk to remove their own edit rights on a finance share the finance director owns; procedure lets removals proceed unapproved. What should the help desk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the finance director to approve the removal first
options.B: Remove the coordinator's edit rights on every finance share
options.C: Refuse, since the owner alone may change access to the share
options.D: Remove the edit rights on that one share, as requested

questions.key_concept: Owner approval guards new access; removing rights someone no longer needs lowers risk and can proceed as the procedure allows.
questions.pre_read: Recall why access requests need an owner's approval.
questions.correct_explanation: Approval guards the granting of access, because new rights add risk; giving up rights lowers risk, and here the procedure lets removals go ahead without approval. The analyst removes the edit rights on that share, as requested. Asking the finance director first is the runner-up, because they own the share, but the procedure does not require it, and waiting keeps unneeded rights open.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the finance director owns the share. But the procedure lets removals proceed without approval, since removing unneeded rights lowers risk; waiting keeps them open.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems thorough. But the request covers one share; removing rights on other shares goes beyond it and may disrupt work the coordinator still does.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owners control access to their data. But the procedure allows removals without approval; owner sign-off guards grants, not giving rights up.

tips: Eliminate: B removes rights on shares the request never covered, and C refuses a removal the procedure allows.
Final two: D beats A because owner approval guards new access; this procedure lets the help desk remove unneeded rights straight away.
Exam cue: approvals protect grants; when a procedure lets you remove access someone no longer needs, remove it and record it.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.2 (Establish an Access Revoking Process); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the owner approves new access and a different person fulfills; removing unneeded rights lowers risk' (notes 3.1.14 Access Requests and Approvals). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bell foundry adds a partner workshop's staff as guests on its collaboration platform, whose default lets guests browse the staff directory and every open team space. What should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Restrict each guest to the projects shared with them
options.B: Have the workshop sign a confidentiality agreement first
options.C: Require guests to use multifactor authentication at every sign-in
options.D: Stop guest access and email the files to the partners instead

questions.key_concept: Third parties should reach only the work they are part of; agreements and MFA add to that limit, not replace it.
questions.pre_read: Recall how far guest access should reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Guests should reach only what their work needs, so the platform should limit each guest to the projects shared with them, not the whole directory and every open space. A confidentiality agreement is the runner-up, because it sets duties and consequences, but it is a promise; it does not stop anyone browsing. MFA proves who the guest is, not what they can open.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an agreement sets the partner's duties. But it is a promise, not a technical limit; guests could still browse everything.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because MFA strengthens guest sign-in. But it proves who the guest is; it does not narrow what they can open.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids guest accounts. But emailed files leave the foundry's control and cannot be withdrawn later.

tips: Eliminate: C strengthens sign-in without narrowing what guests reach, and D emails files out of the foundry's control.
Final two: A beats B because a technical limit stops browsing; an agreement only promises it will not happen.
Exam cue: for third parties, limit access to what the work needs first; contracts and MFA add to that, they do not replace it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-8 (Identification and Authentication (Non-organizational Users)); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'guests need limited access to what their work needs; the risk sits on your systems' (notes 3.1.15 Third-Party, Guest and Federated Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: After a phished salesperson's password is reset, a colleague warns the help desk technician that the attacker may still be in their web mail. Which reply from the technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disagree, as a reset cancels every sign-in made with the old password
options.B: Agree, as sessions the attacker already holds may keep working
options.C: Agree, as the attacker may still use the old password for days
options.D: Disagree, as web mail sessions end when the browser window is closed

questions.key_concept: Resetting a password stops new sign-ins, but open sessions can continue until they are ended or time out.
questions.pre_read: Recall how long a session lasts after sign-in.
questions.correct_explanation: The colleague is right. A password reset stops new sign-ins with the old password, but a session already open can keep working until it times out or is ended, so an attacker holding a session token may carry on. The sessions must be ended too. Disagreeing because a reset cancels earlier sign-ins is the runner-up: some systems do this, but many do not, so it must be checked and done, not assumed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: some systems end sessions on a reset. But many do not, and an attacker's existing session can keep working until it is ended.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it agrees with the colleague. But the reason is wrong: a reset takes effect for new sign-ins at once; it is the open session that survives.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because closing a window feels like leaving. But it is the attacker's browser, and many sessions stay valid until they time out or are ended.

tips: Eliminate: C agrees for the wrong reason, since a reset stops new sign-ins with the old password at once, and D assumes the attacker will close their own browser window.
Final two: B beats A because a reset does not reliably end sessions already open; they must be ended too.
Exam cue: after a takeover, reset the credential and end every open session; one without the other leaves the door open.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 6.4 (Session Attacks: hijacking after an authentication event); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-12 (Session Termination)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a session lasts until it times out or is ended; a password change alone may not end it' (notes 3.1.16 Sessions, Timeouts and Reauthentication). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sports league moved staff to passkeys, but its help desk enrolls a new passkey for any caller giving a staff name and number. Which risk should the security analyst rate MOST serious?

options.A: Impostors can have passkeys enrolled on other people's accounts
options.B: Passkeys synced between staff devices could be copied by attackers
options.C: Staff could still be phished for passwords they no longer use
options.D: Passkeys enrolled for the real site will fail on look-alike pages

questions.key_concept: A weak recovery or enrollment path lets attackers bypass even phishing-resistant sign-in.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes a sign-in method phishing-resistant.
questions.correct_explanation: Passkeys stop look-alike pages, but an account is only as strong as its weakest way in. A name and staff number are easy to find, so any impostor can phone the help desk and have their own passkey enrolled, skipping the phishing protection entirely. Copying of synced passkeys is the runner-up, because syncing does move keys between devices, but they stay protected by the person's provider account and device unlock.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: synced passkeys do travel between devices. But they stay protected by the person's provider account and device unlock; the help desk path needs no secret at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because phishing often targets passwords. But staff who sign in with passkeys have no password in use for attackers to capture.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a failed sign-in sounds like a fault. But refusing look-alike pages is exactly how passkeys resist phishing; it is the protection.

tips: Eliminate: C worries about passwords no longer in use, and D treats the passkey's refusal of look-alike sites, its main protection, as a risk.
Final two: A beats B because a weak help desk path lets anyone enroll a passkey with easily found facts; synced passkeys stay behind the owner's unlock.
Exam cue: strong sign-in is only as strong as recovery and enrollment; check how a new authenticator gets added.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 4.2 (Account Recovery: recovery uses recovery codes, recovery contacts or repeated identity proofing, and always notifies the subscriber); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'phishing-resistant sign-in is only as strong as the way new authenticators are enrolled and recovered' (notes 3.1.5 Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Identities and accounts
questions.question: A school plans to reissue the username 'kpatel', held by a teacher who left last year and still named in its kept logs, to a new teacher. What should the access analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Give the new teacher a different username not held before
options.B: Reuse the username after deleting the old account and its files
options.C: Give the new teacher the old account with a fresh password set
options.D: Use a shared 'teacher' login while the old records remain

questions.key_concept: A leaver's username is not reissued to another person, at least for the period the organization sets, so past records keep pointing to one person.
questions.pre_read: Recall how identifiers support accountability.
questions.correct_explanation: A departed person's username should not be reissued while records still name them: logs, tickets and records that say 'kpatel' would then point to two people, and any access still tied to that name could pass to the newcomer. A fresh, unique username keeps each record tied to one person. Reusing it after deleting the old account is the runner-up, because the old access is gone, but past logs and records would still become ambiguous.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: deleting the old account removes its access. But past logs and records naming 'kpatel' would then point to two people.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a new password locks out the old teacher. But the new teacher inherits the old account's access, files and history.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids the clash. But a shared login hides who acted, the very accountability unique usernames give.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the old account's access and history to someone else, and D swaps the problem for a shared login.
Final two: A beats B because a reused name confuses old logs and records even after the old account is gone.
Exam cue: one identifier, one person; don't reissue a leaver's username while records still name them, so give newcomers a new one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-4 (Identifier Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an identity represents one person, so its identifier never passes to someone else' (notes 3.1.1 Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A licensing agency's case app checks clerks' rights only at sign-in, so a clerk whose approval right was removed at noon kept approving cases all afternoon. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Limit every session to one hour so rights reload more often
options.B: Require the clerk's password again before each case approval
options.C: Remove rights at the end of each working day instead
options.D: Check the clerk's current rights on every action

questions.key_concept: Authorization should be decided on each request against current rights, not once at sign-in.
questions.pre_read: Recall the difference between authentication and authorization.
questions.correct_explanation: An access decision should be made for every request, against the rights as they stand now; checking once at sign-in lets removed rights keep working all session. Checking current rights on each request closes the gap. Hourly session ends are the runner-up, because they shrink the window, but a removed right would still work for up to an hour, and staff would sign in far more often.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: shorter sessions shrink the gap. But a removed right still works until the hour ends, and frequent sign-ins burden every clerk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it adds a check before approvals. But a password proves who the clerk is, not what the clerk may still do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it batches changes. But it keeps removed rights working even longer, the opposite of the fix.

tips: Eliminate: B re-proves identity without rechecking rights, and C delays removals, keeping the gap open longer.
Final two: D beats A because checking each request leaves no window; shorter sessions only shrink it.
Exam cue: authentication happens once per session, but authorization should be decided on every request against current rights.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-24 (Access Control Decisions); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'logical access controls decide each request: may this subject perform this action on this object' (notes 3.2.1 Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ticketing startup's developers keep write access to the production database to investigate faults and make fixes, though every fix should ship through a tested release. Which change should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep write access, limited to working hours when leads watch
options.B: Log every developer change made to the production database
options.C: Remove developer access to the production database
options.D: Give developers read-only production database access

questions.key_concept: When changes must go through releases, standing write access to production is more than anyone's task needs.
questions.pre_read: Recall how least privilege applies to production systems.
questions.correct_explanation: Least privilege gives each person only the access their task needs. Developers investigate faults in production but ship fixes through tested releases, so read access is all they need there. Keeping write access to working hours is the runner-up, because it narrows when the right can be used, but the unneeded right remains, and an untested change or a stolen account can still alter live data in those hours.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it narrows when the right can be used. But the unneeded write right remains, and a stolen developer account can still change live data during working hours.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a log shows who changed what. But it records changes after they happen; the unneeded write right stays, so live data can still be altered.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes the risky right. But developers still investigate faults in production; least privilege means the access a task needs, not none.

tips: Eliminate: B only records changes made with a right nobody needs, and C also cuts the read access developers need to investigate faults.
Final two: D beats A because removing an unneeded right prevents harm; limiting its hours only narrows the window.
Exam cue: least privilege is the minimum a task needs, not none; if changes go through releases, nobody needs standing write access to production.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-5 (Access Restrictions for Change)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'least privilege gives the minimum access a task needs' (notes 3.2.2 Least Privilege and Need to Know). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A charity's clerk holds only the two rights the job uses, creating suppliers and paying invoices, and the finance director says this meets separation of duties. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree, as the clerk holds no rights beyond what the job uses
options.B: Agree, as separation of duties covers administrators, not clerks
options.C: Disagree, as the clerk alone can create a supplier and pay it
options.D: Disagree, as the clerk should also review and approve each supplier

questions.key_concept: Minimal rights can still conflict; separation of duties stops one person completing a sensitive task alone.
questions.pre_read: Recall how separation of duties differs from least privilege.
questions.correct_explanation: Separation of duties splits a sensitive process so no one person can complete it alone. Creating a supplier and paying it are such a pair: one clerk could invent a fake supplier and pay it. Agreeing because the clerk has only the rights the job uses is the runner-up, but that describes least privilege; a person can hold minimal rights that still conflict.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the clerk does have least privilege. But minimal rights can still conflict; creating and paying a supplier lets one person complete a fraud.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because administrators are a common focus. But separation of duties applies to any sensitive business process, such as payments.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it mentions a control step. But adding approval to the same clerk combines even more duties in one person.

tips: Eliminate: B limits separation of duties to administrators, and D adds yet another duty to the same clerk.
Final two: C beats A because least privilege limits how much one person holds; separation of duties stops one person finishing a sensitive task alone.
Exam cue: least privilege asks how much one person holds; separation of duties asks whether one person can do the whole risky job.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'least privilege and separation of duties differ: minimal rights can still conflict' (notes 3.2.3 Separation of Duties and Two-Person Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: option D reworded; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: Every designer at a jewelry studio has local administrator rights on their laptop so they can install fonts and design plug-ins. Which change should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep the rights and train designers to pick approved software
options.B: Remove the rights and offer approved installs from a catalog
options.C: Keep the rights and scan every laptop for malware each week
options.D: Remove the rights and let designers borrow the IT admin password

questions.key_concept: Meet the task that needs admin rights, such as installing software, without leaving users standing privilege.
questions.pre_read: Recall how least privilege applies to everyday users' own devices.
questions.correct_explanation: Local administrator rights let anything a designer runs, including malware from a bad plug-in, change the whole laptop. Removing them and offering approved software from a self-service catalog meets the real need without standing privilege. Training is the runner-up, because careful users make fewer mistakes, but it leaves every laptop one bad download away from full compromise.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: training helps designers choose safer software. But admin rights stay in place, so one mistaken install can still take over the laptop.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because scanning finds infections. But it detects harm after it happens; removing admin rights prevents much of it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes standing rights. But a borrowed admin password spreads privilege further and hides who installed what.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on weekly detection instead of prevention, and D replaces personal admin rights with a shared admin password.
Final two: B beats A because removing standing admin rights prevents harm; training only lowers the odds of a bad install.
Exam cue: when users need admin rights for one task, provide that task safely instead of leaving them full privilege.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-11 (User-installed Software)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'privileged rights belong only where needed; everyday users should not hold administrator rights' (notes 3.2.4 Privileged Access Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A community radio station's volunteers create and share their own show folders, choosing who may open each one. Which statement about this discretionary access control should the access analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: It is the strictest model, but slow for owners to change later
options.B: It lets a central team decide who may open each folder
options.C: It stops owners sharing with anyone who lacks a clearance
options.D: It is flexible, but owners can easily overshare by mistake

questions.key_concept: Discretionary access control is flexible because owners decide, and that same choice lets them overshare.
questions.pre_read: Recall the strengths and weaknesses of discretionary access control.
questions.correct_explanation: Under discretionary access control the owner, usually the creator, decides who else may open a resource. That makes it the most flexible model, quick for small teams, but owners can overshare by mistake, and malware runs with their sharing rights. Calling it the strictest model is the runner-up: owners do control their own data, but flexibility is its strength, and owners change sharing in a click.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: owners do control their own data. But discretionary control is the most flexible model, not the strictest, and owners can change sharing in a click.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because many systems are run centrally. But central decisions describe role-based or other non-discretionary models; here each volunteer decides.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some systems block uncleared users. But clearances and labels belong to mandatory access control, not discretionary control.

tips: Eliminate: B describes central, non-discretionary control, and C describes the clearances of mandatory access control.
Final two: D beats A because owner choice makes discretionary control flexible, and the same choice lets owners overshare; strict it is not.
Exam cue: discretionary access control means the owner decides: flexible and easy, but only as careful as each owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'DAC is the most flexible model, not the strictest' (notes 3.2.5 Discretionary Access Control (DAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: On a research lab's Linux server, an attacker controlling the web server process cannot read payroll files that ordinary file permissions would allow. Which explanation should the system administrator give as MOST accurate?

options.A: The payroll team removed the web server from each file's sharing list
options.B: The web server process lacks the Payroll role's permissions
options.C: The server's label policy confines the process despite file permissions
options.D: The attacker does not know the payroll staff's passwords

questions.key_concept: Mandatory access control applies central labels to processes and files, and it holds even where ordinary permissions allow access.
questions.pre_read: Recall how the access control models differ in who decides.
questions.correct_explanation: Mandatory access control adds a central policy, set by administrators, that labels processes and files and is checked as well as ordinary permissions; neither owners nor programs can override it. So even a hijacked web server process stays confined to what the policy allows. A missing role is the runner-up, because roles also limit access, but role grants are ordinary permissions, which here would allow the read.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because owners often control sharing. But ordinary permissions here allow the read, so no owner's sharing choice is blocking it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: roles do limit what accounts can do. But role grants are ordinary permissions, which here would allow the read; something above them blocks it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because passwords guard accounts. But the attacker already runs as the web server process; passwords play no part in this check.

tips: Eliminate: A contradicts the ordinary permissions that allow the read, and D is about sign-in, not what a running process may open.
Final two: C beats B because only a central label policy can block what ordinary permissions, role grants included, would allow.
Exam cue: when access is refused even though owners and permissions allow it, look for mandatory access control set centrally.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'under MAC the system, not the owner, decides access through central labels' (notes 3.2.6 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A community theater's role-based access control system gives every volunteer one Volunteer role, so ushers can open the donor database that only fundraising volunteers use. Which change should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Remove donor rights from the role and grant them to fundraisers directly
options.B: Split the Volunteer role into separate roles for each duty
options.C: Keep the Volunteer role and tell ushers not to open donor data
options.D: Let fundraising volunteers choose who may open the donor database

questions.key_concept: In role-based access control, a role that is too broad is fixed by splitting it into roles that match the work.
questions.pre_read: Recall how role-based access control maps permissions to jobs.
questions.correct_explanation: One role for every volunteer gives ushers rights only fundraisers need. In role-based access control the fix is better roles: an Usher role and a Fundraising role, each holding just what that work needs, so new volunteers get the right access by assignment. Moving donor rights to individual grants is the runner-up, since ushers lose access, but direct grants bypass roles and become hard to track and review.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: ushers would lose donor access. But direct grants sit outside the role model, so they are easy to miss in reviews and when volunteers leave.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is quick. But a request not to look is not a control; ushers could still open donor records.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fundraisers know their data. But that is discretionary control; in role-based control the organization sets roles and assigns people.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a request instead of a control, and D switches to owner-chosen, discretionary sharing.
Final two: B beats A because fixing the roles keeps access manageable; direct grants slip outside role-based reviews.
Exam cue: in role-based access control, when a role is too broad, split the role; do not patch it with one-off grants.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'RBAC attaches permissions to roles that match job functions' (notes 3.2.7 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A science park's attribute-based access control policy opens lab systems to users whose site matches the lab's; contractors' sites now arrive blank. Which rule for a blank site should the access analyst set as BEST?

options.A: Allow the request, but log it for the lab manager's later review
options.B: Treat a blank site as matching every lab on the park
options.C: Let contractors type their own site into their profile
options.D: Deny the request until the trusted source supplies the site

questions.key_concept: When an attribute a policy depends on is missing, the decision should fail safe and the source should be fixed.
questions.pre_read: Recall what attribute-based decisions depend on.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute-based decisions are only as good as their attributes, so a missing value should fail safe: deny until the authoritative source, here the system that supplies contractor records, provides the site. Allowing and logging is the runner-up, because it keeps contractors working and leaves a trail, but it grants access the policy cannot justify and only finds misuse after it happens.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: logging leaves a trail for review. But it grants access the policy cannot justify and finds any misuse only afterward.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it avoids blocking contractors. But it opens every lab to anyone whose data is missing, the widest possible failure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because contractors know their own site. But a user-editable attribute lets anyone grant themselves access to any lab.

tips: Eliminate: B turns missing data into access to every lab, and C lets users set the attribute that decides their own access.
Final two: D beats A because a policy should fail safe when an attribute is missing; logging detects misuse instead of preventing it.
Exam cue: in attribute-based access control, a missing or untrusted attribute means deny, then fix the source.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-162 Section 3.2.3.1 (Confidence in Access Control Decisions: accurate and timely attributes from authoritative sources); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(13) (Access Enforcement | Attribute-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ABAC trusts its attributes, so missing or stale attributes must not grant access' (notes 3.2.8 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A newspaper's new rule blocks weekend file-server sign-ins for all but administrator accounts, and the Sunday backup now fails. The IT manager owns the rule; what should the system administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the IT manager to exempt the backup account from the rule
options.B: Ask the IT manager to make the backup account an administrator
options.C: Run the backup on Fridays under a staff member's account
options.D: Switch the rule off each Sunday while the backup job runs

questions.key_concept: A rule applies to every account it covers, service accounts included, so a side effect needs an owner-approved exception, not extra rights.
questions.pre_read: Recall who a rule-based control applies to.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule-based controls apply to every account they cover, service accounts included, so the backup was caught too. The fix is an exception for the backup's own account, approved by the rule's owner, which keeps the weekend block for everyone else. Making the backup account an administrator is the runner-up, because the owner would approve it and administrators pass the rule, but it hands a backup job far more power than it needs.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it goes to the rule's owner, and administrators pass the rule. But administrator rights give a backup job more power than it needs; an exception adds no rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because weekday sign-ins still work. But a service job should not run under a person's account, which blurs who acted and ties the backup to one staff member's password.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it keeps both working. But a rule switched off every Sunday protects nothing in the hours it was written for, and the administrator does not own it.

tips: Eliminate: C runs a service job under a person's account, and D switches the rule off in the hours it exists to protect.
Final two: A beats B because both go to the rule's owner, but A lets the backup through with the rights it already has; B gives a backup job administrator power it does not need.
Exam cue: rules hit every account, service accounts included; fix a side effect with a narrow exception the rule's owner approves, not extra rights or a dropped rule.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'rule-based control applies the same rules to every subject, so exceptions need the rule owner's approval' (notes 3.2.9 Rule-Based Access Control). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: A ferry operator's AI agent rebooks passengers on its own when sailings are canceled, and only the vendor can halt it, through a support ticket. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Have the vendor commit to halting the agent within one hour
options.B: Cap the number of rebookings the agent can make each hour
options.C: Let on-call staff suspend the agent without vendor help
options.D: Retest the agent's model each time the vendor updates it

questions.key_concept: An agent that acts for the organization runs under an identity the organization itself can suspend, not one only the vendor controls.
questions.pre_read: Recall which safeguards an AI agent that acts on its own needs.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent acting on its own can repeat a fault hundreds of times, and like any account acting for the organization, its identity must be one the organization can suspend itself. Letting on-call staff suspend the agent's account themselves, without vendor help, stops it within seconds. Capping rebookings each hour is the runner-up, because it slows the damage, but wrong rebookings keep coming until the vendor answers the ticket.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a promised response time sounds firm. But a faulty agent can rebook many passengers in an hour, and halting it still depends on the vendor.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a cap slows the damage. But wrong rebookings keep coming each hour until the vendor answers, and staff still cannot stop the agent themselves.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because updates can bring new faults. But testing lowers the chance of a fault; it gives staff no way to halt one that gets through.

tips: Eliminate: A still leaves halting the agent to the vendor, and D tests for faults but gives no way to stop one that slips through.
Final two: C beats B because suspending the agent ends the harm; a cap only slows it until the vendor acts.
Exam cue: any identity that acts for the organization, human or AI, must be one the organization can suspend itself; a vendor's promise or a rate cap does not replace that.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 2.4 (mechanisms are in place and responsibilities assigned to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI systems that perform inconsistently with intended use); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'automation keeps its own identity and a stop switch the organization controls' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded to name the vendor it removes from the loop; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A six-person illustration studio has no IT staff, and each illustrator decides, project by project, which outside reviewers may open their low-sensitivity sketch folders. Which model should a security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Mandatory access control, with a classification on each folder
options.B: Role-based access control, with a role for each reviewer group
options.C: Attribute-based access control on each reviewer's attributes
options.D: Discretionary access control, with an access list on each folder

questions.key_concept: Fit the model to who decides and who can run it: owner-by-owner choices on low-sensitivity data, with no central team, suit discretionary control.
questions.pre_read: Recall who decides access under each model and what each model needs to run.
questions.correct_explanation: Discretionary access control lets each owner decide who opens their own resource, usually through an access list the owner edits, which matches illustrators choosing reviewers project by project. The sketches are low-sensitivity, and the studio has no IT staff to maintain roles or an attribute policy. Role-based control is the runner-up, because it is orderly, but reviewers change every project, so someone would have to edit roles constantly, and nobody holds that job.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is strict. But labels and clearances need a central authority and suit highly sensitive data; neither fits low-sensitivity sketches.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: roles are orderly. But reviewers change each project, and with no IT staff nobody would keep the roles current.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because attributes are flexible. But a policy engine and trusted attribute sources need running, which a six-person studio cannot do.

tips: Eliminate: A needs labels and a central authority for low-sensitivity sketches, and C needs a policy engine and attribute sources nobody can run.
Final two: D beats B because illustrators already decide reviewer by reviewer; roles for ever-changing reviewers need an administrator the studio does not have.
Exam cue: match the model to who decides and who can run it; owner-by-owner choices on low-risk data point to discretionary control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'fit the model to who decides and who can run it; owners choosing on low-risk data suit discretionary control' (notes 3.2.10 Choosing an Access Control Model). Re-angled in review away from the notes 3.2.8 worked example. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: During an identity provider outage, a satellite TV provider's on-call engineer opened the break-glass account as the runbook allows. Single sign-on is now back, but cleanup remains; what should the engineer do FIRST?

options.A: Keep the break-glass account signed in until the cleanup is done
options.B: Share the break-glass password with the day shift for the cleanup
options.C: Switch from the break-glass account to their own for cleanup
options.D: Change the break-glass password to one the team can recall

questions.key_concept: Break-glass access ends when normal access returns; remaining work is done under named accounts.
questions.pre_read: Recall when a break-glass account should and should not be used.
questions.correct_explanation: A break-glass account exists only for when normal access fails. Once single sign-on is back, the engineer should leave it and finish under their own named account, so the remaining work is traced to them and the powerful account is used as little as possible; it can then be resealed. Staying signed in to it is the runner-up, because the work continues smoothly, but the emergency that justified it is over.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it avoids switching mid-task. But the emergency is over, and every further action under the break-glass account adds risk and blurs who acted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the day shift needs to help. But sharing the password spreads an emergency credential and hides who did what.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a memorable password seems handy. But break-glass credentials are meant to stay sealed and strong, not easy to recall.

tips: Eliminate: B spreads an emergency credential to more people, and D weakens a credential that is meant to stay sealed.
Final two: C beats A because break-glass use ends when normal access returns; cleanup belongs under named accounts.
Exam cue: break-glass is for when normal access fails; once it works again, switch back and reseal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(2) (Account Management | Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'break-glass access is for when normal access fails, and its use stays limited' (notes 3.2.12 Just-in-Time and Break-Glass Access). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bank's statement archive refuses more than 500 downloads a day for every account, from tellers to executives, under limits an administrator sets. Which model should the access analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Rule-based access control, as a set condition limits everyone
options.B: Role-based access control, as tellers and executives hold roles
options.C: Mandatory access control, as users cannot change the limit
options.D: Discretionary access control, as an administrator chose the limit

questions.key_concept: One administrator-set condition applied alike to every account is rule-based access control.
questions.pre_read: Recall how to name an access control model from who or what decides.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule-based access control applies the same administrator-set conditions to every subject, whatever their job or label; a daily download cap for all accounts is a classic example. Mandatory access control is the runner-up, because users cannot change it either, but it compares clearances with classification labels, and no labels or clearances are involved here, just one rule for everyone.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because tellers and executives sound like roles. But the cap is the same whatever role a person holds.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: users cannot change the cap, as under mandatory control. But that model matches clearances to labels; this is a single rule applied alike to all.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because someone chose the limit. But discretionary control means each resource owner decides; here one administrator rule covers everyone.

tips: Eliminate: B names roles that make no difference to the cap, and D mistakes an administrator's rule for an owner's choice.
Final two: A beats C because no clearances or labels are compared; one fixed condition applies to every account.
Exam cue: the same condition for everyone, set by an administrator, such as a time window or a cap, points to rule-based access control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'find the decider: one fixed rule for everyone is rule-based' (notes 3.2.13 Access Model Scenarios: Worked Examples). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An energy firm's AI pilot was closed by its owner, and procedure has the access analyst retire its agent account; a data scientist wants it kept for a restart. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Disable the agent's account and revoke its access keys
options.B: Ask the pilot's owner whether a restart is still likely
options.C: Keep the account and rotate its keys for a restart
options.D: Store the agent's keys in the vault, keeping them for later use

questions.key_concept: When a project closes, its AI agent's identity is retired: the account is disabled and its keys revoked.
questions.pre_read: Recall what happens to a non-human identity at the end of its life cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: A closed project's agent identity is retired, so nothing left behind can be misused: the account is disabled and its keys revoked. The procedure gives this task to the access analyst once the owner closes the pilot. Asking the owner about a restart is the runner-up, because owners decide about their agents, but this owner has already closed the pilot; a restart would go through a new, approved request.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: asking the owner fits when nobody knows if an account is still needed. But this owner closed the pilot; a restart gets a new request.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rotating keys sounds secure. But the unused account stays live with its rights, waiting for a restart nobody has approved.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a vault protects secrets. But the keys still work, leaving the idle agent's access open.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps an unused account live with fresh keys, and D vaults keys that still work instead of revoking them.
Final two: A beats B because the owner has already closed the pilot and the procedure assigns retirement to the analyst; a restart is a new request.
Exam cue: when a project ends, its non-human identities end too; disable the account and revoke its secrets, and let any restart come through a new approved request.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.7 (processes and procedures are in place for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'retire a non-human identity when its project ends; any restart comes through a new approved request' (notes 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without a comma clause; distractor D given one; same key and teaching point.

questions.question: A housing association's planning manager owns a new AI agent that needs read access to tenancy records, which the housing director owns. Who should MOST appropriately approve the access request?

options.A: The housing director, as the owner of the tenancy records
options.B: The planning manager, who owns the agent and its tasks
options.C: The help desk analyst who will grant the tenancy records access
options.D: The agent's vendor, which knows what data the agent reads

questions.key_concept: Access to data is approved by the data's owner, even when the requester is an AI agent owned by someone else.
questions.pre_read: Recall the roles in an access request: requester, approver and fulfiller.
questions.correct_explanation: The owner of the data approves access to it, whoever or whatever asks. The tenancy records belong to the housing director, so the director approves the agent's read access. The planning manager is the runner-up, because they own the agent and know its job, but owning the requester gives no authority over someone else's data; the manager requests, and the director decides.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the planning manager owns the agent and knows its tasks. But owning the requester gives no authority over another owner's data; the manager requests, the director approves.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the help desk knows the systems. But the help desk fulfills approved requests; approving access it then grants would remove the check.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the agent. But a vendor has no say over the association's data; the data's owner decides.

tips: Eliminate: C has the person who fulfills the request also approve it, and D hands an access decision to an outside vendor.
Final two: A beats B because the data's owner approves access to it; the agent's owner only requests it.
Exam cue: for any access request, from a person or an AI agent, find who owns the resource being reached; that owner approves.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the resource owner approves an access request, even when an AI agent is the requester' (notes 3.1.14 Access Requests and Approvals). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A beekeeping supplier's contractor, working under a sponsored guest account, is hired as staff, and human resources (HR) sends a start record for Monday. Which setup should the access analyst arrange as BEST?

options.A: Keep the guest account and add the start record's role to it
options.B: Keep both accounts active while the new hire settles in
options.C: Open a staff account from the start record, closing the guest one
options.D: Open a staff account, copying the guest account's current rights

questions.key_concept: A contractor hired as staff gets a staff account from the HR start record, and the guest account is closed.
questions.pre_read: Recall what starts provisioning, and what a change of employment type means for access.
questions.correct_explanation: A move from contractor to staff is a leaver plus a joiner. The staff account is created from the HR start record, the trusted trigger, with the approved role, and the guest account is closed so the contractor-era access ends. Keeping the guest account and adding the new role is the runner-up, because it keeps continuity, but the old project rights and the sponsor-based life cycle stay attached.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it adds the approved role. But the guest account keeps its contractor-era rights and sponsor-based life cycle, and is not tied to the HR record.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it avoids disruption. But one person with two live identities blurs who acted, and the guest account's old rights stay open.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because nothing the person uses breaks. But it copies rights the contractor's project needed, not what the staff role approves.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves one person with two live identities, and D carries contractor-era rights onto the new staff account.
Final two: C beats A because staff access starts from the start record on a staff account; a converted guest account keeps its old rights and life cycle.
Exam cue: a change of employment type is a leaver plus a joiner; end the old identity's access and provision the new one from the trusted record.
